div.head: GREAT STRIKE ENDED.
div.p: THE GREAT STRIKE ENDED.
MEN SECURE RECOGNITION.

div.head: Trains Running and Troops Withdrawn.
div.p: Trains Running and Troops Withdrawn.
SPECIAL COMMI

Suddenly begun, the national .railway strike as happily and as suitlenly ended: The general stoppage lasted little more than two days. News of the settle- ment came on Saturday night as a great relief to all cleaves. From the King to his plorest subjects there was a feeling of personal and national joy. This gladness the striktre themselvee throughout the country shared, and most of them showed their willingness to return to work quickly. There were notable exceptions, includiog Manchester, Hull and Newcastle, u here the men were not at first satisfied with the terms. Eventually points of difference were ' smoothed over. and the railway seri ices quickly resumed, all grades of men stepping loyally it.to their poets.

div.head: CAMP OF THE 10TH LANCERS AT ORFORD.
div.p: THE CAMP OF THE 10TH LANCERS AT ORFORD.
THE CHANCELLORS GREAT EFFORTS.

It was on the Chancellor of the Exchequer, acting for the Premier, that the great task of peacemaking fell, sod within an hour of Saturday midnigl,t, after a fagging day of over fifteen hcurs, his tact and dogged- ness were crowned with success. Railway directors and trade union leaders—for the fir-'t time in Liatcry —met face to face in cocference, and the peace treaty

vas signed. The settlement, the men's representatives state in a manifesto, was not arrived at until a statement had been made by the Board of Trade that the lock-out in Liverpool would be withdrawn immediately the railway dispute was settled.

div.head: HOW RECOGNITION WAS SECURED.
div.p: HOW RECOGNITION WAS SECURED.

They claim alvo that they won what they fought for—' recognition of the right of collective bargain- ing." Their message to over 1,800 branches on Saturday midnight was in the following terms : Joint Committee have se'tled strike. Victory for trade unionism. All men must return to work immediately. It is raid that the men's claim for trade union recognition was the one barrier to peace on Friday night, and that this point was conceded only on Saturday afternoon. Four Labour M.P.'s, including the chairman of the party, did splendid work in helping the Chancellor or bring about a harpy endirg of the stril c.

div.head: TERMS OF AGREEMENT
div.p: TERMS OF AGREEMENT

We set out below the salient paints in the tere.s of settlement. Strike to end at once. Strikers to be reinstated. Conciliation Boards to meet quickly and settle questions now in dispute. Decisions to be lett% spective. Steps to Fe taken to Fettle grievances of men , outside Conciliatha Boards. Special Commission of Inquiry—five members —to start this week an investiga.ron of the working of the 1907 Arbitration and Conciliation Scheme. Assurances given by both parties t ) accept findings of this Commission. Government promise legislation reit SeFsion to allow an increase of charges (within the legal maxima) to meet extra cost of improved conditions of labour. . . . .

The happy ending of industi ial warfare, though it came speedily, came not a moment too soon. Grave events were haprening in many sttike centres ; riots were breaking out, and, unhappily, there was more bloodshed. In Llanelly the troops fired on the crowd cf strikers sod killed two: later an explosion cccurred through the mob fit irg waggons laden with petrol and powder, and four more livt s mere lost.

div.head: FEDERATION OF LABOUR. INTERNATIONAL TRADES UNIONISM. _ OVER 11,000,000 MEMBERS._
div.p: FEDERATION OF LABOUR. INTERNATIONAL TRADES UNIONISM. _ OVER 11,000,000 MEMBERS._

According ton writer in the" Railway Review "the international trades union movement represented, in 1909, a total membership of 6,008,212, as compared with 5,944,262 in 1903. These figures represent member- ship in 20 different Cf untries, the score of federations being all affiliated to the International Secretariat in Between 1001 end 1:03 trade unionism made a great advance, for, in the former year, the number of affiliated federations was only 12, their total member- ship amounting to 213,281. Trade unionists are most numerous In Germany, the figure being 1,832,667 in 1909. The United States came second with a membership of 1,710,433 and Great Britain a6d Ireland third with 733,091. According to the latest data available to the writer, the total mem- bership of trade unions was 1 .085,056 in 1909.

div.head: COMMISSION OF
div.p: THE COMMISSION OF
INQUIRY.

The following are the proposals of the Government with regard to the special commission of inquiry into the working of the conciliation scheme of 11107:— The Commission t be appointed with the following reference To investigate the working of the railway con- ciliatien and arbitration scheme signed on behalf of the principal railway companies and of three trade unions of railway employees at the Board of Trade on November 6, 1607, and to report what changes (if any) are desirable with a view to the prompt

and satisfactory settlement of differences. The Commission to consist of five members, rr presenting employers and workmen in equal numbers, with an impartial chairman. Assurances have been given by both parties that they will accept the findings of the Commission. The Government have given an assurance to the railway companies that they will propcse to Parliament next session legislation providing that an increase in the Cost of labour due to the improvement of conditions for the staff would be valid justification for a reason- able general increase of charges within the legal maxima, if challenged tiLder the Act of 1,91.

div.p: THE COMMISSIONERS AT WORK.

The announce- ment has been received with satisfaction by both masters and men, and with daily sittings it is hoped that the Commissioners will cimplete their task in less than a mouth.

div.head: TRIBUTES TO THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CHANCELLOR.
div.p: TRIBUTES TO THE GOVERNMENT AND THE CHANCELLOR.
Striking Comments on the Settlement.

In the comments of the PreSB on the settlement of the railway ettike the outstanding feature—as will be seen from the extracts given below—is the tribute of Liberal and Tory writers alike to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, " who snatched peace out of the jaws of war." There are one or two in- iguificant excep- tions, where, the old partisan spirit still dominant, the recognition is made grudgingly or denied. " TIIE TIMES " (C.). Congratulations are due t' the Government on the success of their eff jets to cope with an unprece- dented emergency:.

" DAILY " (C.) By general corsent, acknosledgment is chiefly due to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, who has once more shown that his rare gift of conciliating scarring foes is equal to his power, at other times and on other occasions, of exciting the fiercest strife. ,

WES! MIST,I'ER GAZETTE (L.) The Government have done their utmost for con- ciliation, and the public cannot be too grateful for the heroic perseverance, ultimately crowned with success, of Mr. Lloyd George and those who laboured with him in the conference room. 'D*it.r If sir. " (C.). The Government I.as handled the difficulty with energy and firmness. No Government could have done better in the circumstances, and its persistent efforts will be warmly appreciated by the whole nation. Tot MORNING Pon " (C.). In this naional crisis the Ministers of the Crown have intervened, and credit must justly be given to the undoubted power of conciliatory expression that Mr. Lloyd Georg? possesses. YoRKSIIIRE Po,l' (C). The efforts of Mr. Lloyd-George and Mr. Sydney Buxton and their assistants to bring about this result have been hearty and strenuous. For this they are entitled to praise. " MscsirEsTEfl GUARDIA,T (L.) We cannot record this first step to peace with- out some tribute to the capacity of Mr. Lloyd Georee, who has done something bet'er than snatching victory out of defeat. He has snatched peace out of the very jaws of war, and we trust that the political opponents who reserve the very hardest names in their vocabulary for him will at least henceforward recognise the absurdity of denouncing him as a firebrand and a mischief-

maker. MORNING LEADER " (L). In circumstances of extraordinary difficulty, the Government, by the admksion of fle as well at. friend, has won a very notable victory. YORKSHIRE CHISKI:I ER " (L). The prompt, tactful, unsleeping—and successful —efforts of the Govemment to heal this alarming breach compares favourably with the action of aoy previous Administration in a similar situation. - .. _ .

l'A-11. hi %U. GAZE ITE "(C). There is no victory we know, but the strike leaders hove at least fo ced the Government to coerce the railway managers into conference with them, and they have dictated an agreement that expressly Ai, Ids the strikers horn the consequences of their own and their leaders' criminality.

" G LOBE " There is a disposition in some quarters to regard the Chancellor of the Exchequer as the saviour of society. All that Mr. George has dorm is t 3 save the relics of his own agreement of 19)7. EVENINO STANDARD " (C.) There can be no two opinions as to the great service rendered to the nation at the present crisis by the Chancellor rf the Exchequer. " WESTERN MAIL " (C.) It is a pleasure to recognise the importance of the services Mr. Lloyd George has rendered in this historic effort of peacemaking. . . . His sympathy and insight have once more proved invaluable in the delicate process of cocciliatioa. £440,000 IN TRAFFIC DECREASES. startling Figures of Loss in Railway Receipts. The total is thus over £410,000.
The comparatively limited effect of the stiike in the case of the Southern mmpanies is shown by he returns from the South-Eastern and Chatham and the London and South-Western.
THE 18TH HUSSARS IN CAM' AT ORFO:ID.

men's unions passed a resolution declar ir that unrest then prevalentin the railway world had beencreated largely by the vexatious attitude ofmany of the companies towards the working of the scheme of conciliation and arbitration agreed to in 1907. Unless the spirit as well as the letter of the agreement was observed more fully in the future, the resolution declared, the society would have seriously to consider the advisability of repudiating the scheme. Mr. McClean also said the public must clearly understand that there would have been no national strike if the railway companies had consented to meet the men's executives, not to settle the posi- tion in the whole country but to open negotiations with a view to finding a basis of settlement for the centres which were then in dispute. Dealing with the response to the telegram declaring war, Mr. McClean said all the important railway centres were absolutely held up and the official statement that two-thirds of the men were at work was untrue. If the companies could afford to purchase the " loyalty" of employees during disputes by giving them extra pay, they could afford to do it in normal times. As showing the spirit of disinterested sympathy which had animated many strikers, Mr. McClean stated that men who were receiving per day for driving London expresses had struck in order to assist workers in other grades to obtain redress of their grievances. Loud cheers greeted an announcement that the national executives had agreed to pay strike benefits to non-unionists. . . .
Other speakers included Mr. C. Wozencroft (A.S.R.S.) Mr. J. Taylor (A.L.E. & F.U.) and Mr. W. Muskett (chairman of the Strike Committee.)

Mr. Taylor quoted with approval the leading article in that day's" Examiner" which, he said, expressed the truth of the situation. If the arguments therein enunciated were thoroughly understood by the general public their sympathies would be entirely on the side of the railway men. (Cheers). The meeting broke up with a strong determination on the part of every man to continue the struggle to the bitter end, but there was alsd an optimistic spirit that victory would he achieved before many hours had elapsed. Happily that feeling proved to be well-founded, and on Sunday morning the trade union branches were notified by the leaders that a triumph for trade unionism had been won, and the men were advised to return to work forthwith. At a crowded meeting of railway servants held in the Co-operative Hall on Sunday evening a resolution was unanimously passed, agreeing to the terms of settlement, and the men pledged themselves loyally to obey their leaders and return to work at once.
On Monday morning all the men were back at work. Bank Quay station presented a

wonderful transformation, the unwonted I quietness of Friday and Saturday having given place to bustling activity. An! _enormous_volume ofiraffic_was_expeditionalvi dealt with. All the trains were running well to time, and the task of clearing the works sidings, where great quantities of goods had accumulated, was proceeding apace. The low level and Arpley stations, which had been entirely closed during the strike, were re-opened and travelling was accomplished under normal conditions as far as Broadheath. At the Central Station the disinclination of Manchester strikers to accept the settle- ment made it impossible to run the hourly express service on Monday, and there were no excursion bookings or night trains. On Tuesday, however,the Manchester employees yielded to counsels of peace and, to the relief of the many Warrington people making daily use of the line, the trains were soon running as usual, and excursion bookings were resumed.

The Central and L. & N.-W. goods yards reo-pened as usual on Monday but, owing to the inactivity of the preceding week, there were heavy arrears of work to clear off and all bands were very busily occupied. SPECIAL CONSTABLES ENROLLED.

In or.ler to be prepared for emergencies forty specisl constables were sworn in at Warrington on Saturday. An appeal by Mr. Martin Nicholls, the Chief Constables, for volunteers, met with a remark- ably prompt response, the applicants belonging to all grades of society. Practically all the members cf the Warrington Academy were enrolled. The cath was taken before the Mayor and other magistrates, to whom an application was made for the special augmentation of the borough police force by Mr. A. T. Hallaway. the deputy town clerk. In one or two instances the " specials" have performed light duties principally in connection with the removal of prisoner-, sentenced at the Borough Court, to gail. Owing to the unexpected ending of the strike and the peaceful lines on which the dispute was conducted in Warrington, their services were not required to preserve order. Me "specials" will doubtless preserve their certificates, issued after enrolment, as mementoes cl the patriotic part they were willing to play in a serious naticnal crisis.

div.head: PRISONERS AND "SOCIETY" NOVELS.
div.p: PRISONERS AND "SOCIETY" NOVELS.

- The thirty-third report of the General Prisons Board of Ireland, just limed, calla attention to the morbid and immortal tone of a great proportion of modern English " society "novels as inimitable for officers' or prisoners' libraries, and chaplains and goversore hams been advised to replace them by a selection of instructive books on travel, history, biography, SeilMell or si•ndard English novels of healthy tone. An illustrated weekly publication containing news of many current events iv, it is stated, supplied to each prison for circulation among well-conducted prisoners of long sentences some time before their relate. It Ms been urged with some force, the report continues, that keeping prisoners of Icog sentences without any knowledge of current events leads to mental apathy and depression, and places men at a d isad ran tsge on their I elesse.

div.head: g THE MILITARY CAMP AT ORFORD.
div.p: g THE MILITARY CAMP AT ORFORD.

The public dearly likes to see something of the active life of Tommy Atkins, especially if he happens to be in a cavalry regiment, and thousands of Warrington people took the opportunity of. visiting the camp at Orford during the strike period. Two squadrons of the 16th Lancers were drafted to Warrington as a convenient centre for the North-Western area, and last week-end they pitched their tents in a field near Orford Barracks. Here they were able to pass a quiet and uneventful time, relieved only by the inquisitiveness of the public who flocked to the camp to enjoy a sight which was quite a novelty for this district. The horses were tethered in long lines and there was great excitement when occasionally one broke loose and had to be pursued round the field. With the settle- ment of the strike the necessity for retaining many troops in these parts soon vanished and on Thursday the camp was struck and the Lancers took their departure. During the strike over 80 men of the 18th Hussars and the 2nd Battalion Lincoln Regiment (less one company) the 2nd Battalion Welsh Fusiliers, and companies of the King's Own Rifles have passed through Orford Barracks, and have been dispatched to Manchester, Stockport. Burnley and other strike areas.

div.head: ATTACK ON A SIGNAL BOX
div.p: ATTACK ON A SIGNAL BOX

There were exciting soenes at Earlest ,wn junction at one o'clock on Saturday morning, before the news of the strike settlement reached that district. A mob about 500 strong made a desperate attack on two signal boxes and br•fore the Fo'ice and military could arrive from Warringtoo, ons of the boxes was practically wrecked. News of the m nacing situobon first reached Warrington ab ,ut midnight when the Chief Constable (Mr. ALirtin Nicholls) received a message that a body of rioters had take') ioasersion of Earlestown st Ilion and were atoning the signal br.xes. An attack on the Winwick Junction box,with a view to h riding up night expresso ',was a'so threatened. The Chief Constable with a dozen men immediately left hank Quay in a special train. At Winwick Junction they found Sergr. Cooper and P.C. Wooff, of the Lancashire County C, nstatmlary, who reported that a small crowd had gather-id there, but had left a short time previ usly, alter threatening to return and rject theeignaiman. Three men having bsen left at Winwick the train went cautiously on its journey. Near the Vulcan Works atones were thrown at the train, but no one was iujured. The Warringtoo Junction box, at the south end of Earlestown Station was found to be in darkness The sigoalm in hod a graphic story t tell of the doings of the mob. His cabin had suffered extensive damage and the man himself had been threatened with violence. l:very window in the box was shattered. On visiting the Manchester Junction box, the police found that the , signalman had been compelled to desert his post The box was wrecked sod not a whole pane of glass was left. Some of the instruments ha,l also been interfered with, whilst railings in the vicinity had been torn up. , A large crowd had githered outsi le the station, and ' jeered the police who, holte,er. did not come into actual conflict with them. At the rcro.st of the Chief ConstaVe a cAtingent of Welsh Fuciliers from
OmmilMl

Orford Barracks arrived ox the scene to guard the atation and crder was well maintained. At Winwick. 1 junction, a small body of police had to charge a crowd which threatened to wreck the signal box, and \ -an- arrest-was-made-by P.C. Armstrong, of Warring— ton. The intentions of the rioters were defeated and by the time the Fusiliers arrived. quietness hod been restored. The Fusiliers patrolled the line on Sunday hut no further violence or disorder occurred. POLICE COURT SEQUEL.

A sequel to the riots at Earleetown Station w. heart at the Warrington Docersioasi Police Court on 5I grid.% before Mr. F. A. Frost, when a young man named Daniel Ashton, 'calling in Houghtan.atreat, ESfleitoPl3, was charged with mating and disturbing the peace. Inspector Canard stated that shout eleven o'clock or, Saturday nights number of railwaymeo wits were on strike at Earlestown smashed several windows in ths signal boa. The Warrington poles were summoned, and proceeded to Earlestown by special train. On their way they had to pass Winwick Junction signal-boo, and three men were stationed there in case of emergency, along with Police-constable Woof!, of Eeriest... While in the signal-box the officers hear,' a noisy m ib, and were successful in driving them away. The prisoner was one of the leaders of the crowd, and took a prominent part in endeavouring to persuade them ta assault the police and wreck the c thin. P.C. Wooff corroborated this s'atement. He added that about 1.30 on Sunday morning between 150 and 230 strikers walked along the line towards the cabin. He and the other officers charged the mob, which Bed. At the top of the road the priscner returned and endeavoured to persuade the strikers to return, telling his comrades that there were only three officers on duty. He was apprehended by P.C. Anustrcog of the Warring- ton force. Prisoner cross-examined the constable as to whether he heard him speak during the disturbance. Witness replied that he heard the prisoner shouting several times and hews. positive that he was the man. inspector Canard added that the clerk of the magis- trates, Mr. F. G. faylor, was a passenger by the train which was stoned, and he could testify to the fact that bricks and other missiles were thrown at the train. . . _ _ .
Prlroner was remanded to the Newton Petty Sermons to be held on the 31st inst.

div.head: ORDER OUT OF CHAOS. WARRINGTON RAILWAYMEN RETURN TO WORK. Settlement Accepted.
div.p: ORDER OUT OF CHAOS. WARRINGTON RAILWAYMEN RETURN TO WORK. Settlement Accepted.

Just when the outlook in the railway world seemed most hopeless, the glad news reached Warrington that a settlement of the strike had been arrived at. It was after midnight when special editions of the evening papers circulated the momentous announce- ment in all parts of the town, and the general feeling was one of intense relief that the disastrous struggle was at an end. , Throughout Saturday the conditions at the local stations had been depressing in the extreme. There was no attempt to work to the time-table and although on the L. & N.-W. Railway trains were fairly frequent it was only when they actually pulled up at the platform that their destination could be ascertained and tickets issued to those who wished to undertake the journey. The company would only book passengers for long distances at their own risk, and many who had arranged to spend holidays in remote parts concluded that it would he extremely hazardous to attempt to travel, and telegrams were dispatched cancelling arrangements. On the Cheshire Lines very few trains were got through before the afternoon and then it was found impossible to maintain anything approaching the usual service. What made the outlook in War- rington particularly gloomy was that owing to the difficulty in getting hold of raw material and dispatching finished goods, several of the largest works had.heen obliged to close down and thousands of workingmen were confronted with a period of enforced idleness. On Saturday evening railwaymen of all grades who had come out on strike held a large and enthusiastic meeting in the Co-operative Hall. Mr. W. Adams presided and an address explaining the steps which led to the declaration of the strike was delivered by Mr. W. McClean, secretary of the Liverpool No. 1 branch of
the AAR.S. He defined that the strike .afforded evidence of trade union solidarity such as had never before been witnessed in
-railway circles. The .remarkable and out-
standing feature of the strike—apart from the victory which was not far off—was the loyal co-operation of the unions involved. . .
Elitherto t-hey. had been content to work
separately, mid sometimes in opposition, but the present dispute had consolidated them

div.head: MR. W. P. RYLANDS AMD LESSONS
div.p: MR. W. P. RYLANDS AMD LESSONS
OF THE STRIKE.
Compulsory Arbitration Advocated.

Presiding at the annual meeting of the Working- men's Committee cf the Warrington District Nursing Aascciation, held at the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon, Mr. W. P. Rylands said they sere met under circumstances of grave anxiety and the outlook was somewhat dark, lie apprehended that as a broad and gPneral pAition the ultimate method of settling &Rareness between art employer and his men must be the Mt ike or lock-out. A man could not be compelled to work for a lower wage than he thought he ought to receive, nor under conditions which were distasteful to Itim, and if he was not prepred to accept the conditions of employment, recourse was had t 3 the strike. It was

A BASS \SOUS 511,11. a and he profoundly hoped that as time went on saner counsels would prevail and methods r f conciliation, discussion and the like would gradually and entirely supersede such brutal ways of settling differences. But still as a general principle, it must be accepted ' that the strike was for the present the ultimate court I of appeal in all disputes between masters and their men. He, however, was going to draw a very clear distinction between the class of industry in which that law must be allowed still to prevail and the class cf of industry in which he maintrined it should not he permitted to prevail. "If you take an isolated industry," Mr. Rylands continued—" and so as not to be invidious, let me take my own, and !et us suppose my men refuse to stork under the conrEtions laid down, and I was not prepared to modify them. Then let us suppose they went on strike. The injury which would result from that strike would be entirely con- fined to flirts) men and myself. It would be an isolated conflagration. The injury, so far as the community would ha concerned, would be localized to the asset field of the strike. I should have no right tocomplain, the community wood have no right to ccmplain, if I could not settle my differences with my men. Presumably that must be the last court of appeal and it would not affr.ct anybody else materially beyor,d my men and those whose money be invested in the enterprise in which they are employed. But if we look at certain types of industry we see that a diepute of that kind is not isolated. The effects are nut confined to the parties to the quarrel." There were certain great industries, said fill.. Rylands, upon which the com- munity as a whole were absolutely dependent fur their existence, and time who were engaged in those industries ought to be regrrded as trustees of a certain charge which was entrusted to their care.'lhe lATCREsTa ot lilt OMMUNITY MUST OVI:11-1111.1. EVECS "rum itS WES %TEO,. In the case of a great industry which was absolutely essential to the webbeing of the community, and when any dislocation struck hard at the people who had no concern whatever in the quarrel which might arise, then the community c'uld say that that strike should not be, and that there must be some com- pulsory method laid down by which that grave injury to the community could be avoided. (Hear. hear.) There were two great industries and a few lesser ones to which those conditions applied. The one above all others was the railway system. It was a most abominable thing that there was not some method of bringing to a close and preventing entirely any absolute cessation of the working of the rsilwar system. whatever might be the reason, and especially on account of a difference of opinion between the masters and ram. Ile knew nothing of the merits or demerits of the quarrel. That was not a matter with which he was concerned and with which the meeting was not concerned, but they as members of the com- munity could rightly claim that it was a function of the Government to prevent the whole of the community being put to grave inconvenience, enormous loss,great distress and possibly peril of Hs through a purely trade quarrel between two sets of men with whom they had no concern whatever, lie viewed the situation with grave distress. He could not help thinking that the result would he that
AU,FIT 10 Tim ovw UN IT

which would make the community say in future tit t those things should cot be. (Hear. hear.) In War- ingion they had no put in the dispute, and yet from Monday be had very little doubt there would be 10,000 working men without employment. Ten thou- sand working men would have no wages to draw for the next week and for so long as the .trike lasted. Carryingthe position of affairs to the logical conclu- sion it might be said that if such • strike was to be permitted at all, what was there to prevent it going on for a fortnight or three weeks. reducing the whole of Wart ington an I enemy

other town in the countty— to atarvation and possibly resulting in the death of a large number, of the weaker people? It was a lamentable thing, and they ought to consider the matter horn the wider point of view. It was public opinion that effected solutions of those difficulties. If public opinion was arowted and it held the view which be hail submitted, that the interests of the community must stand first, then public opinion would insist upon such regulations being laid down that differences betwer n railway ccm- psnies and their men—and differences between the shipowners and their men cught to be put in the same category - must be settled by some arbitration board, which would inspire the confidence of evert section Mayor i of athoer associated himself w . fAppla u sei)t. T,, the common sense, logical and humane view outlined by Mr. Rylanda with regard to the strike, lie could not imagine any man, whatever opinions he might hold, whether be sympathized with the strikers or disagreed with them, who, if be was at all sensible. could think of the matter as other than of supreme importance to the- community, or hold any other view than that v iced by Mr. Rylands. Al delegat from ore of the umris slid there were generally two points of view t m be taken into consideration, but be only hopel that the dispute would be speedily settled. Theme were 127,11110,15t0 paid 'annually in wages and £19,01100,000 paid in dividends. Surely it would be possible to afford something of the latter sum to the men who prcalucett.

div.head: CRICKET, BOWLING, AND
div.p: CRICKET, BOWLING, AND
ATHLETICS.
Cricket Notes.
The great strike made railway communication so uncertain on Saturday, that there was no alternative but to caocel the Warriagton club's matches wiih St. Helens.

The Warrington and District League tourney is rapidly nearing the closing stages, and Warrington Conservatives are certain to be the champions. On Saturday they triumphed over Latchford Wesleyan by a majority of 30, C Ho't shining in the battiog -department with a fine innings or 21. W C Brooks wielded the willow smartly for his 15. For the Wesleyans A Fletcher was the top scorer with 15.

Sankey Wire Mil, inflicted a heavy reverse on Wilderspool Brewery, who cut a rely sorry figure, she whole side being dismissed for 41. Johnson (12 not out) was the only player to reach double figures. The Wire Mills responded with the nice round tots' of 106, Bunter heading the scores with a splendid 32. Bradburn (23) and Hawthorn (21) were also useful conts ibutors.

Sankey bad no difficulty in trouncing Walker's Brewery. The villagers declared their innings at 05 f r ll wickets and sent their opponents to the rightabout for 51. The most successful batsmen on the victorious side were Whitfield (22), Forster (29), Plant 18), and Gregson 14). The only Brewery player to gain double figures was W. Wright with 19, but due credit must be given to Wells (8) for keeping his end up, thus enabling Wright to make a respectable score for Walkers. Fortrer (5 wickets for 19) and fifillingtoo k 5 wickets for 219 bowled well for Sankey.

There was a very exciting struggle between Latch- ford Baptists and Runcorn 31.F.C., resulting in a win for Runcorn by the narrow margin of five. J. Hunt distinguished himself with a b:illiant batting display for Latchford, making 42. For Runcorn Hißidge (33) aid W 49011 (21) were the top scorers.

Grappenhall entertained Helsby awl had to bow the knee, the visitors gaining a majority of 14. G. Jackson (2)) headed the individual efforts for the ninners and J. Hutchins knocked up 11 for ~4rappenhall.

Winwick Asylum were the winners of a very poor game with Garswood Hall on Saturday, the combuied effJrts of both teams producing only 96 runs. Winwick batted first and were dismissed for 53. J. Bieck took tao wickets for six rucs ; T. Rigby 3 for 21, and J Dean 3 for 28. Garawood went in to bat after the interval, but thanks to the smart fielding of the home team and the bowling of Dawson, who took 7 wickets for 16 rune, they were all out for 41.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT BOWLING ASSOCIATION. INDIVIDUAL MERIT COMPETITION. DEFEAT OF LAST YEAR'S CHAMPIoN.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT BOWLING ASSOCIATION. INDIVIDUAL MERIT COMPETITION. DEFEAT OF LAST YEAR'S CHAMPIoN.

Thtugh a few drops of rain fell during the early part of Saturday morning, the sun subsequently ,gained the mastery and the weather conditions associated with the third day's play under the War- rington and District Rules at the King and Queen made bowling pleasant enough The patronage NVIIS carat sati,fsctory and the bowling came up to the usual standard.

From a sporting and financiq point of view the afternoon was an unqualified success. The strangers .cvere lcud in their [raises of the King and Queen surroundings thanks to the slight showers which made the tastefully and arranged flower beds adjoin- ing the green look really splendid.

The officials have decided to extend the competition until September 2ad. To-day's rounds will leave only the prize winners which number sixteen. The lucky individuals will then have to toe the line on September 2ad wiled Brune excellent sport is sure to be witnessed. I have heard it expressed from many quarters of the King and Queen green that the way in which tho officials have posted the prize list has met with the competitors' warm praise. Readers will observe from another column that a Preliminary draw has been adopted, so as to bring the competition into line, and thus avoid any snore byes. I might mention that all those players who have not yet completed their second round are desired to put in an appearance between 1 3') and 2.15 p.m. No grace will be given. Also to facilitate matters, and more no now that the days are drawing shorter, players are expected to answer to their names. In this case half-anthour's race will be given. These concluding notes only apply to the third rounders.

Before I detail some of the individual games, I should like to express my admiration towards the young element of bowlers in Warrington who are coming to the front in leaps and bounds. This season I have never seen so many old players taken down by the young bloods. I have heard old players say that these young midgets are becoming too numerous. Of course for generations bowling has been termed an old man's game, but the young fellows have a say now—as they ought to have. To make my notes clear I will endeavour to give a few remarks on the rising young players, and their performances as space ncw permits.
The concluding games in the first round were epesddy diapied of. 'fbe ennui round was reeled off elually as well, the day closing with eight games in abeyance.
C. SU.W V. J. 1A \G!

Neddie Shaw ,commonly known) pt.inted undeniably to his chance against Langley of Hylands Bros. He gained the mastery and drew away with breaks of Jive, which simply outclassed Langley. Never pushed for pints, Shaw won handsomely by 21-7. I have seen Langley make better fights, but bowls is a game which requires a lot of summing up.
GEOROE MONKS V S. RILEY,

I thought this was a good thing far Monks, hot Riley surprised some of his tricst intimate friends. When the game was cried 18, Monks failed to take the advantage offered him and allowed Riley to get home by the odd chalk, 21-20. A very good game !
GE oIICE NOLER.ON V R. ALLEN.

Both of these competitors being representatives of Ryland.; Bros. the game proved more of a friendly bout. It was a one-sided game, Holbrook bringing the game to a close '2l-7 in his favour. I fully expect Holbrook to go well in the prize lists. I don't know a green that suits him better, f he has some wonder- ful achievements to his credit cu the King and Queen _green. Opponents look Out!

div.head: T. ELLISON V. J. ASHTON.
div.p: T. ELLISON V. J. ASHTON.

What a sterling game this was! I was wondering when the game was going to terminate, the card registering 31 ends to decide the winner. It looked as if Ashton would be the conqueror when he reached -20 and Tom Ellison IS, but Ellison, with grand judg- ment. unpinned Ashton for the third round by winning a strenuous game by the odd chalk 21-20.
JA,Ii JOULE V. JOE ELEAVE.

This game came in for much speculation. Jolley, ) was the 1909 champion, is fairly fancied in some quarters to win it again. Both competitors are club mates Bull's Head). .Joe Gleave got away in a spirited fashion, combined ivith good bowling 7-2. Then Jack Jolley found the running and made the .game eight all. The subsequent part of the game was of. ding-dong nature peeling constantly at 10, 11, 14, when Jolley made a determined finish by winning '2l -1.

Tbe efficials kindly consented to a request to meet these two players whit were well down in the programme. Bretherton having to play in the Works Handicap. and Williams going on pleasure bent Williams got badly away, Bretherton reaching 15 against Williams 1, but Herman could not sustain the interest in the game and Brethertnn iptalitied fir the third round by 1- 1 2. I was sorry to learn later on in the day that the Works Association had ercssed Bretherton's name off as absent, his time limit being

overdue. Of course, I don't wish to trespass on the doings of the oflials of the Works Association, hut I was given to understand that there was a compromise between the two bowling hcdies as regards the Works Handicap and the Individual Merit Competition.

kI.BELT GLEE V. fIEV TOUt TS .N. These two playens had their war-paint on. I don't think that during the whole competition, there have been two such desperate triers. It was a fair sporting game all through combined with g od howling knd it was anyb-dy's game, up to the twenty-sixth and. The scorer crying 18 all. With • single and a brace A. Glance (Manchester and district individual winner this year) won a hard game 21-8.
TOM QtATUNE V U EAT,LIFF E

These two young' bowlers have come to the front a lot lately, and Tom is amongst the fancied ones. 11 Ratcliffe was like the cat amongst tbe pigeons. He gave the King and Queen members a shock when the game recorded 15-7 against their club mate Quarrie. But Qutrrie apset all the'r calculations, when he added eleven to his score (18-15). Ratcliffe ,apturing three more chalks made play 18 all, but he had to give way at the criecal period of the game, hard beaten by 3 chalks, 21-18.

Itti T., KN., V. A. JOY LES. This was a remarkable round for the excellent form shown by young Jolley in defeating last year's chambion (G. Ball) WO surprising. I can enly say that it was a brilliant achievement. His bowling was perfect. While Ball was obviously in difficulties when the score recorded 15-s in favour of Jolley, and more so when Jolley was flaying steadily and accurately to a degree. Ball's chance of retaining the championship vanished to zero. Jolley 21, Ball 16.

The conflict of the works being over, the members of the Warrington Works fowling Ass-ciation are now concerned with defending their own honour in the annual handicap commenced last Saturday on the beautiful and spacious green attached to the Florae and Jrckey Inn. div.head: COUNCILLOR STEEL'S CHALLENGE CUP.
div.p: COUNCILLOR STEEL'S CHALLENGE CUP.

For fonr yeara the members of the Constitution Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows (Manchest.r Unity), have vied with each other as to who should hold the handsome silver challenge cop offered by Councillor T S Steel, On Saturday, when the competition was held on the green adjoining the Brook,ands Ho'el, Lovely-lane, the same keen struggle ensued. Thirty-two members competed. In the first mend the greatest surprise was occasioned by A E Burdett. one of the most useful members of the C iale Rubber Company, succumbing by three chalks to Peter Lester who is quite a novice. T. J. Ford, who was in the final the year before last, appeared in the semi-final, but was beaten by J NV Rigby who obtained five more points. The final played between the latter and W. A. Warburton proved to be very exciting. for as both players possess enviable records land were in rod form they did their level best. It ems a neck and neck race till near the finish, when with la series of couples Warburton got away and ran home victor by 4 points. Resides the cup the winner was the recipient of a gold medal again, thanks to the generosity of Councillor Steel. GREENWOOD.

The football season opens a week to-day, and at Wilderspool everything is ready for the visit of Leigh. The ground improvements have been carried out expeditiously and well, and the enclosure at the present time looks a picture of order and spaciousness. In addition to the new stand on the members' ads-- which is a substantial and commodious structure— the playing pitch has been widened, and a new, smart, fence erected all round. Considerably more banking has been done, and there is now accommodation for about 25,000 spectatora—a number somewhat larger than Warrington will be likely to draw )et

" The ground's all right, but what abut the team?' I can hear someone kay. Well, as far as 1 can see tie team it going to be pretty much the same as las season. This will not be pleasant news, for the W'arringtcn forces were everywhere admitted to be below par at the close of last seas at, and the outcry for new men was loud and vehement. During the 'summer great efforts have been made by the Com- mittee to unearth new players, but so far without any notable success. There are s true new juniors on trial but players of ability, or experience, cannot be obtained for love or money. Wet rolgton badly want a couple of threequarters, and negotiations are still open with like'y men in the land of the leek.

I learn that he has said he will not sign on for Warrington, but time will tell if he arrives in this country. It is an open secret that Hull are anxious to secure his transfer. I have by me a report of the last match played by the tourists before leaving Sydney. The side included Frawley, and beat a New Zealand thirteen by 39 points to 7 before 35,000 people. A letter from a correspondent who saw the match and had a few words with Frawley, stales that the Warrington player said he would look out for the writer (now homeward bound) "at Warrington. IRISH AFFAIRS. NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.

THE COMING "NEW MEMBER" It is a far cry from Carrickmacross where five counties demonstrated the other day, down to the underworld of Wellington, New Zealand, whence comes yet another con- gratulatory wire to Mr. John Redmond, yet it makes manifest in a striking way the fact that for I rishmen,wherever they are gathered together, the one subject of political thought and consciousness is the question of Home Rule. And, not less so in the strength of conviction, is it the case with Englishmen. In the National Liberal Club and elsewhere, wherever we have encountered English Liberal minds, Home Rule is clearly recog- nised as the live political issue of the moment. During unpromising years when democratic aspirations had little encouragement the Irish people sowed their seed, and now we are to reap the harvest. "Next session we shall have a Home Rule Bill" declared Mr. Birrell at the \ ational Liberal Club and he proceeded in his own frank style to forecast its prospects and perils. The question he affirmed had" completely altered in all its circumstances and conditions" since 1893 when the last heroic effort of Gladstone was frustrated by the House of Lords. In this change, which, it is interesting, in view of Conservative threats so frequently uttered just now, to note was largely effected by Conservative legislation, Irishmen have more than proved their capacity to manage their own affairs. The most sceptical Tory cannot gainsay the fact or doubt the value of the success with which the local bodies constituted by Lord Salisbury's Administration, have been administered. The measure which Lord Salisbury once declared to be worse than Home Rule and which his nephew hoped would kill the National demand has furnished on Mr. Balfour's own admission, the clinch- ing argument for Irish National Self- Government. Moreover, the general spirit of the age, as reflected in Irish politics, has undergone a great change. In 1893 Imperialism, as the doctrine of Chamberlain and Milner was wrongly called, was rising on the crest of the wave. Since the extravagant military picnic of the South African War,it has steadily declined. To-day, underlying all the movement of politics, there exists a recognition, tacit or explicit, of the feeling for the rights of nationalities to develop their individuality. Jingoism has had its verdict at the bar of commonsense, and ..he propitious moment has arrived for adding a new member to the country of self- governing nations.

- TAB WILD ORANGE MEN. In Mr. Birrell's utterances, however, there is no under-rating of the difficulties of the struggle which now lies before us. " Jaunty ' we remember was the word used to describe his political manner, but there is nothing jaunty about his attitude towards his reponsibilities with respect to I Home Rule. There are new conditions and new hopes; but, no less certain, a great fight still looms ahead. It is true— and what lover of liberty does not rejoice in the fact ?—there is no longer an Absolute Veto to be dreaded, but Mr. Birrell insisted, , addressing his colleagues and friends, "not I without your assistance and loyal support, Parliament Bill or no Parliament Bill can the united Cabinet press forward to "the one great victory" now on the horizon. The powers of the House of Lords for obstruction and delay are not to be despised. The shriekers of a part of Ulster may, however, be well despised, especially by those who know Ireland as it really is. Mr. Shaw Leslie, who knows Ulster better than most, poured ample scorn on them at the meeting just referred to of five counties held in Carrickmacross. The force of Sir J. 13. Lons- dale's declaration that "Home Rule will never be accepted, even if it were passed ten times by the Liberal Govern- ment" may be estimated to a fraction. His threat that if a Parliament is set up in Dublin Irish Unionists "will neither obey its dictates nor pay the taxes it levies" Irish- men may well smile at. To Englishmen, however, just fresh as they are from scenes of violent disorder during the recent strike, these wholly unwarranted incitements to disturbances must appear diabolical. The law of England makes not only a felony punish- able with severe penalties, but also puts under criminal punishment the act of inciting anyone to the commission of a feiony, and it appears strange to us that these wild men of the Orange camp have not already had a practical reminder of this very obvious point. Possibly it is not being taken seriously in England, and it may be that it is recognised here—as it certainly is in every town and village of Ireland—that notwithstanding their braggadocio, as soon as the reins of power pass from Dublin Castle and its flunkeys into the hands of the people, the would-be civil-war men will be "running after the jobs" as persistently, but not so exclusively successfully as they did under the old .regime.

There was no cold caution in Mr. Birrell'a estimate of the difficulties of a genuine national settlement. Centuries of wrong- doing cannot be undone without some trouble. His call for loyal, active and enthusiastic support from his colleagues in the passing of the measure which will, we may hope, put the crown on his reputation, as the Parlia- ment Bill has crowned Mr. Asquith's, will be sure to meet with a worthy response. Liberalism is vibrating with movements directed to that end, to secure that Horne Rule shall be passed, not with any grudging or even apathetic acquiescence by the English people (the Scots and Welsh are already fast with us) but with the whole- hearted enthusiasm of a people who have recently enthroned freedom and fair play on the heights of their national Renate.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SAMIDAY, AUGUST 26, 1911

The Railway Strike THE STRIKE Commission has now TRIBUNAL. settled to its work in good earnest. In announcing the composition of the Commis- sion in the House of Commons Mr Asquirx said that happily the clouds had lifted, hostilities had ceased, and both parties without abandoning any of their contentions had agreed to an immediate investigation by an impartial tribunal. The composition of this tribunal is, to a large extent, unexpected, but it is satisfactory that it is not a tribunal of politicians. The anticipations in some quarters, Liberal as well as Conservative was that Lord ST. ALDWYN would be named as chairman. The Government has done much better. Nobody would doubt Lord ST. ALDWYN'S desire to be thoroughly impartial in such a case. But though he is able and honest, he is not a particularly broad- minded man, and it would not be unreason- able to suppose that he might be influenced by his pre-possessions. The gentleman who has been appointed Chairman is not known in politics, or in connection with industrial- ism. Of the impartiality of Sir DAVID HARREL there cannot be any doubt what- ever. He is absolutely detached from either side, and it is agreed by those who are acquainted with his official career in Ireland that a very wise and even extraordinary discretion has been exercised by the Govern- ment in selecting him for a position of so much importance. -
We can scarcely imagine the possibility of selecting a Commission less sensational in its character than that which has actually been

appointed. It is obvious that what is to take place is not a fight between two sides, but a real investigation. Sir T. RATCLIFFE ELus and Mr. CHARLES BEALE doubtless command the confidence of the railway companies, and have been appointed with their approval. But they have not been involved in the dispute, and there cannot be any reason for suspecting them of anything but a sincere wish to deal fairly in what is probably the most momen- tous investigation that has ever been made in connection with British industry. Mr. ARTHUR HENDERSON will be

generally recognised as one of the most solid and most moderate of the Labour members. Mr. JOHN BURNETT is one of those really great men who do work that is vastly useful to the community and who do not court public recognition. Those who know most of him admire him most. He is quite singularly far-seeing and level-headed He was one of the secretaries of the Labour Department of the Board of Trade. It is one

of his distinctions that as a young man he conducted in a quite orderly manner the long strike with won the nine hours day for the engineers. He has now been outside Trade Union movements for the greater part of his lifetime, but is still justly regarded by Trades Unionists as one of the most remark- able of the men who have risen from their ranks.

The Commission is appointed to inquire into the working of the Railway Conciliation and Arbitration scheme, adopted by both sides in 1907, to report on any changes that may be desirable, with a view to the prompt and satisfactory settlement of differences. This involves the deliverance of a judgment as to whether the refusal of the railway managers to meet representatives of the men is justifiable or proper. But, of course, it involves much more than that. The allegation of the men is that the Conciliation Board has worked against their interest, and that, by deliberate design of the railway companies. This contention will now be subjected to the test of evidence. There is perhaps a lingering suspicion among Labour men that the Com- mission may merely aim at smoothing things over. Mr. RAMSAY MACDONALD said in the House of Commons in a somewhat too- impassioned speech that the Commission . would be acceptable if the inquiry is "carried out honestly and without quibbling or red tape." It may be said with a feeling of ; certainty that the Government could not I have appointed a Commission more likely to . carry out the investigation in a temper of mind such as was suggested. The country will look to this body for recommendations which will bring about not only a temporary settlement, but conditions of permanent peace.

In the course of his THE MAYOR AND speech at the Sankey VACCINATION. Sanatorium on Satur- day, the Mayor (Coun- cillor Dr. Joseph) was led to remark on the fact that the building was available for its present useful purpose because of the practical extinction of small-pox as a result of vaccination. It is a well-known fact that his Worship views the continually increasing number of exemptions with deep concern, and while deprecating the allusion to a contentious topic he added that "He did not think any sane person who had studied the case for a moment could fail to realise the tact that small-pox was to-day a thing of the past was due to vaccination. There is an overt allusion to the anti-v's here which will doubtless impinge violently on their susceptibilities. We hope, however, they will not deluge us with letters on their pet theories! Like the giant gooseberry and the sea-serpent, the anti-vaccination craze periodically bursts forth in the public press. Summer simmering may be the cause ; any- how the "close" season for such topics is approaching.

The Warrington health A FRESH AIR authorities are fighting FACTORY. the scourge of consump- tion with that inexpen- sive but powerful weapon—fresh air. Medical opinion is agreed that it is by the open-air treatment that early cases of the fell disease are best checked, and valuable lives saved to the community. That is the basis upon which the Sankey Sanatorium' now set apart for cases of pulmonary tuber- culosis, is destined to become an invaluable health asset to Warrington. Before consump- tion has got a complete hold of the system, patients will be sent to Sankey where, in a breezy and isolated neighbourhood, they will practically live in the open-air and receive the best of food and the most careful general attention. Under . such favourable conditions, the chances of recovery are exceedingly hopeful. The sanatorium will serve another eminently useful purpose in isolating advanced cases. relieving the patients from the unnecessary suffering at present entailed by depressing surroundings, and protecting the community from risk of infection. The Health Com- mittee is to be congratulated upon its for- ward policy in deciding to make such practical use of the institution, which has happily not been required for its original purpose of dealing with smallpox epidemics. The enterprise is at present being conducted on unambitious lines but if anticipations are fulfilled, Saturday last will be gratefully recalled as the day when the Corporation of Warrington definitely addressed itself to the tremendous task of stamping out the great white plague which is working such devasta- tion in our midst.

Mr. Keir Hardie was A SHOCKING severely taken to task STATEMENT. by Mr. Lloyd-George on Tuesday for his attempts to embitter discussion of the labour troubles. The Government has just effected the settlement of one of the most menacing industrial strikes with which this country has ever been confronted. Nothing, as Mr. Lloyd-George said, could be more disastrous to the men themselves than that they should in a moment of exasperation throw away the fruits which their best advisers regard as a triumph. Mr. Keir Hardie was especially rebuked by Mr. Lloyd-George in the strongest terms which Parliamentary etiquette permits, for his absolutely unfounded statement, in a speech on Satur- day, that the Prime Minister had declared that the railways would be kept open, even if every striker had to be "shot down." On Tuesday Mr. Keir Hardie did not withdraw the statement, but if anything made it worse, if that were possible, by his" explana- tion."

An absurd attempt has WHERE THE been made by some of TARIFF REFORMER the Tariff Reformers to RUSHES IN. make capital out of the strike. In order to make out their case, they concede that the men are underpaid. Wages have not risen along with the improvement in trade and the rise in the cost of living. The strike, accord- ing to those apostles of Tariff Reform, is a proof of a need fora protective tariff which will secure higher wages for the workers by keeping out cheap foreign goods. A more ill-timed advertisement of the Tariff Reform case could not be imagined. The strikers were mainly engaged in the transport services. Their grievances were (1) that trade had improved,without any accompany- ing benefit to themselves. Out of this the *Tariff Reformers can make nothing. (2) That living is dearer, and so their net wages are lower. Tariff Reformers propose to make living dearer still. The workers of this country complain of a 9 per cent, rise in living. The workers in Protectionist America complain of a 50 per cent. rise. Finally, the Tariff Reformers propose to help the men in the transport trades by cutting off the very source and spring of their -employment.

* * * Nothing is ever settled until it is settled Tight. The protective tariff is all wrong. It is wrong in economics, wrong in morals, and a great corrupter in politics. Therefore, the protest against it, and resistance to it, never will cease.—Prof. William G. Sumner, U.S.A. * * _ . .

Young Hopeful: Father, what is a traitor in politics? Veteran Politician : A traitor is a man who leaves our party and goes over to the other one. Young Hopeful: Well, then, what is a man who leaves his party and comes over to yours? Veteran Politician: A convert, my son. 0 0 0 Regular users of Sankey-street have been devoutly wishing they wern't. The only -convenient and spacious section of the thoroughfare has been decimated by the minions of the Water Committee, who are engaged laying the new pipe line from Winwick. An improved water supply will doubtless be a boon, but one shudders to con- template the state of the wood-pavement when the various committees concerned have had their innings

There has been another outbreak of -feverish activity in the neighbourhood of Warrington Bridge this week. Several courses of brickwork have been taken off the wall behind the site of the Bridge Inn, and during the last few days a labourer has -spent hour after hour in the solitary industry of chipping the displaced bricks for future nse. There is something in the air, but of the new bridge as a " concrete " fact one can see no trace. Patience Is the watchword!

COG The railway trouble in Scotland has recalled some stories respecting the North British Railway strike of twelve years ago. An Edinburgh contemporary tells one. In the emergency an amateur engine-driver had been put on duty on a branch line. At one station he ran his train a considerable way past the platform. Stopping at last, he " backed," and went as far beyond at the other end. The old porter, who had remained loyal, eyed the proceedings with cynical amusement. "Stop whaur ye are," he shouted, "an' we'll shift .the station for ye."

* - Father Vaughan, speaking in Inverness I on Sunday on the labour troubles, is reported to have said: "The optimist is teaching false philosophy, and the result must be disaster to the nation. On the other hand, I see the pessimist mounting his tower and unfurling his flag, and shutting his eyes and looking down over the vast multitudes." This is almost as good as the statement of a 'Conservative orator on one occasion who declared that " the British Lion, whether climbing the pine forests of Canada or scouring the Pacific main, would not draw in its horns or retire into its shell."

• - Warrington is not to have a visit from General Booth,after all; the railway troubles having necessitated the cancelling of this week's arrangements for the motor tour. Tho General will begin his tour at Leigh, Lanca- shire, next Monday. It had been his intention to make a start last Saturday from the Barry Dock, Cardiff, but he was prevented by the strike. As a consequence, he drops a week ,out of his programme, which he takes op at the point he would have reached on Monday next if nothing had happened to interfere with his plans. He will not go to •Canada this year. His place will be taken by Mrs. Bramwell Booth, who is about to visit the Dominion for the first time,and will conduct the Salvation Army Congress there this autumn.

...... • * * Salisbury Cathedral, where a new bishop -will shortly be enthroned, is, in the opinion of Oliver Wendell Holmes,the most beautiful building in England. "If one had to name the apple of the eye of England," he writes, I think he would be likely to say that Salisbury Cathedral was as near as he could come to it, and that the white of the eye was Salisbury Clore." An earlier visitor, Nicholas Coulon, who came to England in 1645, describes Salisbury as "one of the most beautiful cities in the world, with running -*3treams in all the streets to freshen and cleanse them, and possessing a superb cathedral, in which there are as many windows as there are days in the year, as -many marble columns as there are hours in the year, and as many doors as there are months."

* - Rossini promised a place in the Opera orchestra to a trombonist, and then forgot about it. At one of his dinner parties the butler announced the visit of the same protege. Rossini, according to the" Musical Courier," hastened to welcome him, and -relieving him of his instrument disappeared a few moments to return with his friends. Handing the instrument to the tro abonist, with a request to let the company hear him, Rossini prepared to listen. Trombone to lips he musician blows—dismay—no sound; cheeks bulging; eyes distended. In vain the unhappy man makes superhuman efforts to produ ze harmonious sounds. At last! 0 effort supreme! With a sound like a hoarse

goose-cackle there shoots from the trombone a mass of sticky macaroni. "No harm, my friend," said Rossini, "you have proved yourself a strong musician." And the next day the coveted position was offered to the trombonist.

• Though one of the most strenuous of fighters, the late Dr. Guinness Rogers was remarkably free from personal bitterness in his antagonisms. On the publication of his autobiography eight years ago, it was noted by one of the reviewers that the most cutting word it contained was the following, respect- ing Mr. Chamberlain : "I regarded his separation from the Liberal Party at the time with deep regret, which, however, is not so strong to-day as it was then." Of his capacity for friendship perhaps the best tribute was that once paid him by the late Dr. Mackennal. "He is a perfect friend. If I were in trouble through no fault of my own there are many to whom I could go for help. If I ware in trouble through my own fault I should go to Rogers." Dr. Guinness Rogers had not been absent from one annual assembly of the Congrega- tional Union of England and Wales from the time that he went to Grafton-square, Clapham, until May of this year—a period lextending from 1865 until 1910. At the last assembly extreme age and weakness rendered , his attendance impossible, but on the motion lof the chairman a resolution of sympathy was sent which cheered him in his retire- ment. Many who were present in the City Temple last year, when the Rev. C. Silvester Home was chairman, will remember the rousing greeting Dr. Rogers received as he came to the platform and spoke. He was then in a frail condition and presented a most venerable appearance, but he much appre- ciated the tokens of affection extended towards him. Dr. Rogers was the oldest ex-chairman of the Congregational Union, having been in office in 1874. All those who followed him until the year 1883, when Dr. Fairbairn was in the chair, have passed away.

- - Those who are endeavouring to make capital for Tariff Reform out of the present industrial unrest would do well (says the "Westminster Gazette ") to consult the ' statistics of strikes in countries in which the blessings of a tariff are enjoyed. We ignore the railway strikes in France and the general strike in Italy as manifestations on an unusual scale, and go back a few years. In the "New Dictionary of Statistics," recently published by Messrs. Webb, the following figures are given as covering the years 1902-6:

_ United Kingdom : Strikes, 406 ; strikers,9B,4so.l Germany': Suites, 2,007 ; strikers, 186,670. France : Strikes, 819; strikers, 244,620. Italy (1900-4) : Strikes, 928; strikers, 245,369. United States (1901-5) : Strikes, 2901; st.ikers, 461,009. Whatever else these figures show, they do not suggest extraordinary discontent in this country. On the contrary, Great Britain has suffered less from labour disturbance than any of its high-tariff neighbours. Taking the population of the two countries, the United States, with its prohibitive tariff and its high wages, has had nearly three times as many strikers as the United Kingdom.

Warrington Man Drowned. A Warringtonian named Joseph Cross, latterly a resident of Lea-road, Egremont was bathing in the river Mersey off the Vale Park, New Brighton, on Wednesday, when he was seen to be in difficulties, and before aid cou'd be rendered he sank an I was drowned. His body was recovered about an hour later. Cross, who was twenty-seven years of age, was a tailor. He was the eon of Mr. Cr s., tailor of Mersey-street, and was a native d Warrington which place he left about two years ay. He leaves a widow and one child. The funeral took place at the cemetery on Friday and was largely attended by his relatives and friends. Many wreaths and cther floral tributes were plac.d on the coffio.

The Coming Bible Contenary. We should like to call the a.tention of our readers to the advertisement on our front page, relating to the coming Centenary of the Warringtoo-A-umilrary of the Blitish and Foreign Bible Society. The Centenary Celebrations will take the form of a Bible Sunday, in which the Church of England and the Nonconformist places of Worship will take part, and a mass meeting, at which the Bishop of (Amster, the Rev. F. W. MacDonald (an en-president of the Wesleyan Conference), the Ten Archdeacon Madden and the local clergy and ministers will asset. It is thought that the occasion might be made the means of raising ,ElCld for the funds of the Parent Society. The secretary, Mr. J. C. Holland, Causeway-avenue, will be pleased to hear from all who desi-e to further the work in any way. Death of an Old Chorister. Many of our readers will regret to helr of the death of Mr. John Pott,r, of 5, Priestley-street, one of the oldest choristers in Warrington, who passed away on Thursday, the 17th inst. while on a visit to his eldest son, at Crewe. For over forty years Mr. Potter, who was OS, had baen a member of the choir of Holy Trinity Church. He was also associated with other choirs in the district from boy- , hood. He was one of the best known bass vocalist's in the district, and was a member of the troupe of ' minstrels formed in the town in the early seventies. An Oddfellow of many years' standing. he held the decree of P.P.G.M. in the Manchester Unity r f that Order. He was a staunch Conservative and took an active part in the elections when the late Sir Gabe' t Greenall sought the suffrage's of the electors. He was also a strong Churchman. Tyro years ago he retired from work as a file forger at the manufactory of Messrs. Peter Stubbs, Limi-ed. The fu,,eral task place at the Warrington Cemetery on Mon lay after- no-n. The first part of the service was held at Holy Trinity Church, the Rev. H. R. Wild officiating. Many beauti'ul floral tributes, including one from the members of Holy Trinity eho.r, were placed on the coffin.

div.head: INCREASE IN PRICE OF MILK
div.p: INCREASE IN PRICE OF MILK

--- The unwelcome announcement is made by the Warrington and district milk retailers that on and after to-morrow (Sunday) the retail price of milk will be raised from 3d. to 4d. per quart. The reason given for the advance is that the farmers in the neighly urhood are demanding a much higher price for the milk. In conversation wiih a prominent milk retailer, a representative of the " Examiner" was informed that the action of the farmers had been compelled y the scarcity of food for cattle, broueit about by the prolonged drought. As the crops of turnips and mangolds are excep- tionally poor, the scarcity is likely to extend through the winter. The housewife is therefore faced with the prospect of paying the increased price for an indefinite but probably long period.

- FATAL MOTOR-CAR ACCIDENT. ENGLISHMAN KILLED IN CANADA. Ottawa, Wednesday.—Mr Arthur Stewart Bitch, son of Mr John Birch, of Mansfield, Nottinghamshire, has been killed in a motorcar accident. Mr. Birch wan driving the car and wan accompanied by a lady friend. A tyre burst and the car wan thrown into a ditch, both the occupants being killed instantly.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
Houghton —Dawson.

The quiet Westraorland village of Heversham was en fate on Thursday, when the marriage was solemnized at the Parish Church, of Mr. James Houghton, jun., eldest son of Mr. James Houghton, Warr, ington,and chief clerk in the Borough Treasurer's department, Warrington, and Miss Beatrice Daw- son, BA., only daughter of Mr. John Dawson, of Leasgill, Westmorland, and late assistant mistress at the Secondary School, Warrington. Great interest was taken in the ceremony and the village bore every siger of rejo'cing, the approach to the church being gaily bedecked with flags and hunting. Within the church a very large congregation had assembled. Sire. W. J. Nelson was at the organ and during the arrival of the gue,ts played Guilmant's Wedding March. As the bridal party entered the church , the hymn " Gracious Spirit, H.tly Ghost " was I sung. The service, which was conducted by the Rev. Canon Gilbert, M.A., Vicar of Heversham, was fully choral. The hymn " 0 Perfect Love" was sung kneeling, and after an impressive address by Canon Gilbert, the organist played the' Bridal Minh" from " Lnhengrin." The newly-married couple left the church to the joyous strains of Mendelssohn's " Wedding March" and the church bells ran.; out a merry peal. The bride, who was given away by her father, was beautifully attired in ivory Cleopatra trAin with yoke and sleeves of Mecklin lace, traced with silver thread. The corsage and train were embro'derel with pearls and Mall wreaths of orange blossom. A wreath of -orange blossom with tiny sprigs of heather was surmounted by a veil of old Limerick lace worn _by tbe_bridegroona's grandmother at her wedding and lent by his aunt, Mrs. Becker, of India. -She carried a handsome bouquet of roses, choice lilies and white heather. The bridesmaids were Miss Holds Elow3hton (sister of the bridegroom), Miss Jesiiie Ifolt (cousin of the bride), and Miss klarg‘ret Germain (a , school friend of the bride). Miss Hcaighmn wore a tunic of white silk embroidered muslin over silk, and the Misses Holt and Germain were attired in tunics of white ninon over satin, trimmed will silver and crystal beading. All the bridesmaids had sashes of eau de nil ribbon, with large picture hats trimmed t mach, and their ornaments were pearl pmdants, the gifts of the bridegroom. M. Charles E. FlouAton, brother of the bridegroom, discharged the duties of best man. After the ceremouy Mr. and Mrs DASVB'II entertained their guests at the Athe.,ream, Leasgill, and the newly married couple were the recipients of hearty congratulations. In the evening, upwards of 100 guests fro-n the neigh's otring distri2ts were , invited to job in whist and dancing, and the gathering was a most happy and ' enjoyable one. During the af tern on, amid the ' plating of church bell+, Mr. and Mrs. J. Houghton, jun., left for Devonshire where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride travelled in a Wedgwo ,1 blue co.tume, t,immed with Paisley brocade, with large ' black picture hat. The p-emote, a very handsome and valuab'e cull- ction, numbered over 150. They ' included gifts from the officials of the Warrington Corporation, the staff, the scho!ars and Form If. B. of ' the Warringto i Secondary School, St. Paul's Sunday School Class and the Sunday School Teachers.

div.head: Banks—Buckley.
div.p: Banks—Buckley.

A wedding of condderable 1 rc,l interest was celebrated on Weloeslay at the Psrish Church, when Miss Ada Buckley, d kughter of the late Mr. Joseph Buckley, sometime licensee of the "Prince of Wales" Inn, School Brow, was married to Mr. Walter Hardman Banks, son of Mr. Davi I Banks of " Eversley " Grappenhall.
