div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" The Heart Bowad Down "

d emetic attraction of much more than average interest is to be seen this week at the Royal Court Theatre, where Mr. and Mrs. Charles Draycott and their company present Mrs. F. G. Kimberley's latest play "The Heart Bowed Down." The most case- hardened theatre-goer finds his attention rivetted I throughout the nine scenes, for the plot is conceived on original lines and its working out gives rise to a aeries of powerful and deeply moving situations. In defiance of the aristocratic prejudices of his mother, Philip Austin, a gentleman, marries Irene Royal, " a true and noble woman of the stage." The mother will not reconcile herself to the match, and refuses to receive the wit-, with the result that a complete e.trangement talus place, and the newly-married couple are forced to spend their days in poverty. Philip cannot endure this life, and is at length pre- vailed upon to desert his wife, who is nobly befriended by Signor Naito Carriello, an Italian actor. Of course, it is not a difficult matter for enemies to put al evil construction on the friendship I,tween the two, and Philip is made to believe that his wife has been false to him. However, a complete retraction of the aspersions is secured by Signor Carriello, in a scene full of thrilling inten,ity and in the end reconciliation lis brought about. Mts. Charles Draycott is a gifted I emotional aetress and infuses dean pathos into her characterisation of Irene Royal without yielding to the temptation to exaggerate. She fills the part to the complete ,atistaction of the sudience and gains loud applause for a beautiful rendering of the song" The heart b 'wed down." Mr. Char'es Drayeott portrays the Italian actor, Signor Nell° Carriello, with an earnestness and fire wh'ch appeal to all and he is repeatedly rand before the curtain. Miss Lily Roselle does full justics to the unpopular part of Margaret Howard,bluntly describmlas "a woman full of wickedues, " and she has an unscrupulous., accom- plice in her brother, George Howard. realistically impersonated by Mr. John Manner.. Mr. Franklyn Bellamy infuses the necessary fervour and dash into his study of Philip Austin. Wee Dorothy Handel, a promising child actress, scores a great success as Sybil, the beloved &did cf Irene. Mi-s Emma Rainbow is admirable as Charlotte Austin. an' the comedy element is well sustained by Mi-,s Vielet Vivienne as Flossie May, and Mr. Robert Sawin as James Butler, the loquacious bookie. The scenery and effects are on a tasteful and elaborate scale. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

The desire of the management to keep the bill of fare well varied is evidenced by next week's attraction which will take the form of Mr. Tom H. Taylor's Company in the successful musical " something to laugh at " entitled " The Dandy Doctor" by Edward Man is. The company which is a strong one, will include Miss Marie Ault as Jane, and Mr. Tom E. Sinclair as the millionaire. The following week Mr. James Welch's Company will present " When knights were bold."
The latest additioa to the types of Londoa's street musicians is a left-handed negro violin's., wbo on Thursday was tryiag his lock in Shoe-lane in the dinner boar.

div.head: WARRItiGTON BRIDGE.
div.p: WARRItiGTON BRIDGE.
'CONTRACTORS GETTING TO WORK.

During the past week there have been welcome signs of an early start being made with the construction ot the new Warrington Bridge. Representatives of Messrs. Alfred Thorne and Sons, of Westminster, the contractors, are now on the scene and on Wednesday morning the position of the bridge was lined out. This work had to be commenced at four o'clock in the morning so as not to interfere with the tramway traffic. The erection of the bridge, we are informed will now proceed without delay.

div.head: WORKS RE-OPENING.
div.p: WORKS RE-OPENING.
Warrington's Recovery tram Strike
Dislocation.

Short as was the duration of the natioaal strike on the railways it was sufficient t 3 di-locate trade in Warrington to an alarming extent. Several of the leading works closed down last Friday ni.tht. and at the beginning of the present week over 5,000 working men must have been walking about the streets without employment. The sattlemeut of the trouble came as a great relief, but- the- accumulation- of manufactured gezels at the most important concerns was great and the shortage of raw material s, serious that it was found impossible to re,ime work immediately. Now, however, the town is recovering frost the state of chaos int, which it was plunged by the paralysis of the railway eystems, and neat week it is hope I that , the conditions will be s3mething approaching normal., Some of the works are a'ready working as usual, whilstothera have partidly resumed operations. The two forges of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd., at D.dlam and Bewsey have remained closed throughout the week, but we under- stand they will re-open on Monday next. This will be welcome news t 3 the 2,050 workingmen and their dependents. About half of the works of Ifesa.s. Rylands Bros., Ltd, Church-street, is at present standing idle, but work will be resumed in all departments oa Monday. Sankey Wire Mills were ii fuq swing yesterday and Whitecr,ss works are in partial operatioa.

div.head: LIVERIML TRAMWAY STRIKE SETTLED.
div.p: LIVERIML TRAMWAY STRIKE SETTLED.
Men Re-instated.

The sole barrier to a comp'ete settlement of the Liverpool industrial war was removed on Thursday, when the Tramways and Electric Power Committee of the Corporation decided to reinstate 250 uniformed trar,way men who had been on strike. On Wednesday the negotiations between the repre- sentatives of the tramway men and the tramway authority broke down, the latter refusing t 3 re-instate those of the strikers who belong to the Transport Federation, numbering 250. The country was once more threatened with a national strike, representatives of the Liverpool strike committee leaving for London to meet the National Transport Workers' Federation. " Arrangements will be immediately commenced," said Mr. Chambers, acting chairman of the Strike Committee, "for a general strike of the whole of the transport workers of this country unless the Liverpool Tramways Committee come to reason. The Tramway- men's Union is federated with the National Federation of Engineers, Firemen, and Kindred Trades," added Mr. Chambers. "They are entitled to the support of this federation. It has been promised and will be given. The federa- tion covers every mall who curtrols the windina machinery at the collieries in England, No-th and South Wales, and Scotland. They will be called upon to net, and every colliery will be laid idle." Before Mr. Mann departed the Strike Committee drew ups manifesto t) the strikers, in which it was said that, negotiations so far having resulted in a definite refusal to reinstate, they have no alternative but to continue the fight with greater vigrr. They were now in communication with the National Transport Workers' Federation and the Joint Executives of the railwaymen's unions for the exten- sion of the fight nationally, no one to return to work till instructed by the Strike Committee. Mr. Asksvith, K.C., whose mediation in the Man- chester carters' dispute was attended with such happy Jesuits, arrived in Liverpool on Thursday morning to use his influence for a settlement. In the afternoon the Tramways Committee agaiu met to consider the question. The meeting evidently found its task a most difil- cult one. Voices in angry protestation and argument could be heard from time to time, and the members of the committee were clearly divided in opinion. The party of concession and the party of " resistance" each fought hard. After three hours discussion, the committee decided in favour of the reinstatement of the uniform men as . and when required.

div.head: GARTERS AND THEIR WAGES.
div.p: GARTERS AND THEIR WAGES.

The Warrington Horse Owners' AsmciAtion, at a meeting held at the Patten Arms Hotel, yesterday afternoon, had under con.ideration a request fr m the Warrington Carters' Union for a revision of wages. It was decided to rsis3 the minimum wage for single horse drivers over twenty-one years of age to 225. per week and pair horse drivers to 251. per week, the working conditions to remain as hitherto.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Many capable gymnasts have appeared from time to time at the Palace and Hippodrome, but without the slightest exaggeration one may truly say that the Michael Richardini Troupe, who head the bill this ' week, are quite equal to any of them. In some respects they surpass their iivals. They Riese wonderful and dating display —one which requires great dexterity and strength. What stem!. out quite as strikingly as the performance itself is the enviable build and pose of the trio. Their superiority over some of their ilk is obvious. There is no puffiness, all is firm muscle, and unlike some of abnormal site, they are as supple as anyone could desire to be. Their performance is occasionally enlivened by humorous tit-bite and throughout the eff,wts of the troupe receive the unrestrained appreciation due to diem. The next turn that should be mentioned, judged by the uandard of popularity, is Waxworks "—a farce which is in the hands of Syd. E Camp and Dora Critic. The wax figures introduced into the sketch are provocative of much amusement and embodying, as it does, afar from stereotyped theme, the audience enjoy the show immensely. Ben Jackson is quite at home on the bulk) and plays bright tunes while his instruments ere in different positions. As a double v,iced vocalist Ditto is txcel'ent, though be sings so well in both registers that the aulienee regards him as a phenomenon. In a pretty and refined vocal scena Carman's Juveniles excel. Their dancing is particularly meritorious. Dascribed as the Southern Serenader, Douglas K. Lwne, contributes a smart song of the light comedy type and follows with a charmingly rendered song of his absent lover, amid picturesque woodland surroundings. His dancing has the stamp of originalty, hiliarity and gracefulness being aptly combined. RI tty Emson is a fascinating damsel- =ti- the popularity attained during her singing is greatly enhanced 1,3, her beautiful d mcing. As a dower in wooden shoes Walter Aubrey gives evidence of con- siderable skill and ability. The orchestra under the able leadership of Mr. E. A. Widdop renders 901336 splendid selections. The pictures are as original and pleasing as of yore.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JAMES WOOD.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JAMES WOOD.

The announcement will be received with deep regret of the death, which took place with painful suddenness, at eight o'clock on Tuesday morning of Mr. James Wood, of lii, Sinkey-street. Mr. Wood, who was 73 years of age, appeare I to be in his usual goad health the previous evening, but during the night he was seized with an attack of cerebral hemorrhage. Dr. E. J. }...)1 was summoned but Mr. Wood was beyond medical aid and passed away aft-r only a few hours illness. The deceased gentleman was a member of an old Warrington family, having been born on the premises which have since been converted into solicit trs' offices and are now oc,mpied by Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., Market Place. In early life he entered the teaching profession, and was for some time headmister of a school in Academy- street. He alsa stu lied at the old Warrington School of Art and was so succe.sful in winning gold medals and certificates that many of his friends anticipated that he would devote his career to art. Over forty years ago he succeeded to the printing and stationary business in Sinkey-street then conducted by his brother, Mr. Henry Wood. During the Turkish War Mr. Wood published a newspaper called " The Evening Post," which ceased issue in, 1881. He enjoyed the respect of a very large circle of friends by whom his unex- pected end will be greatly deplored. He was a staunch Churchman and worshipped at St. Paul's Church. In po'itics he was a Conservative. He leaves a family of two daughters and four sons. Ths funeral took place at the Cemetery yesterday afternoon in the presence of members of the family and sympathising friends. Prior to the interment • there was a short but impressive service in St. Paul's Church. The Revs. W. Bracecamp and H. V. Pigot l officiated. Many beautiful floral tributes were ! placed on the grave.

div.head: Borough Pollee Court.
div.p: Borough Pollee Court.

lIONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) presiding, Aldermen Smethurst, Bolton and Bennett, rNessra A .1 Jolley, W Roberts, Ei Wright, W Furness G Pilling and H Thornton. A W 0174 DING CH ARG E.—John Longrrbaw, 1, Garnett's-yard, was charged with wounding his wife, Agnes Longshaw, by striking her with a stick on Satur- day last. The Chief Constable asked that the case might stand adjourned for seven days to see how the woman progressed. On Saturday the prisoner struck his wife a violent blow across the head with a stick (produced) which necessitated six stitches. The wound however was a scalp wound and be did not think any- thing of a serious nature would ensue. Ile prisoner asked that the C 360 might be proceeded with but the Chief Constable stated that that court WB3 unable to deal with it in its present form as the charge was of too serious a nature but if the wound progressed favourably the charge would be reduced to one of common assault. —The case was remanded for seven days. MiscgcLaNvous.—Ten cases of drunk and disorderly, four cases of simple drunkenness and one each of begging and obscene lang.tage were dealt with.

TT-ESDA Y.—Before Councillor C. Jack on Holmes (in the chair) Messrs W. Richardson, and Mr. T. Looker, and Colonel Edelsten. Ilaut rum. DRUNKARD.—Thomas Flynn, 38, Watkin- street, can summoned by his wife Mary Jane Flynn for being an habitual drunkard. The complainant stetted defendant was drunk about 3 or 4 times every week. lie could earn from 303. to 365. a week. He led the children the lives of dogs and she had to sneak upstairs and hide out of his way. She had never received more than 9s. a week for the last twelve months. There were four children at borne one of whom was working.—The Bench granted a separation order with 12, a week.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Charles White (in the chair), Messrs. W. T. Williams and J. W. Hayward. STRIKERS IN MOUT:I.E.—James Iligharv, 9, Boger- street, and James Mitchell, 14, Barbauld-street, were charged on remand with stealing or receiving Gd. the money of William Wycherley. Both pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable stated that the prisoners were connected with the strike at Walton lay-by and the case had been remanded in order to investigate a charge of robbery with violence. At 4 1500 Tuesday the 15th inst. a man named Wycherley was lying by the river side near to the cricket ground when the prisoners, with whom he bad been drinking, end a number of other men came on the scene. He offered one of the men is. to go and buy some beer. When the beer was obtained they all partook of it. Shortly after Mitchell was seen to rifle Wycherley'a pockets and he evidently took 45. 6d. He handed 25. to iligham and that amount was found in Higham's possession when arrested by P.C. Hewitt. Ile theo tried to throw the money a way. Wycherley was severely assaulted. Mitchell dealt him a blow in the mouth and he was knocked practically insensible. He had looked after the prisoners well and that was how they treated him. He (the Chief Constable),asked that the Bench might deal with the cafe in such a way that it would act ass pre- ventive lathe future. Both prisoners stated that they were drunk at the time. Twenty-three previous convictions were proved against Higham and 33 against Mitchell both of whom were sentenced to two months hard labour. "I WANT MY BiGina''--John Loyden, Thomas White, Fred Archer, Thomas Quinn and the two prisoners in the previous case were charged on remand with having been drunk and disorderly in Arpley-road on the 15th last, while Mitchell was also charged with arsaulting P.C. Hewitt.—Sergeant Stuart said at 6.45 on the day In question whilst on duty with several officers in Arpley-road be saw the prisoners staggering about the rued drunk. Mitchell (commonly known as Coffee Cooler) was shooting "I want my rights and I'll have 'em." Two of the other prisoners were struggling on the bank. Prisoners were taken into custody, and while on the way to the Police Station Ingham tripped P.C. Newitu up, causing him to fall to the ground. Mitchell then took a running kick at the constable which caught him in the ribs. This ata(emeut was corroborated by P.C. Hewitt.—Mitchell : It is all a concoction. Loyden had a record of 13 previous appearances, White 10, Archer 19, and Quinn 20. The Bench sentenced Mitchell to an additional month's hard labour, and all the other prisoners, with the exception of 'Belmar, who was given no further sentence, to seven days' hard labour each. Six MONTHS Fort ASSAULT.—Andrew Clancy, 24 Dolman's-lane was charged on remand with assaulting and heating Bridget Hardy and Mary Crev. He pleaded guilty, hut In self-defence.—The Chief Constable said about 10 o'clock on the 15th inst the prisoner was talking to a young woman in Dolmaes-lane when the prosecntrix passed by. The young woman who worked with the prosecntrix asked her to wait and she would come home with her. Prisoner sae annoyed at this and too" offence at the prosecutrix and treated her in a most brutal manner. The girl was taken home and afterwards while her mother was taking her to the It firmary, the prisoner assaulted the mother. The girl RIM subsequently conveyed to the Infirmary and attended. The knee where the prisoner bad kicked her swelled a great deal and have great pain. She was unable to attend work for a week. This etas borne ont by a number of witnesses. Prise ner stated that he did not kick the prosecutrix, but that she fell on her clog and that caused the injury to the knee. Previous convictions to the number of 21 having been proved against the prisoner he was sentenced to ids months hard labour. LOITERING WITH INTENT.—Sichard Hassell, lodging- house, 15, Bank-street, a labourer, was charged with being drunk in Bridge-street on the 22nd inst. and further with loitering in Atherton's Q ray with intent to commit a felony on the 21st. inst. The Chief Constable said the prisoner was seen on Monday evening last to be loitering in a suspicious manner on Atherton's Quay. It was subsequently discovered that a quantity of brass was aiming and the matter was reported to the police. He asked that the case might stand adjourned pending further investigations. Samuel Mold, watchman at Messrs. Monks' Hall and Co.'s, raid about 6.30 he saw the pr.soner loitering In the vicinity of the works. He questioned him and in reply he said that he was going for a walk. He kept looking round to see if he (Mold) was watching him. The neat day it was discovered that 121155. of brass value 12s. had been removed from the Bin. mill. Prisoner had no right to go the way he went.—Prisoner was remanded for seven days. WIFE DESERTION.—Thomas Kearns, 2, Silver-street, labourer, was charged with deserting his wife.—The complaisant stated that her husband went to gaol and came out a fortnight ago and she had not seen him since, nor bad he sent her any money. Ile was a labourer earning Pis. a week. He had never given her more than 14a. a week since Christmas—The Bench granted • separation order with Ss. a week.

THCRSDAY.—Before Messrs. A. J. Jolley (in the chair), W. T. Williams and Dr. Naden. ALLEGID ASSAULT.—Peter Murray, 5, Oliver.s'reet, was charged with assaulting Edward Stokes. Mr. Steel who appeared for the prisoner, asked that the case might be adjourned, as the prisoner was arrested only the previous night and there had not been time to call any witnesses. 'the case wan remanded until to-day (Saturday), bail being allowed in two sureties of .Ct each.

FatcaY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton, Smethurst, Memos T Locker, W Vurneiu, S Wright, H Thornton, G Pilling and T Wilkinson. PRISONER REMOVED TO UNION HOSPITAI..—Joho Smith, lodging house, Friars-green was charged on remand with being found on the enclosed premises of 19, Kontsford-road. The Chief Constable said that circumstances compelled him to ask for a further adjournment for four weeks. The doctor bad examined prisoner that morning and found him ;to be suffering from au infectious disease. flaring regard to the doctors report the police did not desire the prisoner to be sent to gaol where he would be a great source of annoyance to the prison medical clficer. He would ask the prisoner to give an undertaking that he would go into the Union until he was cured, when he could be again brought before the magistrates. The prisoner consented. - - -

STRONG OBJECTION co BAlL."—Jonathan Broad. burst, green-grocer, Bostock-street, was charged with receiving Plbe. of scrap bearings and 17Ihs. of scrap brasa well-knowing it to have been stolen. Mr Steel represented the prisoner. - The Chief Constable avid that from information received two or three days ago in connection with a prisoner who was at present in custody Apr the theft of this braes the police obtained a ',arch warrant and Inspector Williamson accom- panied by several officers searched the prisoner's premises. About 10.15 the previous morning the prisoner was seen in the neighbourhood of Liverpool- road and was taken to the Police Station. He was there told about the (mg • " but when questioned denied all knowledge of it. Upon arrival at the prisoner's premises the police discovered a kind of workshop and a new piece of wood had been put in the floor as if to conceal something. this was removed and the brass recovered. The prisoner at once said' You have got me fair nod square and I'll give in." It was quite impossible to continue the case as there were a large number of other charges to be preferred against the prisoner, there being no less than four at present. A number of other articles were found on the premises which the police had good reason to believe bad been atolen.—Mr. Steel said that he had no objection to the case being remanded but he would like to make an application for bail. The prisoner was at present under medical trsatment for a bad leg The Chief Constable aaid he objected strongly to bail Ca the ground. that the charge was of a serious nature and the prisoner had denied the questions when put to him. The case was remanded until Thursday the magistrates declining to great bail.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Church.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church.

l'reaching at St. John's last Sunday forenoon. the Rex. W. Reid took for his subject' The hidden manna and the white stone." (Revelations H., 17c.). Both symbols, said the preacher, were borrowed from the Jewish ritual. The central thought was the converting of a mystery into a sacred intimacy, and transferring it from the priest to the whole body of believers. The call of Christianity was to the individual, and in those days they did well to remember that not only militarism, but industrial and social life, sought to stamp out the man's individuality. Christ singled out the soul, and it was led into God's presence, to partake of the sacred food, and to realize that it had a name all in God's purposes—a name determined not by what he bad achieved, but by what he would have done—in short, determined by the vision he had received.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was a fair attendance on Sunday, presided over by the Secretary, who made reference to the railway strike, and the joy it gave to all of them to hear that a" truce" had been arrived at by the disputants while the special Commission endrovoured to come to a good understanding. They were all thankful for the torn of events and hoped wise councils would prevail. Mr. Jolley gave the address upon "Evolution." We had for years experienced material evolution. In the old days requirements were few no there was but little reading of books. People had to put up with slow travel by road and trains. What used to take date of travel could now be accomplished in a few hours. But in the spiritual world of old, the thoughts of men were con- centrated upon a few things, and they were spiritually strong, now, however, men req.ii red a epirit of consecra- tion, a full reliance upon the grace of God to make them strong in this fast age of evolution. Men's minds; were not no fully concentrated upon the work of Christ, as their minds were occupied by 10 many things. Mr. Joynson read the lesson, the Chairman led the wayer and Mr. R. Wallington presided at the organ. One new member received a hearty welcana Prize Ilists were glbeu out.

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday School. Presentation to Secretary.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday School. Presentation to Secretary.

Mr. F. Light, secretary of Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday school, was on Sunday afternoon the recipient of a handsome presentation in recognition of his marriage which takes place to-day. The presentation was made at a special meeting of the teachers and members of the young ladies' and men's Bible classes at the close of the afternoon session. Mr. W. SILCO( IC, the superintendent, said he had known Mr. Light from his earliest childhood, and had watched him grow up amongst them. He had taught him as a scholar and now it gave Mot the highest degree of pleasure to present Itlir.Light, on behalf of the school in general, with a timepiece. He extended to Mr. Light the heartiest good wishes of all concerned that he might live to enjoy a long and happy married

life. The timepiece is encased in oak frame, and contains beautiful chimes and a striking gong of rich soand, and was supplied by Mr. J. Robinson, jeweller, &c., Bridge-street. In acknowledgement of the gift Mr. LIGHT said he had been connected with Sold-street school for over 20 3sars, and for many years had filled the office of secretary. For several years it had been a delight to work wily the teachers and officers on account of the good feeling that existed in their midst. He should always try to do his best for the welfare of the school. Mr. J. C. HOLLAND voiced the good wishes of his men's class to Mr. Light, and trusted that he would be happy in his new surroundings. Miss MILLS expressed the best wishes of the young ladies for Mr. Light's happiness sod that of his bride- elect. Later in the afternoon Mr. Light was the recipient of a case of carvers subscribed to by the members of his Sunday morning clan of young men. The presents lion was made by Mr. R. J. Nolte on behalf of the class adding their congratulations and good wishes for his future welfare.

Rey. F. W. Kernick and the Lessons of the Railway Strike. The Rev. F. W. Kernick preaching at Rewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Sunday evening, said they found that the greatest joy had always sprung up in the human heart. We talked about the dark ages--and they Were dark enough, for then men's reasons could hardly give any account of divine things at all. They missed their way in almost every possible way,' ut they pro- duced the most beautiful hymns we tad. When all I was dark to reason the heart found in God its home. I Continuing, he said that all the Earlier Christians recognised that they were only here on a pilgrimage and the greatest ideal we could have was that we should he spiritually alive and enter into the great heritage of those who had gone before us. And it seemed to him that if the recent railway strike were to mean anything to us it ought to call us to a greater sense of responsibility, to greater ideals of human life and human righteousness. Had not there been a kind of materialism amongst us that had hardened nor hearts ? One knew perfectly well that business life was never so strained as it was to-day and a great deal of the thirst for pleasure was accounted for by that. But at the same time there was a feeling of moral indifference and some of the old watchwords had passed out. If that were so, there wasat any rate a clear call to es. That morning someone said to him that "No property is safe while moo received such a mere pittance." He was not con- cerned with property, bat he could say this, that no great religious church, religious ideal or great moral enthusiasm was safe while many of us went up and down the country enjoying greater freedom than others—while there were thme to whom not only the , privileges of civilisation but the very necessaries of life were denied. We hal got to look away from our interests to a greater ideal for others. There must be a love for Christ who died not for particular classes, ; but for every man.

Welsh Disestablishment. The Prime Minister has at length dellnitely pledged the Government (says the' Parish Church Magazine,") to pass through the House of Commons next year a Bill to disestablish and disendow the Church in Wales, though this grave national question was not before the electors at either of the general elections last year. The magazine contains copies of letters from the Arch- bishops of Canterbury and York commending 1 the work of the Central Church Committee for Defence and Instruction. The Archbishop of Canterbury writes —"We: must unhesitatingly support our Welsh brethren in the impending struggle, because we believe that the retention of ths solemn trust and special responsibility which is theirs is a bounden duty, and because we also believe that the principles for I% hich we contend are righteous and are of incalculable and enduring benefit to the whole people of the land."

div.head: Rev. W Bracecamp and Political and Industrial Unrest.
div.p: Rev. W Bracecamp and Political and Industrial Unrest.

The Vicar of St. Paul's (the Rev. W. Braceoamp), preaching on Sunday morning, took for his test I. Samuel, xii., 25 If ye still do wickedly, ye shall be consumed, both ye and your King." The rev, gentleman lathe course of his remarks said that he felt grievously disappointed that St. Paul's Church was large enough to hold the people who were anxious to be present. Surely every parson who exiled himself a Coristial ought to have been there that morning to intercede with God on behalf of the terrible trouble. It only went to prove the great indifference of the mass of mankind to God and His claims. When were we to learn wisdom ? He further stated that be ventured to predict that men hereafter would look back upon the rear 1911 as one of the great landma-ks of hnglish history. A fortnight since, saw, if not the final, at any rate the decisive moment of battl.., which had been waged Mace 1215 ekes the Church united with the Lords to limit the power of the Crown. Wb ether they agreed with the party of change ur not, they could not deny that a change had taken place of such great magnitude, that its end could hardly le foreseen. In 1532 the power of the Loads was limited as the rower of the Crown six centuries before, and the voice of the people was first heard in any effective way. And now the will of the people was absolutely supreme in the State. The democratic ideal had triumphed. But the triumph of democracy need by no meats be identical with the triumph of righteousness, for if they trusted in the new state of things and trusted no more in God, why then ".` Demos shall go the way of Saul, ye shall be destroyed, ye and your new order, as of old was Is-eel and Israel's God-given King." What bad happened in the political world had been reflected in the social and economical upheaval. The strike was a wonderful manifestation, to suite perhaps an unwelcome revelation, of the power of organised labour. The men had used their rower to secure changes which it was impossible to consider other than just, but the same power could have been used, and might yet be used, to back exorbitant claims, and wrest from the employers extravagant concessions. What the res3lt would be. God alone knew, and He soull determine. The power was undoubtedly with the people. Mistakes would be made no doubt, but the making of mistakes no more invalidated the justice of • cause than it degraded the character of an individual. One thing abuse did that,—the ignoring of all that maker] for good and God, for moral ideal and for ripteousness, for courtesy and consideration. If these things were neglected, there was but one conclusion for " if ye do wickedly, ye shall be destroyed, ye and your people," even Re was Israel of old, and her God-given King. What was the Church to do as she saw

the power of the people prevailing ? Great masses of them repudiated her claims, many were actively hostile, most were utterly indifferent, and there only needed the tiny spark to kindle the indifference into a great flume of unreasoning and bitter opposition. What had they done for the direction and discipline of those vest forces? It had they done to help the people to save them from their sins, and themselves, no lass than from all those cruel conditions of life and labour by which the children of His brothers and His sisters had been strained, starved and stunted ? If they had done evil or failed to make use of their privileges and opportunities, then no amount of outward service, no parade of good intentions would avert the inevitable end of those things which was death.

div.head: HATTON SHOW.
div.p: HATTON SHOW.
PRETTY VILLAGE EXHIBITION.

Where the HaVon Amateur Horticultural Society triumphs over many similar village organisations is in malting the best use of the faculty of observation, as wan again evident at the 17th annual show held in the prettily situated grounds of Mr. James Parr on Saturday last. The members recognise that for such a society to arouse and warrant the enthusiasm of almost every inhabitant they must cater for all sections of the community. Everything that is rurally pro- duced has to be found a place in the show. If the people cultivate ft avers let them exhibit them; if they raise vegetables let them also be shown ; if it be fruit, window plants, poultry or anything else let them be put where the visitors may see and admire and the Pidges adjudicate. On Saturday all the sections afforded satisfac' ion. Three huge tents were requisi- tioned, and in these the various exhibits were dis- criminately arranged. The premier tent, is which the flowers and fruit and plants were stored, presented a picturesque scene, and when gilded with bright sunshine the eff,ct was even enhanced. There were plenty of flowers, though had the summer not been so hot there would have been many more. 'f he vases of sweet peas possessed their perennial charm, and the roses in their delightful freshness, gave of a delicious scent. As to the vegetable section it may be remarked that, strangely enough, considering that they require a lot of moisture, the marrows displayed were the best ever staged at this show. They were particularly robust and no little time was spent by visitors in admiring them. The parsnips were also good and some of those shown by Mr T Wilkinson were no less than two feet long. Beetroots were also of a credit- able quality, but the carrots were lather inferior to those r f other years. In the farmers' classes splendid mangolds and turnips, as well as corn, were much in evidence Both cooking and desert apples were of a grand St indard and the plums were very tempting, combining ample ja'ce with sufficient firmness. • Groupe of plants, were forwarded by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Mr T II Lyn, and Mr F Bought m. During the afternoon and evening the Walton Band discoursed pleasing selections, the young people 'engaging in dancing. Thome were also the usual !attractions which one associates with the fair ground.

div.head: OPENING CEREMONY.
div.p: OPENING CEREMONY.

A large number of people assembled for the open- ing ceremony, presided over by the Rev and Hon F Cross. Mrs T H Lyon declared the show open, and amongst those present were Mr and Mrs R I Wynne Jones, Mr and Mrs John E Seeker, Mrs Shepherd Cross, Miss Bessie Dutton, Mrs John White, Mr lid Wrst, Colonel and Mns Lyon, Lady Denies, Mrs Usher, I Miss McDonald, Miss Stewart, Lady Colquhoun, Mrs Lee Jones, Colonel Ramsden, Colonel Spedding, Rev W S Adams, Rev T W Sturges and Mr J E Hatton (Hon. Secretary) The Chairman said that was a time of many anniversaries, especi lily in the line of shows and sport. Many thought about the 12th August, many about the Ist Sep'ember, and many thought about the Walton and Stockton Heath shows. There they were thinking about Hatton show; they bad come to revisit their old friend, that exhib lion of fruit, vegetables, flowers and poultry. When they saw old friends from time to time they did not always expect to see them in the same state— sometimes they were in fuller and more prosperous circumstances, and sometimes they bad less favourable years. And so it might be they would find that this year the rxhibition was not in some respects as good as last year, while it was in others. In con- clusion, he expressed the thanks of the meeting to Mr and Mrs. James Parr for granting the use of the beautiful field for the show. (Applause). Prior to declaring the show open, Mrs. Lyon . . . . .
delivered a neat speech. She began by referrit. ig to the fact that it was seven years since

she was there be'ore, when the -society was in the midst of a promising youth. It was then in a flourishing condition, and had since grown very rapidly. Applause). There bad been an important development in the poultry section, though it was disappointing to find that there were 40 entries less than last year. In this she a as a little concerned, for what with wars and rumours of wars within and without our land and the railway strike, it behoved them to look to their food supplies. And, therefore, the rearing of poultry would serve a useful purpose, not only as a pastime but it was a capital adjunct to the food supplies. Poultry could be reared very profitably and she thought the question demanded urgent c onsideration. (Applauee). In conclusion Mrs. Lyon referred to the vegetibles which Isere displayed and also to tbe flowers mention- ing that the latter were always a source of pleasure to everybody. (Applause.) In proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Lyon, Mr. R. L Wynne Jones said that the idea of a man opening a flower show was simply unthinkable, for they always associated with flowers, gentleness and loveableness. They could hardly think of a Iran as being loveable. (Lnughter ) A man might properly open a horse show—and possibly a donkey show. (Laughter.) That was about all he was good for. (Reheived laughter.) They were all very glad to have Mrs. Lyon with them ag lin and he could assure them that, she was always willing to assist a venture of that kind (Applause.) Mr. Ditchfield seconded and the motion was agreed to. On the proposition of Mr. James Warburton seconded by Mr. Richard Warburton a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. James Parr for kindly lending the society the field for the show. Mr. Wright in proposing a motion thanking the judges said they had really fine men, who carried' out their duties in a very able and impartial manner. (Applause.) On being seconded by Mr Seeker, the motion etas carried. The Rev T W Sturges (judge of the poultry section) ill response said that the reason there were not as many poultry as last year was because the weather had not been as favourable. The young pullets were not very much exhibited because the hot weather had been against their progress. And the reason for the older birds being fewer in number was because the weather had caused them to moult earlier than usual. (Hear, hear.) He was sorry that the poultry were not exhibited in wire pens as in former years, but they had been delayed in transit owing to the railway sti ike. However, they looked very respectable in the hampers with the wire in front. (Hear, hear.) Evidently even the poultry bad been hampered by the strike. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Newton replying on behalf of the agricultural section, spoke in terms favourable to the epiality of the produce irrespective of the weather. A vote of thanks was also accorded to the secretary and treasurer on the proposition of Mr. Berry, seconded by Mr. Done and a similar resolution was passed to the Hon. and Rev. C. F. Cross for acting as president of the Society. The judges were as follows :—Farmers' prcdttce, Messrs John R Newton, Warburton, and Samuel Davies, Heathy; cottagers' gardens and produce. div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST,
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST,

" GREAT STRIKE." A junior on the staff of the newspaper in connection with which I entered upon my career began with this portentous beading a paragraph reporting how a man engaged in road repairing had seriously injured his big ta by accidentally dealing it a tremendous blow with a mattock which he was using in digging up the surface. I could not help wondering how that genius would have behaved in relation to the unprecedented railway war which was declared just over a week ago, and which has so continued to absorb public attention that I aced not apologise for employing it as a peg on which to hang two or three items. ENGINE DRIVERS AND THEIR WORK, , Shortly after the outbreak of the unparalleled strike I had the advantage of a lengthy conversation with an official of importance in the goods department of one of the great companies involved, and tie declared that to travel by rail in such circumstances WWI really very dangerous. It was absurd to suppose that any but experienced railway men could work the system without grave risk. The comparatively few men who had been induced to assume charge of trains did not know the roads over which they had undertaken to drive, and anyone who understood the situation knew that it svas fraught with peril. In normal conditions the strain upon a skilled locomotive driver is exceed- ingly heavy. A while ago, one such stated that he could recollect when there were some :X) signals to be nnoted between Manchester and Liverpool, whereas ow there are hundreds occurring in a forty minutes run between the two points indicated. THE POINTSSIAN. After all, as everybody knows, safe and efficient railway service depends upon the man in the cabin, and at the critical stage to which I have referred he was for the most part elsewhere. As an expert writing in the " Millgate Monthly " some time ago ' expressed it, whether it be inborn or acquired, the signalman controlling the heavy traffic on a c-owded double, or p ssibly quadruple line, including double sets of signals, up and down, or extensive shunting to work at a big goods station, has a responsibility which most men would be inclined to escape. Much has from time to time been said and written in praise of the block system, and of course I agree with it in the main ; but, as the authority I have quilted pro. ceeded to point out, its adequate working depends on fallible human beings stationed in a series of cabins along the length of the line. And even when the signalman has ttantunitted the telegraphic communi- cations into signals, the latter have to to be noticed and interpreted correctly by fal ible engine drivers for the stopping and starting of trains at critical moments, upon which the safety of the passengers depends. Which all goes to bear out the proposition with which ws started. THE STATIONMASTER. The duties of this functionary are indeed legion. I Even when all is well on the line his day's work leaves him few moments for leisure. As I remember Mr. J. Thornton Burge showing in the "Railway Magazine," perhaps two or three years ago, at a small station the station-master personally superintends the work of every man, and where the staff is limited, has to do a large proportion himself. So, at wayside country stations the station-master often has to assist in loading cattle, to push waggons, and in some cases to clean pottione of his station in addition to doing the general office work and keeping the accounts. During the strike, these officials have had to do that sort of thing at more import. in to Yorkshire, stations. Travelling frcon Manchester Yorkshire, I found that at Rochdale the only members of the staff remaining for the performance of the various tanks demanded of the dozens of men ordinarily at work there were the stationmaster and a goods yard foreman. Those who remained at their posts did their best ; but I was reminded of Professor Palby's statement that in 1881, in which year the first train left Euston for Carlisle, barrelling by way of Rugby, Leicester, York, and Newcastle, the journey occupied 151 hours.

HOLIDAY-MAKERS ON THE ROAD. To resume my narrative. I took occasion to alight at Rochdale for a pop visit to some friends there. It was their holiday week, and being unable to go by train satisfactorily, they had decided to start by road. They happened to be going my way, so we and several others like-minded set forth by tram car. By changing at Littleborough (near Hollingvrorth Lake. the " Weaver's Seaport ") we obtained a lift as far as Summit, the eastern terminus on the Rochdale Corporation's system. Thence we tramped a couple of miles or so, to the western extremity of Todmorden's motor bus route, riding from that point to a place called Sandhed, down the Calder Valley. Another , fairly still walk brought us to Hebden Bridge, which I is connect, d by electric car with the great towns of Yorkshire. Coming in the opposite direction were troops of returning holiday folk. I encountered one party who had left Scarborough early in the morning, and the day was by that time well advanced. They had just managed to hire a carriage to convey them to their destination about nine miles farther on ; but others were glad of help from passing carters. On , the following day I myself rode nearly a dozen miles I on a brewers' motor lorry laden with beer. The rail- way stations, with their accumulated dust, stopped clocks, and deserted appearance, brought to min the days of my childhood, when I revelled in such stories as that of the "Sleeping Beauty." CAMPING OUT. I found that some of my acquaintances in East Lancashire' disappointed as to their intended holidays further afield, had arranged to camp out on the neigh- bouring hillsides. Says one who tried it some years ago :—Did you ever try camping-out? Have you ever struggled to make tea with some triple-patented kettle that belied its claims, tried to fire sticks that would not burn, worried about water that would not boil, amid a wind that upset the crockery and waltzed away with all that was portable? Oh, it's great fun —after the event, when you are reciting your experi- ences. Personally, I have retired from the business. All discomforts notwithstanding, I recognise that the outdoor life is the highway to health, and I sometimes regret that the years that have flown over me prevent my participation in its joys. I dare say I have previously mentioned that I have often spent a week or so in volunteer encampments in the old days, and have thus had memorable experiences at Saari) 'rough, Whitby, Lytham, and elsewhere ; and now-a-days anybody may indulge in that sort of holiday, for many com- panies have been formed to cater for visitors from the towns who wish to spenot a few days—nights, to be precise - under canvas. To my mind a ' more excel- lent way " is to hire the necessary equipment from a local tradesman wh:se advertisement appears on the front page of this paper, and along with two or three I chums to pitch one's solitary tent by some pleasant stream, and for the time lead an absolutely free life, rocky mountain style. As a journalistic friend of mine who has indulged in it observes, you can have your meals when you like, and what you like; you are disturbed in nowise by the t. o early riving of campers, or the too late retiring to rest. To be yore as he is bound to admit, the solitary method has corresponding disadvantages, for provisions are to be I hauled up from town, often carried 1 ng dis'ances over the fields, and a lot of time is consumed in fire- , lighting, especially in wet weather, in cooking, and a strange lot of sundries only realised on trial. No doubt in many ewes this will be thought to lend charm to the life. So (continues my authority) it will for those who have not any distinct sport or work in view. But to the angler, the sportsman, botanist, geologist, climber and men of that ilk, camp life will appear more convenient, though, of course, it entails being thrown with all con- ditions of men. But why not compromise? As my old colleague points out, a separate tent could be secured, and, if preferred, pitched outside the regular camp, or on payment of additional charges, on private ground, meals ordered as required, and all catering passed over to those in charge of the camp. Such camps are generally placed within easy reach of attractions in the way of fishing, shooting, touring, and., the charges are comparatively sma'l, living the free life in one of them comes in very cc ncmically. TRAMCAR JAUNTS. It strikes me that what happened through the mid- way strike as briefly indicated 111,3113 will base served to popularise holiday making by tramcar. As at least one has remarked, it is an easy and exhilarating way of taking the air, and may well become the poor man's way of motoring. in the future. Jr has, moreover, advantages over motoring in the fact that it is cheap, and is free from many of the dangers incidental to motor t,uring on busy country highways. There are other considerations to which attention has now sod again been directed. For example All on a tramcar are on an equality ; there is no distinction of classes: the artizan who pays his penny or Ina twopence is on a par with the rich man, and this rubbing of shoulders is destiuod to have a beneficial effect all round. tends to elim;nate the aloofness which is fostered by railway travelling, and leads to an exchange of ideas which, to anyone of observing turn of mind, is most interesting. Excepting the ten little gaps which,as I have already shown, cccar on the border of the two counties and even these are not so wide on Wednes- day awl Saturday afternoons, when the Todmorden motor 'bus service is extended in each direction—l have found it possible thus to cover almost the entire distance from Liverpool to Leeds. Besides, as one of many writers on the subject has remarked, if one desires to linger in any particular place there are plenty of good hotels available. Apart from the novelty of the trip, there is a sense of freedom and independence about it that one does not experience on a train journey. In the latter case one is whirled from place to place without very much opportunity t f studying the country passed through, or of becoming familiar with the habits and characteristics of the peop'e. A long tram ride is an excellent way of getting an insight into the character of the people in the various towns and country places. The result of observation teaches one that the no-called rough Laccashire artisan is sot half so bad as he is painted. Ile is genial and obliging, always ready to impart information ; and, in fact, never tires of dwelling upon the wonders of his own particular locali,y. A SUPPLEMENTARY NOTE.

I have found it difficult to get rid of the train of reflections induced by the great railway strike, but I must vigorously set aside certain further matters suggested by what I have just wrttten. 'Uncle Caiefs " last week's strry respecting the barrel of russet apples brought to my mind a rather pathetic incident which came under my notice a while agn. A small shopkeeper whose place I pass almost daily is evidently in the habit of dealing out to the slum children in the district snob fruit as has become unsaleable through over-ripeness. Apparently the youngsters imagine that this stuff, fit only tor the manure heap, is specially imported for their delectation by a benevolent tradesmen wealthy beyond the dreams of avarice, for on the occasion in question I overheard one little chap anxiously enquiring of him if his 'rotten apples had come !" METHODIST MINISTERIAL CHANGES.

As will be perceived from an advertisement in this issue of the " Examiner" the nee ly-appointed ministers are t 3 be publicly welcomed at a circuit meeting in the bid-street Wesleyan Church on September 7th. The new Methodist year begins with next month. As a note-writer with whom I worked for years on a Halifax newspaper remarked while I was there, the first Sunday in new circuits must be a peculiar one for ministers and their families. Usually, the congregations are above the average in numbers, and all eyes are turned t wards the pulpit as the minister enters for the first time. Ile Gels conscious that he is being " weighed in the balance" by his people, who have formed various ideas as to what he will be like ; some hoping that he will be young and bright, some that be will be tall and commanding in appearance ; while there are others whose ideal is a " little minister," after the style of J. M. Barrie's ; another section hope he will be clean shaven—because such always" look so nice—and a few who are deaf are chiefly concerned about his voice. Will he speak up ? The Sunday that so shortly is to be will settle the imaginations and anxieties of many. And in the meanwhile let us think sympathetically of the anxious men preparing the discourses which will go far to make or mar them in their new circuits— for, a ith the pt eacher, first impres-- lions count for much.

The old-world town of Shrewsbury was inundated with visitors lrom all parts on Wednesday and Thursday, when the annual floral fOte—the greatest event of its kind in the Kingdom, was held. Com- mencing in 1875, the show has been held yearly in the beautiful park known as " Tne Quarry,' which the Shrewsbury Corporation have lent free to the Floral Society. The prowess of the Bite 311. Ce its inception has been phenomenal, statistics showing that with almost every year making a record above the previous one, the takings rcse from .C... 791 12s. in 1875 to S-5,756 15s. 3d. last year. That the present year should make a financial record could hardly be expected owing to the handicap it has suffered from strikes and other causes, which prevented many intending entrants from the far North and other districts from coming forward with their exhibits. This year's fete was also especially handicapped by the sudden and unexpected death of the chairman (Colonel Cresswell Peele) on Saturday last. div.head: STRIKE SETTLED.
div.p: THE STRIKE SETTLED.

The great Railway Strike has ended. The negotiations which had been proceeding at the Board of Trade have resulted in the men's representatives accepting the terms offered them by Mr. Asquith, viz., a Special Commission of Inquiry to sit at once to consider the demands of all classes of railway servants. The announcement of the settlement was received with relief all over the country by strikers and public alike. Our Picture a Policeman and soldier congratulating one another.

div.head: SERIOUS RIOTS AT LLANELLY.
div.p: SERIOUS RIOTS AT LLANELLY.

Terrible scenes were witnessed on Saturday evening at Llanelly, South Wales, several' people being killed and many injured. A train was storped by the strikers, and this led to a serious collision with the police. Soldiers were called up, and, after the Riot Act had been read, opened fire on the mob, which unfortunately causeA the death of two Innocent men. The crowds then turned their attention to the town, and several shops were looted. Under cover of darkness the railway gcods-sheds wore pillaged and set on fire. The flames finally reached some ammunition, and there was an explosion, which resulted in many being killed and injured. Our picture shows the shop of Mr. Thomas Jones, LP., which was looted.

div.head: Examiner Saturday, August 26, 1911.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, August 26, 1911.
FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, M.P.
THE GREAT RAILWAY STRIKE.

Events fofinVenCh-niti-e.r.Wiiii sudden and sometimes startling development in such a corflict as this railway strike, so that by the time these lines appear in print the situation may have completely changed. At the time I write the strike has paralysed the railway service of the country, the public is suffering enormous inconvenience, the food supply of the people is seriously threatened, and the railway directors refuse to meet the repre- sentatives of the four unions of railway ser- vants are willing and anxious toimeet them.

div.head: CAUSE OF DISCONTENT.
div.p: CAUSE OF DISCONTENT.

The cause of this trouble is not to be found in anything new which has come about in the last few weeks, although certain recent' events in the industrial world have no doubt helped to bring the disaffection among the railway workers to a head. The " settle- ment " which was made four years ago when a railway strike was threatened has done nothing to allay the discontent then existing, but on the contrary has increased it very considerably,. It is notorious that the rail- way men have serious grounds of complaint about their conditions of employment. Their wages are low and their hours are long. The average wage was never very high, and according to the Board of Trade figures, which do not deal with any year later than 1909, the average weekly wage in that year of the men employed in the coaching, goods, locomotive and engineer's departments was 255. 10IAd., which is lower than the average in 1906 and only d. a week higher than in 1899. In the meantime the cost of living has risen very considerably. According to the latest Board of Trade figures the wholesale prices of the articles on which the cost of living is based have risen since 1896 by about 22 per cent.

Rut the grievances of the men in regard to wages become more apparent when we consider how that average of 255. 10W. is made up. Just about 40 per cent, of the men are paid less than 20s. a week. All but 11 per cent are below 303. These facts are appalling. Much of the work of the railway men is of the most responsible character. There are railway guards and signal men working for about a pound a week. There are men working the signals in very important boxes for about 265. a week. On the alertness, skill, judgment, sobriety, and intelligence of these men the lives of the travelling public depend. The average wage of signalmen is only 235. ld. a week. Goods porters, cleaners, passenger porters all come in the class with less than a pound a week, the average wage of the passenger porter being 17s. sd. The normal working day of the railway man is twelve hours, and it is only when more than that number of hours are worked that an entry of excessive hours has to be made. A PATHETIC STRUGGLE. _

Surely it doesn't require any rhetoric to enforce such facts as these. The railway men are as respectable and thrifty a body of working men as there are in the country. It is one of the pathetic things about our social conditions that this great body of men should manage to keep themselves so respectable on the wages they receive. It means that there is a vast amount of unseen pinching somewhere to keep up appearances, and that struggle has been getting harder every year as the purchasing power of the wage has been declining. THE ROOT OF THE TROUBLE.

The root of the conflict is in the refusal of the railway companies to acknowledge the men's societies and to negotiate with their representatives. The railway directors take up the position long ago abandoned by all the great commercial employers of the country, that they will not recognise any trade union among their employers, but will only deal with their men as servants of the company. This attitude on the part of the railway directors and managers explains a great deal. It shows the kind of men they are,and indicates their general attitude of mind to modern labour aspirations. The unions of railway men number about 100,000 men, and yet the managers will not meet the officials elected by these men to represent their views. It ought to be mentioned that there is one railway which is a solitary exception, namely the North Eastern, which for many years has recognised the men's unions and negotiated with their officials to the advantage of both sides. TO THE MEN'S CREDIT.

The " Agreement " which was forced upon the men by the Board of Trade four years ago, although it was signed by the officials of men's unions did not recognise the unions. It was in fact a signing away by the trade union officials of their rights to represent , the men. It is pretty well known now that that" Agreement "was forced upon the men practically at the point of the bayonet. They were given a few minutes to sign it and were not even allowed to leave the room at the Board of Trade to consider it. It was universally condemned by the men, and it should be remembered to their credit now that though the men were never consulted about it, though they were never given any choice in the matter, that though they universally disapproved of it, they loyally set to work to make the best of it, and for two or three years did endeavour to use it as an instrument for redress of their grievances. THE EMPL'IYERS' TACTICS.

But on the other hand, the employers, who also had been compelled to accept the Agree- ment against their wishes (it is said under a threat that if it was not accepted the Government would introduce legislation to reduce hours and to increase the Board of Trade Control), have done everything they could to make the Agreement a failure. They hesitated to set up the Boards, and put every possible obstacle in the way of their smooth and expeditious working. It was over a year after the Agreement was made before the first Award was given, and then the corn- pany4tet their own interpretation upon many of the points, and in other ways tried to evade concessions.

That Board of Trade " Agreement " was supposed to provide the means of dealing with grievances which at the time were so serious that the men had made up their minds to strike if they did not have immedi- ate attention. And instead of something practical and substantial the men were given an agreement they didn't want and which has proved by experience cannot serve their purpose. The railway directors gained in a threefold sense. They avoided-legisla- tion, they got a Conciliation Scheme which was worthless, and they got the union (which they refused to recognise), bound hand and foot as they thought for seven years. Tarn quite prepared to admit all that may be said about thel sacredness of a bind- ing Agreement, but when one party to it deliberately tries to make it useless the other party justified in withdrawing from it. THE BOARD OF TRADE AT FAULT.
Times without number during the last four years the Boar(' of Trade has been

appealed to about the unsatisfactory working of the Agreement, but they have done nothing to mend matters, and there is a good deal of the responsibility for this appalling strike resting at their door. Four years ago they forced the unions to accept an agreement which was offensive and useless, and up to the present they have simply sheltered themselves behind this Agreement, evidently never thinking that the men would become so exasperated as to throw it to the winds. Up to the last moment the Government might have prevented the strike. The men's leaders were the most anxious for peace. If the Board of Trade had made any attempt to bring the railway directors and the men's officials together there probably never would have been a strike. But the Government never Astsked the railway companies to meet the men. It would have been very little for the Board of Trade to do to point out to the directors that the Government recognised trade unions in all their departments, and that it was a piece of out-of-date autocracy for the directors to take up such a high- handed attitude. The Government, up to the time of the strike being declared,believed that the men could be terrorised by menace and threat, and it was only after they found the strike had actually been declared that they began to show anxiety to consider the matter from the men's point of view. MEN'S LEADERS' POSITION.

The men's leaders wore fully conscious of the seriousness of their action when they declared the strike. They did not want a strike. But the unyielding attitude of the companies and the want of sympathy from the Government left them no choice. It has been pointed out in the newspapers, and the statement is quite accurate, that the way in which the offer of a Royal Commission was made to the men was such as to make it impossible for the men to consider it. The strike is in reality a fight for the recognition of trade unionism. The directors take up the old attitude that they are not going to have any outside interference with the management of their affairs. But any large employer who takes up that attitude to-day must be taken in hand by the State and given to understand that he has duties and responsibilities to others, and that he must fall into line with enlightened employers of labour. If the railway directors will meet the men's representatives the strike would be settled at once. If they had done so last week there never would have been a strike. The men are fighting for the elementary rights of combination, but they are entitled to the sympathy of all friends of freedom. I am no advocate or supporter of strikes, as every reader of this journal knows, but in this case the men could not have kept their self-respect if they had not asserted them- selves in the only way left to them.

div.head: CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conductul by UNCLE CALEB. eAd-N,A,v3
div.p: CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conductul by UNCLE CALEB. eAd-N,A,v3
HOW SPIDERS WORK.

The spider is a canny creature and shows a lot of wisdom. Of course, he has reason to be for he has many enemies. When the spider goes for a walk he must look sharply to right and left. A biro will suddenly swallow him or a wasp may kill him. And he must have skill for the building of his nest and web. Watch him at work. The spider's silk, with which he makes his beau- tiful web, is like a piece of your mother's sewing silk—it is made of a lot of very fine strands. And in what a wonderful way the spider spins his web from bush to bush I He throws out a silken thread, and the wind carries it to a leaf where it sticks, then he walks carefully across the thread. To make his tight rone stronger, he pulls the thread with his little claws, as sailors tug at the sail ropes, and fastens it with great care; round and round he goes until the splendid web is made, and, if the wind is blowing, he fastens tiny pieces of stick to the web lest it should blow away. A spider often stretches a thrsad from the web to his home so that when any creature is caught in the web he feels the web shake, and is able to run out to see what has happened.

Spiders are very clever. If you touch a green one he will double up his little legs and fall from the place where you saw him. If you did not notice that he was hanging from his thread, you would perhaps say: "It is only a bit of green leaf." There is a brown spider that does the same thing, , hoping to be taken for a brown leaf. The underground spider makes her house by digging a hole in the ground. She scratches it up with her front legs and carries out the tiny lumps of earth until there is a nice long hole. She lines this with fine silk, which she weaves herself, then makes a little door of leaves and sticks woven together with her silk and fastens it on with a silken hinge. This is a safe, warm home for the baby-spiders, and if the mother hears some dangerous creature trying to get in she holds on to the door with all her might, and the children run to the other end of the house. The spider children are very industrious ; they amuse themselves by making tiny houses just like the one their mother has made so that when they grow up they can make safe, warm houses for their own children.

Some spiders live under the water in little balls made of their own silk; some live under the ground, and others live in trees or in our houses. There are big and little spiders, of wany different colours, and all are equally skilful in their work. Indeed there is no member of the spider tribe but is a marvel in its instincts and its powers. THIS WEEK'S STORY. HOW THE SCHOLAR SCORED.

' Inspectors sometimes try to be clever and catch the scholars, but sometimes the boy or girl scores. ' During a recent examination in the Old Testament the following question was asked, 'What language did nalaam's ass speak ?" After a moment of thought, a smile flashed across the boy's face, and he wrote his answer, " Ass-yrian." ARE YOIJ DOING YOI'R SHARE? There's a great deal of love on this earth. Are you getting your share? There are laughter and music and mirth. Are you getting your share ? There are rya here a-plenty be three-score or twenty ; The world's fell of blissos, Like kind deeds and kisses, And sunshine and roses to spare ; But tell me to thy, As you travel your way, • Are you getting your shake ? There are deeds to do on this earth. Are you doing your share ? There are tasks that your best are all worth. Are you doing your share? There are kind words to use, Whether young man or gray , And kind deeds to dc, 0, the world looks to you To lessen the burdene of care ; Brit tell me to-day, Aa you travel tour way, Are you doing your share ?
