div.head: ACTON AND DORFOLD. – A TYPICAL PIECE OF CHESHIRE.
div.p: ACTON AND DORFOLD. - A TYPICAL PIECE OF CHESHIRE.

Upon a summer day last year we ran over a typical bit of Cheshire roadway from Tarporley to Nantwich—a piece typical in its beauties, its history, its superstitions, its buildings, and for the reader who cares to follow us either in imagination or reality we will serve up the fragments that are freshest in memory.

TARPOiLEY AND THE CHESHIRE HUNT. Tarporley enjoys the quiet of a place that lies two miles from a railway, yet it is sufficiently up-to-date, and if cleanliness and Cheshire air are good for aught it should be a happy place to live in.
There is no time to explore the church, but we give ourselves a moment to linger over two buildings that attract us in the Main street. One is the Old Swan and the other the Manor House.

This latter stands at the end of the street and tells the passer-by that " Ralph Done Esquyer the lorde of this place was an eade to this building," and bears the date 1586. More curious are the letters cut on another beam which say that " Feneys quoth John Newsome bathe kept hys promes just in building of thys howse in August 1586." Concerning Feneys and his promise we defer enquiry for the present. The Old Swan is a fine sample of a coach- ing inn that flavours of Pickwickian days and sets one a-looking for the farm of

William belonged to the old Cheshire family of Mainwarings and succeeded to part of the estates in 1364. Like many another Englishman of the period he seems to have had no school save the camp, and served during the long and harrassing wars with France.

In 1393, though stricken in years, we find him still ready to buckle on armour at the call of his King and he settles his affairs and ' makes his will before departing for Guienno Hitherto this rough man of the field has paid little tribute to the church, but now he makes amends. Feeling the burden of the , rough years that lie behind him, he arranges in his will that for seven years after his death a chantry-priest shall say prayers for his soul. Like the rest of his generatiqp, he bslieved that sins could be expiated b 7 the invocation of saints through the medium of an interceding priest; and so a chapel must be built and prayers are to be said through iseven years.

Not 'only 80, but he gave to the church a most precious relic—a fragment of the true Cross, long preserved in wax. This relic, it may be assumed, had been brought from Spain on the occasion of some military ex ledition. At St. Salvador's, Oveida, there wa 3 treasured, it was 'said, the miraculous arl, which Philip, the Bishop of Jerusalem, had brought away when the Holy City was besieged by the Persian King. This relic had found a resting place in Spain and was said to contain an incredible number of other relics. These, enshrined in gold and silver and ivory caskets, were the wonder of Christendom, and were sung of by poets in exalted verse.
The relict and the written works of saints Toledo's treasure prized beyond All wealth, their living and their dead remain,
Among the treasures thus preserved were a part of the true Cross and of the Crown of Thorns, a part of Elijah's mantle and a sandal of St. Peter.
By what process Sir William got the

div.head: ;HURCH
div.p: ;HURCH
ACTON
Sam Weller. It is the meeting place of the Cheshire Hunt and in a large room over the stables the gentlemen of Cheshire meet to drink their annual toast.

Curiously enough we lighted the other week upon the old hunt-song that fills the air at this great event. It breathes a healthy contempt for all who indulge in any sport save foxhunting, being especially rough upon the pheasant shooter. We hold in abhorrence a'l vulpicid 3 knave, With their guns and their traps and their velveteen
slaves—; They may feed their int Omits ieta, their fer-s destroy, And mar the prima sport they themselves can't enjoy. . . . . .

Pheasant shooters might retort with some- thing equally nasty, and plain and merciful folks like us might call down plagues on both. But it is no use. Are not these fox- torturers the county gentlemen?
fragment of the Cross we do not inquire. Enough that it gave lustre to Acton and brought the devout from far and near to worship at the shrine.
The chantry chapel still stands where they pleaded for Sir William's soul, but the relic has long since travelled afar. ".A PICTURE IN ALABASTER."

, In another clause of the will of 1393 the aged warrior requires that he shall be buried in Acton Church and that his' picture in alabaster shall cover his tomb." He died in 1399, and they placed over him a richly canopied memorial adorned with heraldic shields and mounted with the sculptured crest of the family. _ .

Right happily lid the sculptor carry out the request. The "picture in alabaster" represents him at full length and habited in plate armour. With hands raised in supplication the figure must have been beautiful indeed when it left the sculptor's hands five centuries ago.

But the centuries have not dealt very kindly with it and the vulgar have disfigured it with scratchings. By a bad arrangement the school boys were placed here during service and have helped the pitiful process of ruin by scratching their initials. A CRUSADING STORY. The crest that surmounts it has the Main- Waring sign of an ass's head, and thereby hangs a tale.

During the wars of the Crusaders one of the family had his horse killed under him. Finding an ass at hand he mounted crying " Devant Si je puis " which is Norman- French for" Forward if I can " ; and from that distant day until now the crest and motto have kept the event in memory. One suspects, however, that the crest has not always inspired pride, and in this case the sculptor has made the ass as much like a horse as he could. Possibly he thought that people not versed in history might make wrong inferences. DORFOLD HALL. We are loth to leave the old church and only consent to depart by the expedient of promising ourselves another visit. We come now to the sweet and lordly hall of Dorfold, the old seat of the Wilbrahams, but now inhabited by a branch of the Tollemache family. A mere vagrant cyclist must keep his place and not ask unusual favcurs, but it would be a rare treat to walk through the great chambers of this Elizabethan mansion. It is claimed for it that it is the most harmonious and perfect example that our country holds of the architecture of the days of Queen Bess, and they say that behind the numerous gables and big windows there are rich fittings to match the perfect beauty of the exterior. The Hall sheltered King James I. on one occasion and the room prepared for his visit is one of the show places when the family are not at home.

It would fill a long chapter to narrate the lively doings at Dorfold during the Civil War, for both the Hall and Acton Church were garrisoned for Parliament. From the peaceful garden, now so tranquil, red-hot balls were fired into Nantwich giving con- sternation to the women folks who bravely put out the fires while their husbands manned the fortifications.

div.head: CHESHIRE GHOST.
div.p: A CHESHIRE GHOST.

Well, upon our way to Nantwich we pass through a village that rejoices in the quite Italian name of Verona. Here is one of Cheshire's real haunted houses and we pause to take a look at it. It is a queer place and has a bay window which almost overhangs the roadway. When the London mail coach rolled along the highway the driver pointed to this house and gave decidedly creepy stories to the box passengers of a white figure that flitted about before sun rise and sometimes yen WI her spleen upon the coach ,as it passed. For full two generations the coaches ran by in eerie silence the horn , blower being painfully silent for a full mile before passing Verona and the driver heartily glad to pass from the shadow of the haunted house.

And then the true story came out. The dame who lived in the house had been so annoyed at the tooting of the horn under her Window and the breaking of /her sleep each night that she devised a bold plan. Slipping up her window one dark night she skillfully dropped a white sheet over the horses. The driver lashed them on in blind terror, and in the confusion the sheet dropped away. _
But the terror lingered md for two genera- ons the tooter ceased from tooting and the dwellers there had peace. Seldom has a ghost done better

div.head: DELIGHTFUL CHURCH.
div.p: A DELIGHTFUL CHURCH.

And now we come to Acton Church surely one of the most delightfully interesting of all the small churches of Cheshire. Recently restored it welcomes the visito-: with smiling beauty and offers attraction of the most seductive kind. This little church is far removed from the ordinary, and would hold even the most accomplished and travelled architect as by a spell. Nor could the uninitiated visitor tail to be fascinated by the beautiful carved panelling rescued and cleaned from the paint and whitewash of less enlightened days. A good Norman church stood here, but little of it is left. Carefully treasured within, how- ever, are some carved stones older by far than the Norman builders. The chief treasure of the church is its font, probably of Saxon make. We blush to record it, but until lately this fine old relic was doing duty as a pig trough. Somebody, we suppose, had given a new one, and the old one being considered out of fashion would be given to anyone who would carry the clumsy heavy thing away. It says something for the intelligence of centuries of pigs that they have preserved it from serious harm and it stands once more in its old place, the pride of the village.
SIR WILLIAM MAINWARING AND HIS TOMB.

The other treasure of Acton Church is the tomb of Sir William Maynwaringe. It does not matter how you spell the name so long as yau pronounce it right. There are twenty- five different spellings and you may take from choice so long as you say Man-er-ing. This Sir William conferred lustre on the village by presenting it with a bit of the true cross of Christ, a service that entitles him to I our notice, especially as it was probably procured at the cost of fighting and adventure.

div.head: STOKE HALL.
div.p: STOKE HALL.

There is yet another Hall which we have passed that deserves a passing word. At Stoke Hall lived the Mynshalls, and it is commonly stated that Milton married a member of the family as his third wife. Though so generally believed this is not correct. Elizabeth Mynshall lived at Wistaston, a village which we shall pass as we travel to Crewe, and was a member of another branch of the family. But she was a Cheshire woman, and that is something to be proud of. A. M.

THE FOUNTAIN OF BEAUTY
L. T. MEADE, Author of " The Rebellion of La Carrington," ' A Sweet Girl Graduate," &c.
CHAPTER XIV,

"1 WAY RI 888888 MATTE. AT ANY 11011 INT." The twentieth of February dawned. It was a day much like every other day at that time of year. There was a watery attempt at sunshine, but sleet showers tell at inter- vals. The streets were sloppy. The whole world looked sordid. Even in Rebecca's comfortable house the effects of a long spell of severe weather were felt. Some pipes had broken. The kitchens were not in their usual perfect order. The plumbers were about. But upstairs all was bright and neat as usual, and Rebecca herself, the owner of the pretty house, dressed in her deep mourn- ing, sat in her drawing - room waiting for a visitor. _ _

She felt quite certain that Gerard Lone- dale would come to V. Paddock-row that afternoon. He would keep his word to the letter. She had bnilt a sort of castle in the air around this man. She had read his letter I times, and it seemed to her that she knew his characer. Her father, too, had praised him. He was certainly a person of his word, and he was coming at the last moment to claim his own.

"This is the very last day that I carry IDV burden," thought the girl. "After to-dav, shall begin to live my fresh life. I tfon't quite know what that life will be. All my future seems more or less a blank. Never- theless, I have an assurance within my heart that my time will not be wasted, and that I, who am rich, can do much with my money." Rebecca's reflections were pleasant, her hands lay losely in her lap, her dark beauti- ful eyes were fixed on the fire. She was see- ing pictures in the dancing flames, and each picture represented Gerard Lonsdale in a different attitude -in a new position. It seemed to her that she was looking at his life, watching his adventures, seeing him-- first in hid poverty, then in his gradually ac- quired wealth, then in danger, then in prison. She was wondering to herself what a Persian prison was like. She knew that he was coming to London followed by danger. She hoped that all would be well that very night, and that when her life was free from the burden of the diamond, hie life would also be net at rest. _ _

Presently she bent forward and rang her bell. Lucy, looking prim and bright and pretty, appeared. "Lucy. I am expecting a gentleman to call this afternoon. Ile will give his name as Mr. Lonadale. If he comes, admit him. I shall not be at home to anyone else." "Very well, ma'am." "Yon can bring tea in soon, Lucy. If the gentleman is late, get fresh tea for him when he does come. Thank you; that is all." Lucy retired. She was pleased to see more animation on Rebecca's face than it had hitherto worn. She went down to the kitchen to consult with Cook.

"Our missis is picking up a bit," she said. "And why shouldn't she?" replied Cook. " 'Taint natural for the young to be always grieving, even if they do lose a parient." All the same, it seems pretty quick for her to be reviving," said Lucy; "but I'm glad of it—very glad. It don't suit her to be melanko-ly. Harriet, have you ever remarked our miesis a face?" _

"What do you take me foe" said Harriet in a lofty tone as she whisked some cakes, done to a turn, out of the oven. "Ain't she a perfect beauty—to my way o' thinking." "And to mine," said Luce, "and I'm own maid to her, and ought to know. But all the same our Miss Rebecca have a queer face, un- like most.'' _ _ .

... "Queer means ugly, and I wouldn't give tongues to these sort o' remarks ef I was you. Lucy." "It don't mean ugly," said Lucy. "I can't put it into right words, but it's a sort of expression that mikes you want to turn and look at her and wonder about her, times and again." You always was a strange, fanciful sort of girl," Baia Harriet. "Hadn't von best be getting your tea together and leaving our s features alone." "I know the word I want now," said Lucy " It's 'contradiksheous.' T hata what I mean." _ _ .
'Never heard tell o' that word," said Cook.

"Oh, well; it expreses my meaning—mouth sad; eyes glad. Didn't you never see it for yourself?" "My word, no." "But its true—the saddest mouth I ever looked at, and the merriest eyes. What drove me most distracted after master was took, was that her eyes and mouth were both sad. Harriet, I'll take up the tea now. Yon watch for yourself the next time you see the minis. It gives her a mighty peculiar look. And—Harriet: she's expecting a young man to call!"

"Now, is she!" said Harriet. She put her arms akimbo and looked thoughtful. "And no one else is to be let in to-day," continued Lucy. " 'l'm expecting of him, Lucy." she sal& and his name is Mr. Lone- dale,' she said; and :sou're not to let no one else _in.' "
"Oh, my word!" said Cook. "He's a for. tune hunter. You tell me what sort of ex- pression he has on his face when he calls, _

"I will," said Lucy. Our missus is in great danger," said Cook, "hein' so rich; she'll have them for- tune hunters surrounding her like bees—or wasps. rather, I should say. Each of them want, not her, but her money. I know Poor young lady. it's a pity the master didn't wed her to some one afore the Lord took him."
-.7boe's a deal too young to be wed," said Lucy. "She's ouly twenty." "She looks her age," said Cook. "and could do very well with a husband if he worn't a fortune hunter."
"There's ring at the front door," said Luty. . . . .

She rushed upstairs and opened the door. Rebecca felt herself trembling. She stood up, undecided whether to rewire her visitor standing or sitting. She wan about to seat herself again when Lucy flung open the door. Mr. Lonsdale," she said, and a man entered.

He was very tall and thin, but broad shouldered and muscular looking. His face had a great deal of life about it. His eyes were dark and animated. His eyes were good, but the rest of his features were plain. 'they were irregular; he had high cheek bones. His colour was had, too, being dull and sallow in tone. His forehead was high and slightly bald, his dark hair fine. His chin, too, was firm. Altogether. Rebecca felt that she liked the face of Gerard Lonsdale.
"Sit down, won't you?" she said. "I have been expecting you." He gave her a very courteous glance, bowed, and took a chair which she indi- cated.

"I called at your father's office to-day," he said, after • moment's pause, "where your letter was at once given to me. I cannot even try to express my sorrow at not seeing him again." Rebecca had begged of all her friends not to condole with her on the subject of her father's death; but. somehow, she liked these words from the lips of the stranger. "Hr. Lottedsle." she said suddenly (her eyes filled with tram the slight artificiality which hail characterisiwl her until this moment melted, she was her natural and best self). "you were One a the last people my father spoke of before he died. He took • great liking to you. He wished to see you Wu. ",
"He used in,' said Lansdale, with ler- 'Our.
He drew his chair impulsively • little nearer to the fire.

"Shall I tell you all about it?" he said. after a pause. "or would you rather I didn't? It may be painful for you to hear your fathers name mentioned. He only died a very short time ago." "Not a month IV, yet," said Rebecca. "One of the last tir.ip he read wan your Cr, pressibly." Lucy entered with tea. She glanced at the stranger, observed that her mistress had a faint touch of colour in her face, and felt a sense of satisfaction. Having arranged the tea equipage, she went downstairs. "I hod a good look at him," she said to Cook, "and he ain't no fortune hunter."

"Before you say anything more to me," said Rebecca to Lonsdale, "you must have some tea. It is a cold day; you look cold." The stranger had shivered slightly. Rebecca poured out tea, and gave it to him He found himself talking to her in a gentle. mellow sort of voice, a voice with no harsh- ness in it—the refined voice of an Englist gentleman. Already he seemed to under stand Rebecca, her reticence, and her grief. It seemed to Lonedale that his office wee to draw her out of herself, to get her to talk of matters ethers than those which immediately pressed round her. He thought her environ- ment too narrow for her personality. Her character, he felt certain, wan strong. He was interested, too, in her face, although it puzzled him. When the eyes danced, he looked at the .ad mouth, and felt bewildered:
"That girl is complex, but she is good," he said to himself. _ _ _
—.....-- Not until tea was over, and Lucy had re- moved all traces of the little meal, did Re- becca alter her manner.

"Now," she id;sa "you hare come to see me on business, have you not?" "I have come to see you, Miss Henshall on the subject of my letter." "I understand," said Rebecca. "I have the letter by me. May I fetch it?" Lonsdale bowed. Rebecca went to her davenport, opened a drawer, and took out the letter which bore the postmark of Tehe- ran. She returned to her seat and read the letter slowly over. Slw had read it many. many times, and felt that she knew it bs heart. When she had finished, she raised her eyes and fixed them on Lonulale's face.

"Were my father alive, you would, accord. mg to that letter, have a strange tale to tell him—one which you did not dare to put on paper. You have, however, informed him that von have been in prison and in peril of your life, and that even when you wrote you were a hunted man; you say further that when you hold the diamond in your clasp and give it to the one who demands it back, you will be able to breathe freely." "That is quite true," said Lonsdale. "You have repeated the important part of my letter with admirable exactitude. I want the diamond back. When it is mine once more, I shall return it to the man who— stole it." "The max who stole it!" said Rebecca. "Yes; he is waiting for me in London. I hope to give it to him to-night." "But why?" said Rebecca. "Pardon me. Why should you give it to a thief, who in his turn will make restitution?" "The diamond will find its proper owner again. The fact is, Miss Henshall. my life is in danger; I may be assassinated at any moment unless that diamond is restored to this man, who is all powerful, and in very high authority at Teheran. You have it safe, have you not!"

Rebecca raised her hand and just touched that portion of her dregs beneath which the diamond rested. "I have it safe." she said. The stranger gave a sigh of the utmost re- lief. "Thank God for that I feel that I can breathe again. I cannot tell you what hot, rors I have undergone on my homeward journey; not that I for a single moment doubted your father, but in a case of this kind, and where Orientals are concerned, it is almost impossible to be guarded against their wiles. They can employ means of as- sassination. for instance, unknown to an western race. They are absolutely unscru- pulous; their wisdom is almost unfathom- able, and when once they determine to track a victim, that victim cannot by any possi- bility escape them. I have found that out dur- ing my residence in Persia. lam telling you what I know."
Rebecca was silent for a time. Then she wild:
"After all, you did not understand my tether."

"What do you mean?" said Lolled&Ie. You distress me." "In all the world," said Rebecca, "there never was anyone wiser or more honourable. In his hands the stone you value was safe. It is safe now with me. It will be in your possession almost immediately ; but first, may I ask you a question?" "You may ask me a thousand questions. and I will answer them to the fullest of my ability. But what I wish to say before you ask me any question in this: I did trust your father most absolutely. I only feared that he might be unwittingly tricked by the dangerous enemies of whom I spoke. I dared not write to him, for my letters would have been traced. I knew that if once the nian who is waiting for me in London was aware that your father possessed the diamond, he would not keep it for many hours. I believe firmly now that no one in London had any clue to the fact that your father possessed the stone—that he guarded his secret well." "Until almost the end," said Rebecca in a whisper. "Now—one person knows; indeed. I ought to add that I believe two people know:'

"My God! What do you mean?' "Never mind." said Rebecca. "They tried to get the stone from me, but —failed. I want to listen to your story now. I assure you the diamond is safe; I looked at it only an hour ago." "I will tell you as briefly as I can how matters stand," said Lonsdale. "I was en- gaged in a mercantile house at Teheran, and was doing well. I was only twenty-two years of age. I found the climate suited me admirably, and I did not suffer as many Europeans do. Then I got into difficulties. I trusted a fellow—an Armenian. He in. duced me to put • little money that I pos- sessed into an investment of his own. I need not worry you with these sordid details Having got my money from me—oh! I was a y oung greenhorn at the time !—he made away with it and made me responsble for many debts which lw had incurred. If those debts were not met I should lose my employ- ment and be obliged to return to England. a disgraced and dishonoured man, and my poor old mother, who was alive then, would be left without the necessities of existence.

"You can imagine my position—the ter- rible sensations at being sorely done, and my hopeless outlook. Five hundred pounds would save me. would enable me to pay off everything—would s;lence the tongue of evil rumour which, let me tell you, Miss Hen- shall, in a place like Teheran. often means imprisonment and death to a foreigner. But I had aa little chance of getting five hundred pounds as I had of turning the stone in the streets into gold. "1 was seated on my verandah. musing over my position and wondering how long I could avert the burst of the storm when a sly-looking Persian of a low grade ' sala- amed ' before me in the street. He called out to know if h- might come up and speak to me. I nodded compliance. I had learn. d that my best plan was, as far as possible. to humour these people. The man appeared. He came gingerly forward. closing the door which led to the verandah behind him. He took from a lidt which he w ore round his waist the diamond which you now have in your keeping. lie offered it to me for a sum which represents about five pounds in English money. I beat him down to less than that

sum, and took the stone, thinking that might some day in England sell it at a profit. I knew nothing about diamonds, but I could not help remarking on its size and brilliancy. I thrust it into my pocket and went out.

"On that very evening at • restaurant I met your father. It wan a sort of half Eng- lish, half French honae, where the cooking was tolerably good. I used to frequent this place every day for dinner. I went there now, the diamond in my pocket. No one suspected me or seemed to observe me. I found myself at a small table opposite to your father, who, finding that I was English, greeted me cordially. We took a liking to each other on the spot. Before the meal wan over, I found that I was giving him my con- fidence. I did so without the ghoot of an idea that he would personally help me. lie listened to my story and accompanied me as far as my rooms.

"As I was parting from him he asked Iwo If I would call on rum me fotiowing nay, ant. gave me his card. Ile was staying in the best hotel at Teheran. I went to him at the appointed time and he received me in a private molt!.

'Now, Mr. Lonsdale,' he said, '1 inns' es well tell you at once that I am interested in von. I once knew people of your name who lived in Yorkshire. Can you possibly be- long to the same family?' "We had a little discussion over this, and I was able to prove to him that I was a dis- tant relation.

That clinches it,' he said. Now listen. You have got into a mess. I am an English- man, and I don't like to see a young fellow of my country in hopeless hot water. What will set you on your legs?' "I named the sum, trembling as I did so He looked very grave. You are sure that is sufficient?' he said. Amply sufficient,' I replied. 'But I have no security to give you—nothing, and I am a stranger to you.' "He bent forward then, and spoke earnestly.

"'I believe I have • kind heart, Mr. Lens- dale,' he said, ' but above all things I am a man of business. I should infinitely prefer both for your sake and mine to make this a business transaction. Rave you nothing of ant sort that you can give me as security for the money?'
"While' he spoke I suddenly thought of the diamond which lay unguarded in my waist- coat pocket. I don't believe I have got anything,' I replied—' but stay—do you know anything of gems?' . . .
'"A good deal," he said, his eyes spark- ling lam particularly interested in dia- monds—in fact, their sale makes part of my trade.'
Then you will tell me if this iA valuable or not.' I said; and I laid the sparkling gem in his hand.

"He gave a perceptible start, and changed colour. He got up abruptly and went to the window. He caught up a piece of dark vel- vet and put it behind the diamond. Then, cloning his hand firmly over it, he returned to where I sat, _ _
_ How did You come by this ?• he said, sternly. I looked at him in astonishment. What do _you mean, Mr._llenshall?'

, " I mean this. he replied.'You have offered me one of the most magnificent dia- monds I have ever looked at. It is worth a very large sum of money. It is abundant security for the fire hundred pounds which I propose to lend you. But before I touch it I must find out how it came into your pos- session.'
" I didn't steal—air—if that ia what you mean! I bought it from a Persian, a low fellow, who offered it to me for a small sum of money yesterday.'

I sitail leave Teheran to-night,' Tour father said, 'and will take this with •Ine. You have told no one that it got into your possession?' ' No one,' I replied. "Very well: these are my terms. I re- turn to England with the diamond. I keep it for you for seven years from this date.' 'lt was the twentieth of February, seven years ago, when our interview took. place, Miss Henshall. 'Any time between the pre- sent moment and seven years hence you can give me back the capital I have lent von with five per cent, interest,' said your father. 'At the end of seven years, if you du not appear, and I hear nothing whatever of you, I shall conclude that you are dead and will regard this stone as my property. Is that a bar- ga,itff . _

". "We made it so, Miss lienshall, and I left your father's hotel a happy and saved man. k paid all the debts which had been put upon my shoulders by that cured Armenian. I saved my character, and went on with my work. I had, however, a strange feeling that I must be careful not to speak of the diamond, nor did I remark to anyone the fact that I had visited the Englishman at the hotel. I learned, however, that your father left Teheran that very evening, and owned to a sense of relief that he had taken the stone with him. " A few days later I was told that the Per- sian who had sold me the diamond had been assassinated; his body was found in a corner of one of the old streets of the town. The person who gave me the news said that the man was a thief and had stolen a dia- mond of great value from the palace of the Miry* Kara Yusuf, one of the most infiuen- tian men in Teheran, and who was closely connected with the Shah himself. There was a hue and cry with regard to the missing stone, and as the Persian spoke to me, be fixed his eyes on my face. I don't know what he read there, for I believe I have an Englishman's power of keeping my thoughts to myself ; but it was quite evident that from that moment he suspected me. "Nothing happened, however, for a year— for two years—for three years; but I learnt from different whispers that the missing stone was of enormous value and that in the first instance it had been stolen from the Shah himself. I was further told that were the Shah to discover the thefts, the great Mirza Kara Yusuf would instantly be be- headed. To make a long story short, sus- picion began gradually but surely to fasten upon me, and one day some armed ruffians came into my private quarters, tore about my things, and even examined my person, tel- ling me that it was well-known I had bought the stone from the murdered Persian. They could find nothing, but I was committed to prison and was even put to the torture. I do not know what my end wont& have been were it not for the fact that a private friend, of the Shah's—one Nadir Julaver—came to see me and told me that he hated Mir.* Kara Yusuf, and could get me released at once from prison by applying to the Shah. "I wondered at his kindness, which was considerable. lie did not allude to the dia- mond, and simply regarded me as an unfor- tunate Englishman who was treated very cruelly by the Shall'S favourite minister. "I was given back my liberty, and I almost forgot the diamond, although I couid never, never forget your father's great goodness, and the splend'd way in which he managed to put me on my legs. "In my letter, I told you that I had col- lected a considerable fortune. I am, in truth, very well off, and it is not necessary for Inc to work any more. I do not wish, however, to lead a life of idleness, and will seek em- ployment as soon as possible, in England. But my mother is dead, Miss lienshall ; I have no near friends to go to; I am a lonely man, although I own to a sense of safety in this country which I could never feel in the land of the barbariap. I will now, if you please, conclude my narrative, and, fulfilling your father's conditiona, hand you over the five hundred pounds which he gave me, with tit.. full internat."

As Lonsdaie spoke. he took a pocket book, opened it, and handed Rebecca some notes amounting to five hundred pounds with five per cent. interest for seven years. Rebecca received them with ..a hand that trembled. . _

"I, too, am rich," she said slowly. "I am my father's only child. I am lonely. as you are lonely, Mr. Lonwlale. This money means less than nothing to me." "Nevertheless, you must take it," he said. "My honour demands it." "I understand," she said softly; "and, of course, I will take it."

She 'then slipped her hand inside the neck of her dress, pulled out the black ribbon, un- fastened the silver case which her father had made for the diamond, and taking out the gem, gave it to Lonsdale. "There,": she said.

Mimi Kara Yusut is in London. I will tell you inure of my story to-morrow if I may call," said Lonsdale. "I will give him this stone to-night." "Ah, do;' she answered. "It was a weight too heavy for me. The misery I have under- gone during the last three weeks on account of it I can never describe. But now, it is yours. Yes, come and see me to-morrow." . .
Lonsdale 'slipped the diamond into his. poc- ket, shook hands with Rebecca, and left her.

Gcnersl Topsy Turvydom.- It has been seriously suggested that the prolonged drought and unusual heat, have much to answer for in regard to the labour troubles, which culminated in the great national railway strike. If that is so, we shall all be thankful to use the tropical summer over, and to get back to normal conditions., both as regards the weather, and the carry- ing on of the deity life and business of the nation. Happily the deadlock on the railways was short lived, but the interference with the holiday season will not soon be forgotten, and there are few people who have not suffered] more or less from the general unrest, which it is difficult to believe, is in any great degree due to the irritation, and unsettled feeling caused by an aboornsal summer. Those who have escaped hardships have endured innumerable inconveniences whilst the shortage of provisions has made itself inconveniences, in every direction by a not inconsiderable rise in prices. As every housewife knows, when prices have been put up, it takes a long time for them to come dos-n again, and this, Rect of the labour troubles is not likely to wholly pass sway this aide of Cbriatmay. The Camera Fiends.—There have been complaints at some of the more fashionable seaside resorts from people who have been annoyed by the attentions of the photographers end snapshottere. When one cannot enjoy a morning bathe without having a camera focused upon you, with the possibility of seeing yourself repro- duced in the illustrated press in not too dignified attire, it becomes an impertinence to sensitive people. This is a nuisance from which Royalty suffer a first deal more than ordinary people, and soapahottiog. when it first came into vogue was a great annoyance to Queen Victoria, and also to King Edwsrd, when be was l'rince of Wales. Grsduelly the camera obtained a recognised place stall brilliant functions, but it is often carried too far in prying into the privacy of members of the Royal Family. At Cowes, no attempt was made to snap- shot the King and Prince of Wales whilst bathing, and on another occasion, someone got near enough to take the Royal party coming out of church, proceedings which can be only characterised ala piece of shameless impudence. Footgear and Bathing Dress.—A great deal of atten- tion is devoted just now to women's footwear, and this department of dross offers far more scope for novelty than the majority of people imagine. Orse noticeable feature is the decline of the Louis heel, and another, the vogue for coloured stockings. It would seem that black stockings are quite defunct, Lot doubtless they will return with the cold weather. The low cut shoes that are so popular, with slightly squared toes, very moderate heels, and fiat bows, are the most comfortable ever invented. The newest and smartest evening shoes are trimmed with narrow edging of ostrich feathers, which is a delightful mode of introducing colour. Bathing shoes this summer have been made in satin, to harmonise with the dresses worn. Pearl studs fasten these shorn. Bathing dresses become every year more elegant and expensive, although to thoroughly enjoy the morning dip in the sea an expensive dress is not necessary. I About Sashes.—This simmer will be remembered for its bright colours, and dainty graceful fashions, but it has not been characterised by any radical changes in the style of dress, nor is this to be regretted since the modes of the hour ase particularly graceful and becoming to most women. Of course there have he'll modifications of styles,and many details and accessories have been introduced, but these are not of sufficient importance to affect the styles. Among accessories, saliva take piide of place, for they have added immensely to the charm of the cool, coloured or white, dresses that have had such a vogue this summer. One of the prettiest novelties at present, is the draped sash, which is quite narrow with boss and ends behind, and finished at the edges with a rather wide and not very full frill of Valenciennes lace. Another equally charm- ing sash could le fashioned from apiece of Fenian silk in greens, blues, and pinks, or any other combina- tion that harmonises with the dress. This is quite full round the %east, and worn higher on the right than on the left side, the long full made being arranged in s double box-pleat at the beck, and floating to the edge of the dress. Odd lengths of brocade too make hand- some sashes of this descriptioe. Boleros and Shirts—The revival of the bolero may be due to the short coat which has been steadily growing shorter and shorter. The revival should be hailed with satisfaction, for this style of coat is most becoming, and has the further advantage of not-Climbing the most fragile bodice worn beneath it. It can also be quite successfully built by the home dressmaker, provided a good pattern is securei. The new bolero has sometimes one seam in the heck, but usually only I on the shoulders, and under the arms. Another garment I that should be made at home is the shirt which is no neat and smart when cut and well fitted. If a high 'price be given, good materials, cut, end fit. mey I usually be depended apes, but the low priced garment

Forthcoming Modes.—A revival that will be seen as autumn approaches, is reversible cloth, and braids will in consequence be much lees used. There is no donbt that immense possibr Wes lie in eh ths that have two different patterns and that can be used on either side. There cloths and the lafge cheques have had the effect of bringing back the black cloth, taffeta or satin jacket, which with different skirts have already made their : appearance in Vienna and Paris. The long cloak of satin or other handsome materials is too useful, and too convenient a garment to he lishtly relegated to a second piece in our affections sad will be as popular in the autumn as at present. For evening &elm in Empire style, some models have a little apron of lace, with embroidered edges, which makes almost the only trimming. Although this is a season of collarless dresses, many linen gowns are being made with rather thick plain collarbands, and there is more than a hint of • refs a of the Toby frill in the near future. Nothing at the pri rent montent is more useful in transforming an old-fashioned bodice, and bringing it lup-to-date, than a dainty fichu, but it must be well drawn dean over the arms and dainty folds.

At relt hionab le Weddings.— Brides rossessed of originel Ideas have been much in evidence of late. To give an example or two, one bride, well known in Society, " roped " her maids together, while another stood with the bridegroom to receive congratulations beneath what looked liken huge white satin umbrella, a little silver bell being suspended from the top of each rib. In the breeze obtained from open doors and windows, the umbrella waved slightly and the tinkle of the bells woe audible amid the hum of conversation and happy lsughter. The notion of "roping " the maids, vas perhaps not quite such a fortunate one. True the ropes themselves were very artistic, being silver cords twisted with smilax and roses, but the ides when carried out savoured too much of the"reins and horses" game, beloved by small folks. At all fashionable weddings nowadays baskets of r,as leaves or petals of any flo sem prefet red, with silver paper horseshoes, arc provided for the guests 'ten the " sending off " moment arrives, also very dainty and artistic paper slippers, to be sant after the depleting carriage or motor ear.

THE PROTECTION OF ANIMALS ACT. Most important provisions affecting animals are ccn- tained in the Protection of Animals Act (introduced by ' Mr. G. Greeneond, M.P.), which has just received the Royal Assent. The maximum punishment for cruelty has been increased from three to six months, and a fine of £25, while the period in which proceedings can to taken has been increased to two months. Power is given to a private person to give another person into custody, on condition that the person no doing carries out the prosecution. In addition to providing for the destiention of enimals which have been cruelly treated, S very importatt principle haa ben established by a clause inserted during the passage of the Bill through the House if Lords, by Lord Leigh on behalf of the National Canine Defence League, embodying the provisions of the bill promoted some time ago by that tociety, the object of which was to prevent dogs or other animsls being subject to revenge- ful treatment after conviction of the owner, and also to provides deterrent to cruel treatment of performing or other valuable animals, the loss of which would mean a greater penalty than would the imposition of a simple line, I oder this disuse an order can be made depriving the owner of the possession of the animal which was the subject of the charge, If there is reason to believe that it would be the victim of further cruelty if left with its owner. In the case of an order being made for the forfeiture of dogs the Canine Defence League is offering to nod good homes tor the anini•ls and to bear all expenses connected therewith. The new Act also provides for the inspection of spring traps every twelve bourn, arid imposes penalties I on those who sell poisoned grain or seed, or place poison I without taking reasonable precautions against access '1 there to by dogs, cats, fowls or other domestic animals.

WALKING DAY.—This popular annual festival was , observed on Tuesday afternoon. The children assembled at the schools a little after one, end a procession was formed. Those taking part were smartly attired, and a pleasing feature was the display of banners sad flower,, for which prizes were given by Mrs Lyon, of Appleton Hall. The Warrington Blue Coat School Band heeded the procession, which marched to church for service, conducted by the Vicar, the Bev. and Hon. C, F. Cross. An address was given by the Rev. J. C. Trumplesaure, Vicar of Whitley. The children left church for the Vicarage where refreshments were served on the lawn. Subse: quently the youngsters started for the usual parade round the village to a field lent for the occasion by Mr. G. Blackshaw. At four o'clock a return was made to the school, where the children and band sat d..mn to tea. After tea the children returned to the field, where all kinis of sports were indulged in.

div.head: FLOWER SHOW.
div.p: THE FLOWER SHOW.

The animal show promoted by the Penketh, Sankey and District Garden and Cage Birds Society took place in a field opposite the Infanta' school on Saturday under ideal conditions nod proved a pronounced success in every way. The entries were well up to the standard of previous years in the horticultural claarea, but the cage bird section, which covers a much wider radius, suffered by the railway strike. There was a fine display of cut ti3tvers and plants, the sweet peas, roses, and chysanthemums calling forth special commenda- tion. The exhibits were very tastefully arranged and presented a picture of great beauty The fudges had a difficult task in deciding the merits of the respective gardens, as the interest taken in this departure is very keen and the village boasts many trim and well laid- out gardens. The vegetable and fruit section was very creditable. In the cage classes hues the canaries were the most prominent, a number of beautiful plumaged birds being on view.

div.head: OPENING CEREMONY.
div.p: OPENING CEREMONY.

The interest taken in the show by the inhabitants of the district was manifest by the large attendance which assembled at the opening ceremony, which was per- formed.by Mrs. Sankey (the president). Among those present we noticed, Mrs. Garnett, the Rev. J. Jones, Messrs C F. Parker, J G Withinshaw, II Sankey, .1 Backhouse, It Aldcroft and W Woods. In declating the show open, Mrs. Sankey said she appreciated very much being the president of that society, as aloe had always token the keenest interest in gardening. Whilst away in Jersey a few weeks ago she noticed that nearly all the flowers had gone, end it male her feel very anxious for that show for fear the same result would to experienced there. She was glad to see, however, that that was not the coos, and she could assure them that the display there was one of which they could feel highly proud. There were many enthusiastic gardeners in Penketh and district, and by the loving care she had noticed being bestowed upon the sweet peas this veer, she thought that the Daily Mail " prize might have come to Penketh. (Laughter and applause). Although that had not proved so, she thought that they had not been very far away front it, as they could judge when they examined the boautiful blooms set out for exhibition. (Appplause). Mrs. Garnett said the show had made rapid strides during the last few years. She could remember the first show eighteen years ago when it was held in the Infants' School. It commenced with one table and a few plaits. Tney must continue to w irk her I and learn to lebour and to wait, and the result was sure to be crowned with success. . .

A vote of thanks was passed to Mrs. Sankey for open- ing the show. SCARLET Fun —During the week two children from Nevrtield have been removed to the hlspital with scarlet fever. The oases are very alight, and no cause for alarm need be felt in the district.

CONGREGATIONAL CHRISTIAN SERVICE BAND.-- This meeting was resumed on Monday evening last, when a good number of young people were present. There was no address given, but favourite &raptors nt the scriptures were read by Misses E. Moores, F. Sutton, B. Miller, Mrs.C. Lewis, Messrs. J. DR. Smith, G. Wiliam, C. Lerather, H. Rushton. M iss Emma Miller rendered a solo " For you I ern praying," in a most effective way. Mr. Cyril Howcroft dresided. The meeting concluded with prayer.

div.head: Hatton.
div.p: Hatton.

BURGLARY.—Great consternation prevailed through- out the little village of Hatton, when it became known that a burglary had been perpetrated at the resieence of Mr. John Kippax, money to the amount of £l7 Its. having been stolen. £1 17s. of this wee money that Mr. Kippax had collected in subscriptions for t.e Hatton show. The rest was his hard earned savings from prizs money, &c. ; fortunately this years' prize money was not included as it wls only given on Friday night. The money, which was kept in a box and deposited in a still larger box, was alright on Thursday lastweek,eay of Wal a show It appears that en Friday night Mr. Hippos heard a rumbling noise and got up to investigate, hot seeing no one got into bed agnin. On Wedi.esday Mrs. Kippax went to the box for some ' money to settle an account with a tradesman, and to her horror found it empty. The police were sent for, but as let are at a loss to account for the robbery. Much sympathy is felt with Mr. and Mrs. Kippsx in their loss.

- - FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR. LomAS.—The funeral took place at Grappenhall Church on Saturday last. As a mark of respect and sympathy most of the residents had drawn their blinds, and a good many of the villagers awaited the cortege at the church Ow. The following members of the Ancient Order of Foresters (Mount Hermon Court 864) acted as bearers :—Bros William Fairharst, P.C.R. ; Fred Fairhurst, P.S.C.R. ; Joseph Leigh, P.C.R.; Thomas Brierler, P.C.R.; James Burrows, treasurer; and Thomas Shakeshaft, secretary. The chief mourners were :—Mrs Lomas (widow), Walker Lomas, George W Lomas, Matthew Lomas (Cons), Minn Lomas (daughter), Willi ,m Lomas (brother), Mn Kinsey (sister), W Kinsey (nephew), lit Fairhuot (niece), Miss Kinsey (vister-in-law), Mrs George Lomas (daughter-in-law). Meters Joseph Crostleld nod Sons, Limited same represented by Messrs Platt, Clayton and Warren (of the commercial staff). Others present were —Messrs Thomas Ireland, Thompson, J Leyland, F Smith, J Wilding and 0 A Leach. The cortege was received at the gate by the Rector and full choir. The service in the church was very impressive, as also was that at the graveside. The choir sang the psalm . .

Mr George Pilling, presided end those present were :—Mesers H Clarke WH J Westbrook, J J Whitley, J McDermid, 0 J Brown, b' Rose, .1 Hallows, C W Hallows, J It Wood F J Pearson and F Ashton (clerk) •.• . _ .

The Clerk read a letter from the Town Clerk of Warrington, dated August Vat, no follows t—Referring to the interview which took place on the let June last between a deputation from your Council and the Gas Committee of tlis Corporation I have to inform you with regard to the amount rendered the committee are prepared to agree to the price 3ou tuggest upon the understanding that new terms are arranged immedi- ately which shall apply to all 'neonate autsequent to December 1910. In this carte the agreement at present ern be terminated by mutual consent, on satisfactory arrangements belng made. In order, however, to safe- guard the interests of the Corporation I have to give you formal notice in accordance with the provisions of the agreements dated 27th December 1892 and on the 14th February 1906 c n the intention of the Corpora- tion to terminate the said agreements as and from the 31st August 1912. HOCSES FLOODED Ity_ THE STORM.

The Clerk read the Sareyor's report which stated that during the heavy storm on Monday evening (the 2lst inst.) all the sowers in the parish appeared to have baen filled no that tSe present arrangement. for atom overflows appeared to be inadequate. Consequently cry house, where the back yards sloped towards the botmes, was flooded by the water from the back to the front doors. Espe.iially was this so at the houses II to 21, at the top of Dundonald-avenue and the homes, 16 to al, Elleemere-road. The latter houses were particularly affected, through a piece of timber getting across the outlet of the bottom manhole in Egerton-street, thereby checking the flow. Consequently all the service water from West Avenue had to pass through this manhole. Thin caused back pressure on the low sower and forced water through the lowest back-yard grids. The syphon st Twenty-steps Bridge proved to he flowing freely and the storm overflow from Ellesmere-road working at full flow. The storm oval flow pipe at the syphon, how- ever, was cloned. The Surveyor wso strongly of opinion that Creosbrook water course should be main- tained upon an IS-inch pipe laid up the valley to receive

I storm overflows from West Avenue, Walton New-road, I Nfhiteffeld-road and intended Lew road, in White%lds and other vacant land up the valley. I The Clerk also read a letter ffom Mr. Wray, tenant of 21, Ellesmere-road, which stated that through the sewers being inadequate to take the water away, his house was flooded to a depth of I inches. Something I would certainly have to be done to remedy that state of things, as his carpets on the ground Ilacir were ruined, and he was not alone in that respect. He was sure the I committee would do their best to remedy matters, as if I they had a recurrence of the floods they could not be expected to put up with matters quietly. I Mr. Joseph Houghton also wrote to the committee 'taut.; that his tenant, Mr. Fergcsson, of 17, Ellesmere- ruse, had tent in notice of removal because of the I recent flood. Flooding, he raid, was not likely to ,I enhance the value of property. ' Mr. Brown said that with regard to Ellesmere-road several people had been to him to complain. He attributed the flood pertly to their being insufflaient grids, both in the side Streets and in Ellesmere-road. Besides, the cinders from the unpaved passages ran down the channels and clogged what grids there were. A short discussion ensued and it was decided that when tLe Surveyor returned from his holidays he should make a thorough investigation Into the matter.

Bradley's clothier's establishment in Widnes- road, sometime between Saturday midnight and I a.m. Sunday, the 20th inst., and doing damage to the extent of .E 2.2.
Superuttendant Strickland asked for a remand uutil Thursday In order that inquiries might be made. Hogan applied for bail, but was refused.
RUNCORN FOOTBALLER'S PLUCK. SAVED A SECOND LIFE.

James Dixon, a well-known Runcorn footballer pluckily rescued a six-year-old boy from drowning in the Big Pool, Rancorn, on Tuesday evening. The little lad, whose name is Peers, WAS sailing a boat when he over-balanced and fell into the water. Dixon, who , cannot swim, entered the pool up to bin neck, and grasped the boy is he was sinking for the second time. This is the second life Dixon has saved in similar fashion.

WIDNES HORTICULTURAL SHOW. The twelfth yearly exhibition of plants, flowers, vegetables, Zsc., promoted by the Widnes Horticultural Society was held on Thursday In Victoria Park. The Mayor (Councillor F. Neil) presided, and the show was formally opened by Mrs. F. H. (tonnage. The quality of the exhibits,especially in the vegetable section, was extremely good. In the cottagers' section Mr H Feeney was very successful, securing ten firsts ; while Mr J Flewitt won seven, and T Sparkes six. In the amateur class, Mr G Roscoe was the most prominent, and had nine firsts to his credit. Mr Feeney was very successful in this section also with six Brats. Mr F Discos Natal! (St. Helens), who won the prize for the beet collection of plants arranged for, secured nine firsts in the open section.
Toe honey wen of very high quality. The first prize was won by Mr F Hatton, Hill Cliffe, near Warrington.

div.head: SOCIALISM AND STRIKES.
div.p: SOCIALISM AND STRIKES.
LORD WOLMER'S VIEW OF THE TROUBLE.

Viscount Weimer, the member for Newton, speaking at a Conservative demonstra.ion on Saturday in Garswood Park, &Mon, referred to the railway strike. It was, he said, of no use to indulge in mutual recrimiostions. They knew perfectly well that these poor fellows were not striking for the fun of it. There nsmt be something wrong somewhere. Yet he could not help but think that a great deal of it was due to the Socialist agitation propaganda that had been going on. Mr. Lloyd George, at Liam- house, told the people things they would never have thought of for themselves, things that took Mr. Lloyd-George's genius and imagination to invent ; and then they were eurprised that they bed at last succeeded in stirring up class hatred and plunging the whole country, from North to South, into an internecine quarrel between class and class. This ought to boa lesson to all, and to these irresponsible politician, who did not weigh their words before they , uttered them. Men who had the " gift of the gab " , like Mr. Lloyd-George or Mr. Churchill, were ept to net in motion forces which they could not afterwards control, and however much those men might deplore the hardship of the strike ,on the unhappy people, they were responsible in the first instance for having caused it. These men who had been preaching class hatred were beginning to reap their harvest now, and they were finding once swain that it was a great deal easier to destroy than t build up. Ile hoped that the issue of these unheppy circum- stances would ultimately be that the outpourings of Socialist agitators would receive less attention in the future than they had in the past, and that men would realise what that sort of thing led to if persis:ed in. (Applause).

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
DAMAGE TO FARMS.

Thomas IVilton end William M'Cano, two young colliers living in Essex-street, pleaded guilty at St. Helena. on Monday, to stealing growing potatoes and doing 2s. Bd. damage. The Chief Constable mid that a terrible amount of damage was being done to the farms of the neighbourhood. Fined 20s. each, with the alternative of fourteen days imprisonment.

- - SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A HUSBAND. John Dillon, a young man of 29, Hardy-street, was remanded at St. Helene on Monday on a charge of feloniously wounding his wife. It was alleged that because of a very trivial matter at midnight on Satur- day the man kicked bin wife most brutally about the head at.cl face. TRIPLE PIT-BROW TRAGEDY. An adjourned three-fold inquest was resumed at St. Helene, on Tuesday, by Mr. Brighouse, on John Daffy (12), 2"' Mount-street; Joseph Henry Armstrong (35/. 139, Park-road ; end Stephen Kelly (52), 244, Clock Face-road. Mr. Peace represented the Sutton Heath end Lea Green Colliery Company, at whose pit the men were fatally injured on June 17th by a cabin falling off the pit-brow, which was being reconstructed. James Sephtoo, joiner, 23, Cbester-street, Prescot said he had worked for the colliery company fifteen years. On June 15th, Mr. Laycock, the engineer, went to his workshop end asked him to go to the Queen pit- brow, which wee loving r 'constructed. Thai were to construct an airlock for the upeast ehaft, and in order to do this had to cut an opening 27 feet long in the platform on the brow, between the pit and the cabin whera the workmsn got their meals. They nailed down the ends of the planks that were cut through, end put in runners ready for the opening to be filled with con- crete. On Saturday, the 17th, Mr. Laycock found that the opening was not wide enough, and told him to saw oft another six itches from the planks on the cabin side. Ile had done thiAby about half an hour after 11001), and he went with another joiner, named Roberts to the shop for some 6-inch nails and other material. A few minutes afterwards they heard a shoat, and found that the cabin had toppled over from the top of the brow and fal'en about left. to the ground. Armstrong was under as cabin, and was badly hurt, and one of the men in the cab'n was killed by the stove falling OD M.

div.head: OVERHANGING CABIN.
div.p: THE OVERHANGING CABIN.

Witness, in eross-esamination, said that be bad not the nails on the job, because when he went to the brow in the morning he did not know they would be wantad. The cabin wag 6ft. by Mt., and overhung from the brow It. It bad bean in use about two year., and it was never thought necessary to prop under the side that overhung. They bed to put a runner under the ends of the planks from one end to the other before they could nail them down so that it c.,uld not be done as they went along. The Coroner said he did not see how Mr. Laycock came ioto the buiiness. lie did not norm to blame.

Heory Creighton, colliery surface band, 160, Park. road, tZt. Helens' dercribed the accident, and said that no one appeared to think the cabin in an unsafe condition. William A. Roberts, ioiner, 65. Crosaley-rond, said this was a " push "job, and until they canted the nails ail their attention ens concentrated on Emile, the opening cot to the proper size. None of them thought ' there was any danger of the cabin going over. 'I hey I did Dot warn the men working on the brow because they Dever thought it was likely to more. The Coroner raid it seemed clear that so one ever I dreamed that the cabin would fall.

The jury returned a verdict that the affair was purely accidental, and that Mr. Laycock, the engineer, vu in no way to blame. The Coroner said it would no doubt be • great satisfaction if he asked Sergeant Staveley to visit Mr. Laycock in hospital and tell him that.

div.head: Warrington Rugby Football Club.
div.p: Warrington Rugby Football Club.

Sir, —1 notice that several nen- committee men have been appointed to our local Notthern Union Football Club. At the end of last season the club lost a most valuable member of the committee in the person of Mr. T. Bowers. Mr. Bowers, who, I understand, resigned his membership owing to the pressure of business, has been a devoted member and has bad the welfare of the club at heart for over 20 years. 1, think this length of service should not be passed by without some recognition, not tn!y from the club but from the members at large wh^, I am sure, will only be too pleased to show their appreciation of his valued services by subscribing to a fitting testimonial. The writer will be pleased to subset ibe half a-guinea and suggests that the club treasurer be asked to receive subscriptions.—Yoars Ac„ ENTHUSIAST. Aumst 2ith, 1011.

div.head: Railwaymen's Strike.
div.p: The Railwaymen's Strike.

Sir,—Having taken some little part in connection with the Railwaymen's strike at WarringVn perhaps you would allow me through your valuable paper to state the reasons why railwaymen took such a united stand and so broughtabout a National Sirike on the railw.iys. The cry has gone abroad that we did not know why we did cone out on strike. Nicer was there a greater misleading statement made. One of the reasons could tot be given in a more definite and correct statement than that given by the Right Honourable John Bum (Presidect of the Local Government Board). He was asked the other day (I understand by that valuable paper the " Daily News") what was the reason the railway men of the country were out on strike ? His answer was something like this :—Because there were 100,000 men on the railways getting less than £.l per week and GOO,OOO getting less than 25a. per week and I have not seen that statemer.t denied. Another reason :—The Conciliation Boards of 1907 have been a failute. The prccednre taken with the grievances, was altogether too long before they were dealt with, and many were not put forward. The men were out of patience with it knowing only too well that they would not get fair play. The machinery of the Conciliation Boards was altogether tor complicated. What we ask for is an agreement viz : Minimum rate of wage, guaranteed seek, all over-time plid for irrespective of number nf hones worked, all men to have the same chance to rise to higher position according to service and ability and not to be penalised because they take an active part in Trade Union work. Let the companies drop that out-of- date, idea that if men take part in organizing men its trade unionism they are tot as valuable to them. I say the very opposite is the case. Let the com- pathes give us fair play all round between man and man and then they will find that the men will be loyal to them and will watch their interests more than ever. I say, without fear of contradictioo, that if the Companies and the Government had agreed at once to recognise the men's representatives there would not have been a National strike.—Yours
-C-NiToZiCROFT.
renketh, Warrington. August 25th, 191 t

div.head: Tariff Reform and Foreign Missions
div.p: Tariff Reform and Foreign Missions

Sir,—Tariff Reform "means "—more Church missions to the heathen ! That is the latest develop- ment. So, at least, one gathers from the "Monthly Letter" which appears in a recent number of the "Shanklin Old Church Magazine," or, if this be not a strictly accurate interpretation, it is at any rate made quite clear that more missions to the heathen mean Tariff Reform. The writer of this tru'y remarkable "Monthly Letter," who signs himself " your affectionate friend and pastor, W. Barry Cole," says " God will take care that we prosper if we take care to do what lie has given us to do. Be will give us Tariff Reform and Colonial Preference and every good thing, if we give the Gospel b the heathen." One has often heard of people keeping a debit and credit account with God, but surely it is a new ! departure to ask the Almighty for a p ptl pro quo for services rendered to the heathen! Na one but a Tariff Reformer could have evolved such • brilliant idea. The Rev. Barry (who must be an interesting preacher, if his sermons are anything like his "Monthly Letter,") evidently regards Tariff Reform and Colonial Preference as heavenly blessings which are only withheld by a Divine Providence because of a regrettable tendency on the part of erring humanity to be chary of contributing funds for missionary purposes ; and Ido not for a moment doubt that the reverend gentleman would be quite prepared to "prove" conclusively that this characteristic is an outcome, and one of the evils, of Free Trade. This newest of New iheobgies opens up a splendid opportunity for the Tariff Reform League. Instead of sending out a horde of speakers and tons of literature, the league will now be able—by the simple process of contributing a good round sum to be clevoied to the spread of the Gospel among the heathen —to secure, at one stroke, all that it has been striving after during the eight years ii its existence. Subscribers to the league vvill then feel that, in a double sense, they are respondir g to the cry of those who
" . . . . Call us to delierr Their land flora error's chain."

In view of the Rev. W. Barry Cole's remarks, it would be interesting to know whether he proposes, in the m Mar of missuns, to give to the heathen in the Colonies any Pleference over those in foreign lands. Might one sugge.t that, judging by recent utterances in the Hcuse of Commons and elsewhere, them is plenty of scope for a home missionary campaign, to be conducted amongst the heathen within the ranks of the party to whi.h the reverend gentle- man so obviously belongs; for it has been made abundant'y clear that whatever Tariff Reform may or may not stand for, it certainly does nut " mean " good manners. _
The" affectionate friend and pastor •' cf the Shanklin Old CLurch has begun well, and beyond all _ _ . . . . . .

manner of dimin-theve is a (i-hopric in Mori; kr him if ever the Tariff Reform Party gets into power. Let '•4 him meantime pursue the path he has chosen, and each bight as he retiies to rest he vvill be able to console himself with the reflection : " If I but serve my God e ith half the zeal I serve my party, -He will not is mine age, Leave me naked to mine enemies."
Yours etc., WILLIAII J. RIDGWAY
Gorton, Manchester.

div.head: DROWNED WHILE BATHING Attempts at Rescue Fail.
div.p: DROWNED WHILE BATHING Attempts at Rescue Fail.

An inquest was held at Cross Ferro, Appleton yesterday, by the District Coroner (Mr. Thomas, Ridgway), touching the death of Thomas Jones,sged 20, C. COU IMP, Appleton, a ',tinter, who was drowned while bathing in Brooks' l'it, Appleton, on the 23rd inst.

Arthur Jones, Cross Cottage, Appleton, paid the deceased was his brother and was employed as a painter by his father. He last saw him alive on Wedneeday, the 23rd lost. at twenty minutes to seven in the even- ing, when the deceased left linuiP on Li 3 bicycle alone. Ile went in the direction of Brooks' Pit where he knew he bad been learning to swim for about a week. William Tomlinson (2l), Ilatton Farm, Appleton, said that about seven o'clock on the evening of the .3rd not,. he was bailing with several others in Brooks Pit, Appleton, when the deceased arriv-i. Deceased stripped and went into the water with a pair of water wings, remarking " I'll go across on these." He plunged in end swam to the centre of the pit when he said he could not go soy farther and cried "Come here, Billy" (meaning the witness). Witnesc went to his assistance. Deceased sank but witness managed to get hold of him when he came up again. Witness had to let go, haw ever, as the deceased was pulling him down. Witness's brother got hold of deceased, but was obliged to leave him. None of them could swim well. Assistance was sent for and the body was recovered after Vi minutes search. The juiy returned a verdict of " Accidentally drowned " and the Coroner expressed sympathy with the family in their bereavement.

div.head: GREAT WHITE PLAGUE.
div.p: THE GREAT WHITE PLAGUE.
WARRINGTON CORPORATION'S EFFORT TO FIGHT CONSUMPTION.
Opening of Sankey Sanatorium.

" Our chief medicine here will be fresh air " said Dr. J. Coote Hibbert, medical officer of health, at the opening of the Sankey Sanatorium for consumptives on Saturday afternoon. The Warrington authorities' effi rt to arrest the dread disease in its early stages will largely take the form of open-air treatment and it would be hard to discover in the vicinity of a gt imy manufacturing town a building more suitably situated for that purpose than the Sankey Sanatorium. It stands near a secluded and little traversed road about a mile from Sankey station, in a pleasant rural spot where no smoke pollutes the atmosphere and it is difficult to imagine that the works of Warrington are so near. The main building was erected in order that the Corporation might be prepared at any time to cope with a smallpox epidemic, but fortunately the town ha some years enjoyed an immunity from that disease, sad rather than allow the sanatorium to remain unoccupied any longer, the Health Committee wisely decided to devote it to tile treatment yf consumptive cases During the last five or six years the Committee have treated, during the summer months, a few cases of pulmonary tuberculosis in a hut situated in the grounds of the Aikin-street Isolation Hospital. The accommodation there has, however, been very limited, and naturally it has been impossible to receive more than a few patients diving the year. Moreover th conditions in the centre of the town are scarcely suitable for the open-air treatment of this Msease. During the present year consumptive patients have been received in the small pavilion at Sankey Sanatorium, but so long as there was no administra- tive block or accommodation for nurses at the sanatotMm, it was impossible to admit any but early c tees of the disease, which would not require skilltd nursing. This latter difficulty has, however, now been overcome by the erection at a cost of 11.800 of an administrative block with quarters for nurses, and the Committee are now prop sing to admit both early and advanced ctses into the sanatorium, the small ploilion, with its six beds, being reserved fir early cases, and the large pavilion with twelve beds for advanced cases of the disease. The new administrative block has been provided with • an especially large and well fitted-cut kitchen, (Ire., no that in the event of the hospital being extended at any future date there will be ample kitchen provision. There is also in this block a combined dining and sitting-roam and five bedrooms for the resident staff It is a one-storey building and so arranged that further bsdroams may be added if required. The two , pavilions, each with its two wards, provi le accom- • modation for eighteen patients. The buildings also include a laundry and diFinfecting station, and the I disinfector is shortly to In install-d. An old farmhouse forms the lodge where the caretaker lives. On Saturday afternoon the Mayor (Councillor Dr. • Joseph) formally opened tin new administrative block. Many members of the Health Committee and . town councillors, along with officials, medical men, - and several ladies assembled at the Tows Hell and I drove in open conveyances to Sankey. The Mayor was accompanied by the Mayoress. On arrival at the sanatorium, the party immediately 'assembled out-ide the administrative blcck and several interesting speeches were delivered. t Alderman JAMES EVANS (chairman of the Health Committee), who presided, said that whilst the health authorities had been coping with many things it seemed to some people that they had sadly lett alone the particulsr disease with which that institution was to deal. They hoped that the departure they were now making would be the means of materially diminishing the death-rate from that _TEIII,IIILE 5(101:11GE, _

consumption. (Hear, hear). If they were successful, that day would indeed be remembered us a red letter day in the history of the town. It might be thought that they were taking a step in the dark or going in advance of public opinion, but he thought they could not move too quickly in such a serioas matter. (Hear, hear.) Consumption accounted for inure deaths than all the other infectious diseases put together. That fact alone showed the necessity for all tlght.minded men putting their shoulders to the wheel and earnestly endealouring not only to cultivate public opinion, but to bring about a better state of things. (applause). The MAYOR then unlocked the door of the building. In the course of an address, his Worship said the . . . . .

chairman of the Health Cmimittee might well have taken upon himself the task of opening that huileinr, as no-one was more worthy to do so, but with his usual large-mindedness Alderman Evans had kindly passed on the duty to him (the Mayor). The new institution was a small one, hut in its objects and aspirations be believed it marked THE DANt N OF A VERY BIG UNDERTAKING

(Hear, bear.) There were arm-chair and drawing-room critics and others who from snug retresta—he did not know whether they thought be meant bar parlours— (langhter)—and at a safe distance, romote from toe scene of active work, thought fit to criticise the "city . .

fathers." Whatever opinion those people night have of the Council End of their actions, gam and present, he did not think the finger of scorn could justly he pointed to the health authorities of the Wen. He had been in touch with the town and its sanitary conditions forover thirty-seven years and he thought he could speak with some show of authority. (Hear, hear.) There was no doubt that
WARRINGTON HAD BEEN SINGOLARLY FORTUNATH lO the past in its public men, but in none more no than in those nho had been connected 'gbh the health affairs _

of the town. 71-ite-y-ii;d-;1;;;;-b-egO;Tn the forefront, the van of sanitary progress, and they might fittingly be called pioneers. The present Health Committee formed no exception. In their real earnestness and in their efforts to maintain the sanitary progress of the town, they outstripped even their predecessors. It was only right that the Town Council should have very large-heartedly and generously supported the recom- mendations of the Health Committee. With regard to the medical cfficer of health, Dr. Hibbert was the sixth holder of that office in Warrington. In that small line of medical officers there had been more than one earnest, fearless end contcientious sanitary reformer and he thought the present medical officer worthily upheld the traditions of his predecessors. (Hear, hear.) The people ef Warrington also had some share in that insti- Lion being used for the purpose for which it was now being set apart. Indirectly the mere fact of the inhabitants of Warrington being law-abiding, broad minded citizens in the matter of AGREEING TO VACCINATION, WITTI A MINIMUM OF PROTEST AND OBJECTION, . .

was the reason the Corpoiati, n could devote that building to the relief of tuberculous cages instead of smallpox. He did not want to enter into any con- tentions ',object. Goodness knows, it ought not to be cc ntentinus. (Hear, hear.) He did not think soy sane person who had studied the case for a moment could fail to realize that the fact that smallpox wee to-day a , thing of the pa t was doe to vaccinati. n. The only fear he had was that with an increasing number of " conscientious objectors," the Corporation might, instead of tieing that hulloing for the diminution of the greatest scourge of the world, bane to turn out the tubercular cases to that smallpox patients might be admitted. Metaphorically speaking, a constant warfare was going no around and within us I etween health and diease. Fortunately for us, health had the mastery, otherwise many of them would not bathers that day. (Laughter.) We were gliding through all kinds of dangers almost dAly—dangers which we did not see and which did not have any effect upon us because we had protecting armour in the shape of good general health and great vital powers. It was most important that efforts should be made to deal with tubercular disease. in view of the fact that

in the world were due to it They must fight con- surnption with a strong hand and he regardEd that institution as Warrington's share in the general con- flict against that great enemy. They ought to consider bow the disease was brought abut and the relative value of cure and prevention. Tubercle, as a rife, Was transmitted by the sputum from patient to patient.
