div.p: TUBILRCL:LO,S MUM.

..... That was, of cour,e, a danger, but a comparatively small one as compared with the other. Meat was even less dangerous Lima milk. Although many cases of consumption were curable, there were others which were incurable. 1 lin acute cases and those in which there was a strong hereditary pre-disposition to con- tract the d:sease wore practically hopelesa from the first, to far as present knowledge went, and upon that ground be would call attention to the fact that prevention was better than cure. (Hear, hear). The great thing was to keep the general health of the public at a high level and thus preserve the armour which day by day, ucknown to ourselvet, protected us from the onslaught of hidden enemies. One consumptive patient could give off countleas millions of bacilli daily. If those were all dried, pretested acd wafted about in the tun ía badly ventilated house where a patient lived, there was extreme danger to the public. In order to prevent that, the authorities most

div.head: EDUCATiyHE PEOPLE
div.p: EDUCATiyHE PEOPLE

- not only to look after their own health but to instruct sufferers from the disease to net in such a way as to pro- trot those whom they loved meat from the same danger. The institution which they were formally opening that day was a kind of pioneer—he did cot suppose there was another town of the site of Warrington which had an institution like it. Ile hoped it would not t sly be a blessing and a protection to the town but that researches and experiments into the dread disease which might be

conducted there wOuld be for the benefit of the country and the world in general. (Applause.) Dr. J. COoTE Hi mint , medical oflicer of health, said it had been extremely helpful to him and to the Health Committee to have on that committee the senior medical practitioner and the first medical officer of Warrington. The sanatorium had been opened in the interests of the general public, just as the fever hospital was at present being conducted, and not so mu, h for the benefit of the individual sufferer. Of course, in sanatoria generally the individual sufferer WAS chiefly considered. He was admitted with a view to cure. In the present instance the Corporation had not only that *eject in view but the far more important one of isolating the infectious patient who was advanced in the d sense, from the general ptblic, especially from those who live I in the same house. Having described the accommodation of the building, Dr. Hibbert said that in dealing with tuberculosis they had several problems before them. There was the problem of the early case which one hoped to cure. There was Cite further problem of the advanced cases which were far beyond cure but which they wanted to isolate for the sake of the general public. There was also a long list of intermediate cases which were beyond hope of cure but still CAPABLE OF PERFORMING USEFUL trunk UNDER
FAVOURABIR CIRCUMSTANCES

—.—..—...- --- and by means of the help thus afforded them. The early cases would practically live in the fresh air, have the best of food and receive the most careful general treatment. They would have to be kept in the institu- tion for considerable periods in order to effect any good results, so he was afraid not many patients could hope to pass through in the course of a year. 'lke , patients whom it was hoped to cure must be kept abe, lately apart from the advanced cases which would be dealt with in the large pavilion. Other- wise they would be exposed to infection which would do away to a large extent with sny hope of cure. The main object would be to atimulate the vital powe.s to overmaster the disease. The advanced cases would be chosen chiefly from those homes where the surroundings were such that the spread of infection was most likely to occur. They would have to remain in the places considerable time, because it would be almost impossible, or at any rate undesirable, to send them back to their homes again. Intermediate cases could not be dealt with there at present. The health department .

VISITED THOSE CASES IN THEIR HOMES, supplied spit bottles and disinfectants und gave advice as to the best way of preventing the spread of infection. Perhaps later the committee might build some wooden erections in the grounds for the accommodation of intermediate cases. As to the future of patients when they were apparently cured, if they were sent home to bad conditions of life they would relapse and again suffer. Son e means should be devised of getting them suitable work under proper conditicns and perhaps feeding them for a time.
THE CHIEF MEDICINE AT THE SANATORIUM WOULD

That remedy which they hoped to apply by way of cure could also act by way of prevention and he would urge that every dwelling and school in the borough might, if possible, he made a little sanatorium in itself not with the idea of riming but of preventing disease. If in the post our dwellings, our schools and cowshed• had been properly ventilated, there might have been ne need for that ceremony. (Applause). Alderman P 16121.3 INT, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Mayor ai.d Mayores‘, said he had lived long enough in Warrington to see it grow from one of the dirtiest-11e said it advisedly—towns in Lancashire to be a

WELT, ORDERED, PROGRESSIVE AND CLEAN TOWN. H • was old enough to recollect the cholera epidemic in the early forties. He recollected quite well the fever epidemic, when a house of recovery wan estab- lished on Cockhedge as the only metals of coping with It. He had a very lively and dissgreeable recollection of the smallpox eptdemic, which was the original cause of the p 'merit proceedings. It was the terrible time they went through in Warrington end the great expense to which the town was put, thot forced upon the Council the necessity of establishing the smallpox hospital at Sankey. Tfte institution hal been there mousy years hot fortunately the occasi In for its use hai not arisen. The committee were wise in try ieg, to disoover means whereby the I- ttilding, no long smoccupiel, could be utilise I for the beneflt of the tow,, and they could not have devoted it to any better object than the core of phthisical disemes. Some people might say the Council had gone to great expense, but where the health of the ! community was et not rned, Fe did not think the ques- tion of expense hai any right to come in. They were managing the town to the hest of their ability, sal the respoosibilit v rested upon them to do all they could to support the Health Committee in the good work they wets doing. The question of expense might appear to le something of a bughear to the chairma 1, but be (Alderman Plerpoint)would say to him "Go on and you will fl sd the Commil will do all they can to help in the good work you have started to-day ' (Applause. ) Aldermen BENNETT seconded. He raid it was the absolute duty of the civic authority to do whatever it could to promote the health, happiness, pleasure and prosperity of the whole m.pelation. We had innumer- able difficulties to face but no men was worth calling a man or. titimn who would not, to the utmost of his ability and the full extent of his powers, do something to remrdy the evils and remove the difficulties under which we leboured. It ens difficult to imagine the terrible suffering involved in th a wort tuberculosis. It was the greatest scourge in the country at the present time an] every medical eel municipal authority and every man of goodwill ought to strain themselves to the utmost to endeavour to devise tome method of alleviating the evil. Ile was glad to find
WARRINGTON IN THE FOREFRONT

in this as in iaa-m-a-n-y-o—tholm—taie-ri—kiinhitill its (inns the town bad many great virtues and there were many things about it of which they were proud. He did not think, however, that there was anything tipno which thoy could more legitimately c trier dole. thems tl v. than upon the fact thrt they were leafing tha way in fiAting that a scial scaurgx. lit did no, know whether Mr. Lloyd George got his idea from Warrington, hut be (the sneaker) was pleased to see hi n taking up what the Warrington Corporation was doing on a local scale and applying it nationally. (Applause). The vote was heartily accorded. The MAYOR, in responding, said the most valuable way in which they could fight not only tuberculosis but cancer and other mortal disoaoes as well, was by trying to prevent them. Once they got into the systera he could not imogine the possibilit y of any certsin cure of some forms of phthisis, especially tho acute form and larymeal phaisis. The same applied to severe forms hf cancer and to diabetes. On the othor hand they were getting to know the causes of the diseases. With rega,d to consumption, more an iti,bt and fresh sir, and healthy modes of life were the chief weapons with which to fight it. Consumption and tuberculosis generally were much on the decrease and, es saoitory improvements went on, consumption must necessarily recede. (Applause.) Aldermen James Evans was thanked for presiding, on the prnposition of Alderman W. BOLTON. The vieitors then inspected the buildings, and alter light refreshments had been partaken of, the return driVe was made to Warrington. It should Its noted that the sanatorium is primarily a small-pox hospital, and should there be in the future any outbreak of this disease in the borough the con- sumptive patients will have to be immediately sent home no that the small-pox cues can he admitted. A warning to this effect will be given to each conaumptive patient before admission into the sanatorium.

div.head: WARRINGTON EVENING SCHOOLS.
div.p: WARRINGTON EVENING SCHOOLS.
The Coming Session's Work.

As will be seen from an advertisement in another column the evening schools of the Warrington Education Committee (inclnding the Branch Technical Schools, the Commercial Institute and the Technical Institute) will be opened for the session on Monday September 11th. The prospectus ims already been issued and affords convincing evidence of the wide scope and eminently useful character of the course of instruction to be gives in the schools. The Breech Technical Schools have been organised with a view to providing opportunities for boys and ' girls, who are not able to attend Secondary Schools, to have the education they have received in the Elementary Sohools continued, no that they may be prepared to pass on to the Commercial or Technical Institutes to receive their professional training. The Branch Technical Schools for boys special lee on the Comn3erisiel ' and Technical side, whilst those for girls specialise on the Domestic Training side, and those who are , successful in their studies will pass to the Commercial Institute. The Commercial and Technical Institutes have been orgsnized no that the requirements of mokt boys will be met. It is absolutely (agendal that every student should be properly qualified to take up the course of study. A student who is not properly qualified in the preliminary subjects not only wastes his own time but wastes that of his fellow students. Consequently no students will be admitted to the courses at the Com- mercial or Technical Institutes unless the Principals are Eatisfied that they are qualifitd. An entrance esamination to the Technical Institute will be held for all students desiring admission who cannot produce evidence of qualificaCon. Hon.ewcrk exercises will be set end students will not be allowtd to continue in attendance unless they do the Homework. . . _
Numerous pluses and scholarsbirsare tflered. THE SCHOOL OF ART.

The School of Art also re-opens in September. It provide, systematic instructian in day and evening classes In pure and applied art, with a view of such education being of practical one in manufactures and decoration, and the more complete union of art with craft : also affording a thoroughly practical knowledge of drawing, painting, design and modelling to those who desire such study as • branch of general education, Students are prepared for all the art examinations of the Board of Eduost ion, and for admission to the Ronal College of Art. and the Royal Academy Schools : also for the kt.1.8.A. diploma,.

div.head: OPEN-AIK POLITICS.
div.p: OPEN-AIK POLITICS.
SATISFACTION AT SETTLEMENT OF
THE STRIKE.
The Lords and the People.

The weather was so forbidding during the early part of Monday evening that it seemed probable that the Progressive labour League would have to cancel its usual meeting at Bridge Foot. However, a welcome improvement net in, and as a large crowd collected it was decided to proceed with the meeting, which proved to be a most enthusiastic end successful one. Mr. E. Wynne-Jones presided, and the principil speaker WAS Mr. Robert Lewis, of Manchester. The CHAIRMAN Said that every Liberal at the present time must be proud of the Liberal Government. (Hear, herr). They had succeeded in smashing once and for all the veto of the House of Lords. (Applause). Their opponents had been talking a great deal about revolution. There was, however, nothing revolutionary about the Veto Rill. It was fair, just and equitable and it ought to have been placed on the statute book long ago. (Hear, hear.) If there wee any revolution at all, it was to he found inside the Tory party, whose members seemed to be at sixes and sevenr. Now that the G,,vernment had

CLIPPED I,IE WINOS OF THE lIOEsE OF LORDS and reduced its powers of mischief, there would be a chance of carrying the Liberal programme into law. They were going to abolish plural voting. (Applause.) Every man should count an one man in the government of the nation and 63 no more. Lord Wolmer was supposed to represent the Newton Division, but in that constituency there were 1,000 plural voters, 800 of whom were known Tories. Lord Wolmer's majority was only lit so he could not be slid to represent the people of Newton Division and if plural voting had been abolished Lord Wolmer would not ba the member for Neaten toeisy. (Applause). The Tories talked about the over-represeotation of Ireland but they had nothing to say about the

UNDER-REPRESENTATION OF LIBERALISM in the English counties. The Liberal member for the Romford division represented as many electors as fauiteen Tory members. It should also be made easier for working men to get on the register. (Hear, hear.) Ile did not see why nearly two years sh mid have to elapse before a man was entitled to exercise the franchise. Three months should be quite sufficient to qualify him. Once a man was on the register be onght to be able to carry his vote with him wherever he went, instead of being disfranchised because he removed from one constituency to another. They were glad, continued the chairman, that there were

SIGNS OF PEACE IN THE I•REAT LABOUR. STRPG,LE. (A Volts: "Whet are the men getting ?') They had won the right of recognition for their leaders. (The INTERRUPTER r "They are not getting the money they came out for, though"). It was a great thing to have gained the point of recognition. The discussion at the Board of Trade on Saturday ehoeved that when the employers were met by men who were able to argue and state the men's case, the result was very soon seen. He el,d not see why the railway com- panies should refuse to recognize the men's leaders, when almost every other trade was prepared to recognise them. The men had no far won a splendid victory and when the Commission had finished its work he believed the wages which they were agitating for would be granted. (A Voice " I don't think they will.") " That is a matter of opinion " said the Chairman, '' You don't represent the world." When the workin.'classes got more wages the benefit was not confined to them, but every section of the community shared in it. The opinion of every business man ought to be on the side of the workers in the present struggle. He hoped that when the award was given it would be IMPOSSIBLE FOR ME RAILWAY COMPANIES TO GET

div.head: BEHIND IT
div.p: BEHIND IT

as they bad done in stonier cases in the past. Great credit was due to the men who had nothing to gain by Hy) strike hut who came out in sympathy a ith their fellows. He hoped the time would COMO when such struggles would he impossible and when all differenm s would be settled in a nobler and be-ter way. (Appl.use.) Mr. R. LEWIS, who had a hearty reception, hews an interesting speech with a reference ta the strike. He said that for three days he walked home from Manchester rather than ride in a train driven by non- unionists. (Applause.) His own conviction was that , the natural outcome of the present upheaval was that I the railways of this country, being a national service I nod convenience, must sooner or later come under national control. (Applause.) H 9 did not want to blame or praise anybody, hut he had never known ally great industrial battle to be settled r•erely by the arbitrament of arms. When the skilled advisers of eitla-r si ie came together they could settle their differences without very much trouble. The appeal to comrron sense must be the great deciding factor in the solution of our troubles. Ilse people might rest assured that their political liberties were not going to be sacrifised. The House of Lords was Fettled ; the power of the Peers was broken. They would never again be able !belly nod ultimately to reject tire proposals which the people of this country desired. The House of Commons had arid to the House of Lords " Hands off the money c'est." (Applause.) Some of them had dipped their hands fairly deep into that. (Laughter.) there was a d.scussion in the House of Commons last week as to the

div.head: PAYMENT OF. MEMBERS..
div.p: PAYMENT OF. MEMBERS..

One of :he Tory members who objected to it was Mr. Peel, the son of an ex-Speaker of the House of Commons. and the other was Lord Widmer, member for Newton Division awl son of Lord Selborne, one of the "dip-bards." (Lauelper.) "It is marvellous to me," continued Mr. Lewis "when these Lords begin to talk ahout dying-hard. [don't vice koo-v what, they mean. (Laughter.) They have no intention of dying in the list ditch or in the ditch before it. (Laughter.) They want to live—and to live on the product of your labour and enterprise. (Hear, hear.) Lord Wolmer in the House of Commons got up end wanted a reduction from £4OO a year to leas. lie thought it was unjust, imnroper, and a violation of everything that was good sad great to gel) rid of volunt try service and bogie to pay for it. Want you pay for, h iwewer, you have a right tojcontrol and von will also have th 3 advantage of making the best selection out of the meterial Cott is submitted t ) you. When Mr. William Peel and Lord Willmar got up and began to point across at the Labour benches and say how wicked the Labour men were, Air. Philip Snowden cove them the finest dressing down they ever had in their lives. (Hear, hear.) He gave some informa- tion as well—that one of the objectors who talked 53 much about voluntary service was the son of a man who drew £50,000 during ten years of service as Speaker of the House and who since he has left that position, Ins drawn pensions amounting to £41,000. Mr. Snowden wanted to know whether in the judgment of this m the service his father had rendered to the State was a wrong and improper service to render. It ins different matter when the money is coming into my family instead of into yours. (Laughter.) If it were coming to the Tory side of the House it would be saintly act, but because it is going to the others and the people of this country will have the right of selecting a man bemuse be has got brains and character and not merely because he has got money, these men are opposed to it. Theo Mr. Snowden
BEGAN TO ORAL WITH LORD NVOLNIER.

I don't know how Lord Wolmer felt, but if he did not feel small he ought to have done, because Mr. Snowden demonstrated that during a given number of years the Selborne family had drawn out of the public revenues £308,000, and going on, he demonstrated that what are called the governing cleaves—tie rich, the people who grab everything tlvrt they possibly cue and binder others from having their just share—had walked awry with £108,000,000. And now they n re going to the House of Commons to declsre that the payment of members is unjust, improper. unconstitutional and all the rest of the hard words that these Tories can use when they don't agree with what the Liberals are doing. If the House of Lords hod its way you I would have to take a min not Because of his head hut because of his pocket, not because of his character but because of his politice,not because of his position but because he was sent to you by some party organization in some part of the country. In future, however, the electorate of this country will have the right of choosing from all the candidates that come before them the best man, whatever his money or position may be. I am not going to say anything against the honorary cornice given in the pest, but how much of it has been honorary service wish some members of the aristocracy 1: The oaly opportunity they wanted wants lay their hands on the public purse but now by the passing of the Parliament Bill, ono, and for ever there bas been net down in blsck and white the record that the House of Lords will never again have the right or power to interfere with the enancial arrangements of the country." (Applause.) Continuing, at-. Lowis said the:: so f .r as general legislation was concerned, the HOUS3 of Loris would in future only have a suspensory veto. Tnere were some people who said the new conditions meant single chamber government, and Lord Rosabery had declared that the Parliament Bill would be the end of all things. (Laughter, and a Voice : " file lonely furrow.") Ves, and because of his loneliness they must pity him, for he was very lonely indeed. (Laughter.) It wos, however, worth recalling that in 1891 Lori Rosebery maid the time had come ashen theright of the House of Lords to oppose an absolute veto to the legislation of the House of Commons should fur ever cease. (Applause) Even Lord Lonadowne bed come round to the principle that no man should become a legislator merely because his father had been one, and that he must be elected, if only by the House of Lords before be could legislate ia future. The Lansdowne pmposals would. however, still have left the Tories with a majority in the reformed House of Lord., which was obviously unfair. The Liberals had carried their policy that the absolute veto of the House of Lords should be destroyed, precisely on the lioos laid Idown by Lori Rosehery in 1891. The people had come Into their own and had at last obtained the rights and privilegesof citizenship, to govern and control them- I selves. The House of Lords could still delay measures.' lint he would not advise them to doss. They had also the power to criticise. (A VOX( U All to no use.")

The interrupter W 69 absolutely wrong. When did the Liberal Government ever reject the matured judgment of an intelligent man The House of Lords could criticise in detail any Bill that came before them and if it was clearly demonstrated that the people were against it, the Bill would be killed. But it the opposi- tion was merely a sectional, querulous quarrelling sith particular provisions, or a

SELFISH INTartrsT seeking to undermine or over-ride the clear will of the people, it would not suec.ei. Any Bill that could stand (be racket of public discussion in this country had a perfect right to be insaribed on the statute book. Could anybody say that Home Rule had lost ita bold on the country ? On Saturday Lord Londonderry used a ' phrase about Mr. Annith which was no credit to Lord Londonderry. (Hear, hear.) Nothing had pleased him (the -speaker) more in all the strike doqc My than the fact that the men on strike had mainly kept their heads. It was the hooligans who bad caused trouble. and disorder. The strikers who believed in their rause and knew that it would win if it ware right, had been co-operating with the representatives of the law in keeping the law. How had the Tory party helped the trooble ?

div.head: LORD JIUGH CECIL, MR. T. E. SMITH
div.p: LORD JIUGH CECIL, MR. T. E. SMITH

and the other Die-Hards had done their beet 'to invite the Colonists of Ireland ts resist by arms the decision of the House of Commons when it granted Home Rule. They had threatened disorder. He (the speaker) recom- mended the attitude of the men on strike in the ' Manchester area—and be included Warrington—to Lord Hugh Cecil, Mr. F. E. Smith and his brother. If there had been no disorder it was because the men bad had more sense than to follow the blatant examples of the 'fories he had mstitionel. H inse Rule, co I tintiad Mr. Lewis, was the only just and legit imste way of meeting the national aspirations of a brave and devoted people. He (the speaker) bad tang been a Howe Ruler and , would continue to be one until every section of the enited Eingdorn—England,Scotland,lreland and Wales, had separate control of its own efitirs. The power of the House of Lards to prevent the healing of Ireland by the granting of self-government which had had such wonderful and blessed results in South Africa, had been destroyed for ever, and never again would they be able to throw out such a beneficent measure. Touching upon
W ELSH DISESTABLISH MET,

I Mr. Lewis described the Church in Wslei as an alien Church, devoted to alien pirposes —Mien to the spirit and temper of the people, and to the noble purposes of the founder. No longer was it a tribal Church, but an Anglicised institution, utilised for Tory electoral purposes, and the oppression of that institution had been felt for many a year in Wales. Sines MO Wales had consistently returned a majority of members in favour of Disestablisbmsnt. The people were asking Vast in their land there should be no suoh privileged institution, there should be no parish priest standing as a Tory garrison in the heart of Wales, but that the people should be free to worship God in the way they deemed best without the tryanny of. Slate institution. The House of Lords had now made its foal kick against the growth and development of national senti- ments and aspiration.. In Scotland hundreds of thousands of acres of land which people should be tilling to preside 'mead for their families, had been given up to the domination of the Yankee millionaire. Under the power of an oligarchic laud system, the people had been driven from the soil.

IN PLACE OF PEOPLE THEY NOW FOUND GAME, and Scotland was asking for a reformed land lag that would ena'sle her t a enjoy full access to the land. Now that the pewer of the House of Lords had been broken Scotland would get what she desired. The Government were also determined to get rid of privileged monopolies in education and in liquor. Nobody ought to be allowed to make a profit out of the ruin and degradation of the people. They had only to look at the places where disorder had occurred during the strike, and they would find liquor was at the bottom of it. It was being forced upon the national conscience that the Licensing Bill of len was a fair and just proposal to meet en admitted evil, and it must eventually become law. It could not now be killed at tbe Lansdowne Arms. (Laughter and applause). Having dealt with the question of plural voting and with the disgraceful and degrading condunt of the Tories who honied down the Premier in the House of Commons, Hi. Lewis concluded wirh an appeal to his audience to support the policy of Liberalism which did not protect selfish interests, but considered the welfare and freedom of all. (Applause). Mr. iIA RR Y New, referring to the labour trouble, said that whereas a week ago the country was threatened with the greatest national disaster that had ever occurred, we ha mow arrived at a solution—not perhaps as satisfactory as some trade unionists would desire, tut we had at any rate reached the position that the employers had at last to recoenize the claims of the workers. The Government had been blamed for calling out the military, but they would have been blamed even more if they bad left life and limb at the mercy of a few hooligans who were not trade unionists but were always eager to get something for nothing. He did not believe fore moment that the sane, level- headed trade uniooists had caused the havoc. The r.)ilway men bad by the strife obtained recognition for their leaders. They had not 3et received an increase of wages, bit he believed the way had been paved for it. Having referred to the inconsistency of employers who paid low wages end then used starvation as an argument for tariff reform, Mr. New said he was c mvince I that when the next election CARIB %Varring ton would have nothing to do with Protection. Further lie doubted whether the ManMester Tariff Reform League would again send anyone hsre to 02m00 VIM policy, vol be questioned whether they had anyone in Landon who *would have the heart to come north to support Protection. (L aughter.) He hrpsd that the Warrington electors would resist the blandishments of those who sought to buy them by cheap charity and that they would return to Parliament a really democratic member to support the strongest and noblest Government of modern times. (Applause).

div.head: DISTRICT NURSES.
div.p: THE DISTRICT NURSES.
Warrington Workingmen's Support ot a Worthy Institution.

Ths self-swriflcing work of the Warrington district nurses is an inestimable boon to tine working-classes and it is only nsturnl that they should seek to repay it to some extent by supporting the funds of that splendid institution—the Warrington District Nursing Associa- tion—through whose benefiaient agency that visitation and care of the sicil is undertaken. As the result of the past twelve months' effort, the Workingmen's Com- mittee has been able to band over to the treasurer of the association the sum of £307 63. 7d. Thu amount was raised by systematic collections at the works, bandit performances,and subscriptions. Thu committee's I work is run on most economical lines, the exam More during the year being only £4 6i. 41. At the annual meeting of the committee, held at the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon, there was a large attendanco of delegatr from the various works sod plams of busi- ness. Mr. VV. Pater Ryland., presiled ani wal sup- ported by the Mayor (Couacillor D. Joseph), the Rev. John Yonge and Mr. Henry if spa, hon, treasurer of the I committee.

Mr. F. MOcKS, the founder of the Association, wrote - exprealing regret that he could not attend. "I must leave the active work of the association to the young man 'he wrote : I have dons my full share of public work when I was younger and now that I am old I can, with a clear conacien:e, look on and appreci- ate what the young men are doing." Letters of apology were also releivel from Mr. F. W. Monte, Councillor Henry Roberts, Yliu Milne, Mr. George Walker chsirman of the committee) and Mr. JA. Ransom?.

Tbe statement of accounts, which was aloptad on the Ipr >position of the chairman seconded by Nfr. A. C. Blake, was supplemented with the followiag brief report :—" The nursed are doing excellent work in tie town and district, especially among the peer and work- ing classes, as hundreds of working M4Il and their wives can vouch. All urgent ant needful nines (except infectious di•ases, receive prompt nod the best possible attention. Doustions gad subscriptions will be thankfully remeived ad acknowledged by the tretsurer.

Th;jgyç w irmly convatailstel the committee upon the splendid result of the last year's work. Tney hal been working for sit years, he sail, an leech vest the result was better then the previous one. That was most eocouraging aril gratifying. Toe Nursing Association was the second of the great charities in Warrington. ft was second only to tee Infirmary. To his mini the work done by infirm tries ant mimes wee. class of work width was almost priceless, and the spxreciatiox of that work in the minds of those to whom it was extended must be, and be was convicced was, very great indeed. U. was sorry to note that the ilk [OW in lucerne —E3O7 6a. 71. this year an compared with £257 7a.91 last year—bad bee, mere as the result of certain special elf arta then a steal, increase in the general entrees of revenue. Ho hoped that there was not the 'lightest tendency to apathy on the port of acme of the sources of their contributions. It. trusted that the committee would do everything prmelble to stir up the intermit of the w 'thin; nano of Worrinztos in the work and try to see to it that the subscription list I would alt low a steady sod • healthy progression which I was necessary if the werk was to be don. properly for the increasing population. The &Lavoie moved the re-electi en of Mr. W. Peter Rylande as president of the committee. Ho said that any institution repairing a president could not have • better gentleman at the head of fakirs than Mr. Rylandf, who pesasesed all the seal qualities to mike an organization successful. What Mr. itylands lead done for the Infirmary wag simply marvellous. With regard to the aseociation be had always had a good apanion of it, and as time went on his opinion grew stronger still in its favour. The few words in the report were literally correct and modestly put. No class of mem was more intimete with the work of the

institution than the medical men and if the public could only see the readiness ant cheerfulness with which the nurses dad their work, they wonld appreciate it even more. He thought the usefulness of the association would be extended if one or two of the nurses were set apart to devote odd nights to nursing for mothers who were tired out with nursing children or wives woo bad sick husbands to look after and who could not afford to pay for trained nurses. One or two night's relief would ba greatly appreciated by such hard worked people and they would then be enabled to take up their task with all the greater zeal. When he first made the suggestion he was told it was against the rub, of the association. It was a pity and he hoped the rules could be altered to give effect to his suggestion. The resolution was heartily agreed to. _
